articles.title: Cómo votar en los Premios Steam 2026 y elegir el mejor juego de la década
articles.text:
Los Premios Steam 2026 ya permiten que la comunidad nomine títulos en 14 categorías, incluida una nueva votación para elegir el mejor juego de la década. La iniciativa de Valve abre el proceso que definirá los finalistas y, más adelante, los ganadores de una ceremonia basada por completo en las decisiones de los usuarios de PC.
La convocatoria adquiere relevancia por el décimo aniversario de los galardones y por la incorporación del premio Salón de la Fama. Esta categoría reúne a los títulos que ganaron el reconocimiento principal en ediciones anteriores y los enfrenta en una votación que busca identificar al juego más destacado de los últimos diez años dentro de la plataforma.
Cómo participar para elegir el mejor videojuego
Para participar, es necesario acceder a la página de nominaciones de los Premios Steam desde una cuenta de la plataforma que no tenga restricciones. Valve permite seleccionar un juego por categoría, aunque un mismo título puede recibir nominaciones en más de un apartado si encaja con los criterios de cada premio.
La primera etapa termina el 30 de noviembre a las 19:00 en España peninsular, equivalente a las 10:00 en la costa oeste de Estados Unidos. Hasta ese momento, los usuarios pueden modificar sus decisiones cuantas veces consideren necesario desde la misma sección de la tienda digital.
El sistema muestra recomendaciones a partir de los juegos que cada persona tiene en su biblioteca y de los títulos más populares de Steam. También incluye un buscador para encontrar cualquier juego elegible. Esa opción permite nominar producciones jugadas fuera de la plataforma, siempre que cumplan los requisitos de publicación establecidos para cada categoría.
En la mayoría de los premios, los candidatos deben haberse lanzado entre el cierre de las rebajas de otoño de 2025 y el inicio de las nominaciones de 2026. Hay dos excepciones: Con amor y dedicación reconoce juegos antiguos que siguen recibiendo contenido, mientras que Salón de la Fama tiene una lista cerrada.
Salón de la Fama enfrenta a los ganadores de otras ediciones
La categoría más singular de esta edición es Salón de la Fama, creada para celebrar los diez años de los premios. Allí competirán los ganadores históricos del reconocimiento principal o, en los primeros años, los títulos equivalentes elegidos por la comunidad antes de que existiera la categoría Juego del Año.
La lista incluye a Grand Theft Auto V, The Witcher III: Wild Hunt, PUBG: Battlegrounds, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Red Dead Redemption 2, Resident Evil Village, Elden Ring, Baldur’s Gate 3, Black Myth: Wukong y Hollow Knight: Silksong.
Cada uno representa una etapa distinta de la plataforma, desde los grandes mundos abiertos y los juegos multijugador hasta las aventuras de acción, los títulos de rol y las producciones independientes. A diferencia del resto de apartados, los usuarios no pueden añadir otros nombres a esta selección.
El resultado permitirá conocer cuál de esos juegos recibe el respaldo de los jugadores de Steam como el mejor título de la década. La votación también convierte a los premios en una revisión de la evolución del catálogo de PC y de las preferencias de una comunidad que participa directamente en la elección.
Catorce categorías cubren desde realidad virtual hasta juegos relajantes
La edición 2026 incorpora tres premios inspirados en categorías populares de años anteriores. Son Solo cinco minutos más, para juegos que invitan a prolongar una partida; Difícil de describir, para propuestas que escapan de un género definido; y Mi nuevo trabajo, centrada en simuladores de actividades cotidianas.
El resto de la lista mantiene apartados habituales. Los usuarios podrán nominar candidatos a Juego del Año, Juego de Realidad Virtual del Año, Con amor y dedicación, Mejor juego para dispositivos portátiles, Mejor con amigos, Estilo visual excepcional, Mejor juego difícil, Mejor banda sonora, Juego excepcional con buena trama y Siéntate y relájate.
La categoría dedicada a dispositivos portátiles tendrá especial atención entre quienes juegan desde Steam Deck y otros equipos compatibles. Por su parte, Mejor juego difícil reconoce propuestas que exigen perseverancia, mientras que Siéntate y relájate distingue experiencias de ritmo pausado.
Cuando cierre el plazo de nominaciones, Valve realizará el recuento y seleccionará los cinco juegos con más apoyo en cada categoría. Los finalistas se publicarán el 17 de diciembre, fecha que coincide con el inicio de las rebajas de invierno de Steam.
La fase definitiva permanecerá abierta hasta el 2 de enero de 2027 a las 19:00 en España peninsular. Al finalizar ese periodo, Valve anunciará los ganadores de los 14 premios, incluido el primer título que ingresará en el Salón de la Fama.

articles.title: GTA 6 shatters PlayStation records with 39 million players and 683 million hours played in 3 days
articles.text:
Bottom line: Sony has announced that GTA 6 is the biggest launch in PlayStation history, attracting more than 39 million unique PS5 players since its November 19 debut. The company also revealed that players logged a staggering 683 million hours of cumulative gameplay on PS5 during the first three days after launch, averaging 17.4 hours per player between November 19 and November 22.
GTA 6 smashed several other PS5 records, including the highest peak concurrent player count of any PlayStation game, surpassing previous records across multiplayer, free-to-play, and single-player titles. The launch also reportedly resulted in the highest number of new PS5 consoles connected on a single day outside the holiday season, with Sony stating that GTA 6 was played on approximately 70% of those newly connected consoles.
Grand Theft Auto VI was always expected to be a massive hit, but the full extent of its success is only now becoming apparent, thanks to official reports from developers and publishers. Late last week, Take-Two confirmed that day-one retail sales of GTA 6 reached an estimated $3.79 billion, making it the most successful launch in entertainment history.
Before its release, the game had reportedly set another record with 32.5 million pre-orders across both consoles. According to Circana's Player Engagement Tracker, 61% of active US PlayStation 5 owners and 56% of active Xbox owners worldwide played the game on launch day.
Reports also confirmed that the anticipated spike in sick leave on launch day actually materialized, with BrightHR reporting a 56% increase in sick leave across the UK on November 19 compared with the previous Thursday. Attendance data from school management firm Arbor also showed that approximately 35,000 more secondary school students were absent on launch day than earlier that week.
Grand Theft Auto VI launched on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S following years of delays. The game, which took 13 years and an estimated $1.2 billion to develop, generated so much hype that it prompted other publishers to postpone their highly anticipated releases to avoid competing with it.
Some of the most notable games reportedly pushed out of the late-2026 release window and into 2027 to avoid clashing with GTA 6 include Star Citizen spinoff Squadron 42, the reboot of the classic fantasy action RPG Fable, dark fantasy action RPG Crimson Desert, and Danganronpa 2x2, an expanded remake of Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair.

articles.title: ASRock Industrial Unveils Robotics-in-a-Box to Democratize Physical AI Development
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 24th 2026
ASRock Industrial Unveils Robotics-in-a-Box to Democratize Physical AI Development
ASRock Industrial, a global provider of industrial computing and edge AI solutions, today announced the launch of RBK-100 Robotics-in-a-Box. Designed to simplify robotic AI development and make hands-on experimentation more accessible to researchers, educators, and developers, RBK-100 is an integrated Physical AI development platform powered by the ASRock Industrial NUC BOX-358H featuring the Intel Core Ultra X7 Processor 358H. RBK-100 integrates local AI computing, an RGB depth camera, a 6-DOF leader-and-follower robotic arm set, and pre-installed AiRoboStarter software in a ready-to-use development platform. By integrating edge AI computing, visual perception, robotic manipulation, and software workflows, RBK-100 reduces system integration complexity and enables users to focus on AI model experimentation, robotic skill development, and real-world Physical AI applications.Key Capabilities of RBK-100 Robotics-in-a-Box
- AI-Ready Edge Computing: Powered by the Intel Core Ultra X7 Processor 358H in the NUC BOX-358H, RBK-100 delivers local AI computing capabilities for robotic development, AI model experimentation, and Physical AI workflows. The platform comes with 32 GB DDR5 memory in the standard configuration or 64 GB DDR5 memory in the Advanced configuration, along with a 512 GB PCIe Gen 4 SSD.
- Integrated Robotic Vision and Manipulation: An integrated RGB-D camera captures color and depth information for robotic perception and object interaction. Combined with a 6-DOF leader-and-follower robotic arm set, the platform enables developers to record demonstrations and explore AI-based pick-and-place, object handling, and learned robotic skills.
- Physical AI Development with AiRoboStarter: The standard configuration includes 32 GB DDR5 memory and pre-installed AiRoboStarter software, providing a streamlined environment for developing, training, and executing robotic skills. Its workflow spans demonstration recording, dataset review, model training, and robot skill execution, with support for model workflows including ACT, Pi0.5, and SmolVLA support planned for a future release.
- Optional Agentic AI Integration with AiRoboStarter Advanced: Available with the 64 GB configuration, AiRoboStarter Advanced extends the development environment with an integrated agentic AI workflow connecting voice interaction, AI reasoning, visual perception, and trained robotic skills. Capabilities include speech-to-text (STT), text-to-speech (TTS), large language models (LLMs), vision, object detection, web search, custom APIs, and robot skill integration. Supported models, features, and performance depend on the software release and validated configuration.
"Physical AI represents an important step forward in bringing intelligence into the physical world," said James Lee, Chairman of ASRock Industrial. "Building on our expertise in edge AI computing, we see tremendous potential in making Physical AI development more accessible and practical. Through Robotics-in-a-Box, developed in collaboration with Intel, we aim to simplify the development journey from AI experimentation to real-world robotic applications, empowering researchers, educators, and developers to explore new possibilities and accelerate innovation in Physical AI."
"Scaling Physical AI requires more than powerful AI. It requires an open technology foundation that makes complex robotic systems easier to develop and deploy," said John Healy, vice president and general manager of the Industrial and Robotics Division, Intel. "Powered by Intel Core Ultra processors, ASRock's Industrial Robotics-in-a-Box gives researchers and developers an integrated platform to accelerate experimentation and turn promising robotics concepts into practical, real-world applications."

articles.title: What’s going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
articles.text:
Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.
It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.
Tackling Riemann
The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”
The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.
But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.
The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.
Proof factories
It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.
But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.
When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.
AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.
The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.
Deriving worries
Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.
Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.
But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.
By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of new ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.
Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.
How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.
This is all new and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.
But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.
Yep, it has! Imagining just such a situation, or perhaps one where a human was the one to prove it, there's a longstanding statement of the Riemann Hypothesis in the standard Mathlib library. It's been confirmed that Alpoge's proof (Claude's proof?) aligns to it. 
There's a confirmation from the Mathlib initiative here, which gives more detail.

articles.title: I'm an avid PC gamer, but can the Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless make me better?
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless lives up to its name, delivering high-end gaming performance and great battery life in a phenomenally lightweight chassis. It also packs Corsair's new PureVector tech, which promises to improve your in-game accuracy by monitoring your inputs and adjusting directional sensitivity to compensate for poor aim. However, in my testing, I found the software to be a bit lacking, and the mouse itself is very expensive for the limited feature set it offers.
Reasons to buy
- + Comfortable design
- + Incredibly low package weight of 37g
- + Snappy performance
- + Excellent battery life
Reasons to avoid
- - Very expensive for what it offers
- - PureVector software is half-baked
- - Thumb buttons feel a little flimsy
Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless review: Two-minute review
The Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless largely does what it says on the box: it's wireless, it's incredibly lightweight, it's marketed towards pro-level and aspiring esports gamers, and it's the third iteration of Corsair's Sabre gaming mouse.
But does it deserve a place among the best gaming mice? Honestly, I'm not too sure. On paper, it's quite impressive: with a total weight of just 37g, it's easily one of the lightest gaming mice I've ever used, and with a high-end Corsair Marksman X sensor and up to 140 hours of battery life, the specs speak for themselves.
In real-world use, it feels good; the extremely low weight, 8K polling rate wireless receiver, and snappy, reactive performance all work together to create a gaming mouse that should never be a barrier to your in-game skill.
However, there are a few too many niggling issues sticking to this mouse for my liking, and these have ultimately forced me to drag down my score a bit – despite my initial enjoyment when I first started testing this third-generation Sabre.
For starters, it's too expensive. As you might expect from the ultralight design, this isn't exactly a feature-rich mouse; you get four buttons, a scroll wheel, and that's basically it. No RGB lighting, no sniper button, no Bluetooth, no fancy haptic trigger system (as seen on my beloved Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike).
Now, that's not inherently a huge problem. In this era of feature bloat and over-designed hardware, I'm not against a product that aims to keep things simple. What I am against is charging a whopping $179.99 / £159.99 / AU$289.99 for it.
That's too much money, Corsair! It's one of the most expensive mice you offer, and it does the least stuff! Heck, if you want to spring for the (less lightweight) carbon fiber or magnesium alloy skeleton models, it'll cost even more. The price alone makes it very difficult to justify this as a purchase over any other gaming mouse.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Of course, Corsair has an explanation for this mouse's steep asking price. The Sabre V3 Pro is the first mouse to come packed with the brand's new PureVector software, which makes the incredibly bold claim that it'll actually make you better at gaming.
How does it work? Well, Corsair has collaborated with developer Statespace, best known for its hugely popular aim training tool Aimlabs, to produce a smart algorithm from over four billion data points from Aimlabs users. It promises to improve your aiming by up to 81 milliseconds (or 33% faster, though I have no idea how they landed on that percentage) by reading your performance and adjusting the Sabre's directional sensitivity to compensate for over- or under-aiming.
It's clever tech, and unsurprisingly Corsair has several soundbite-worthy quotes from pro esports players on their website, all espousing how wonderful PureVector is and how much it improved their aim. In my experience, though... I wasn't too impressed.
I should say at this point that I'm a decidedly middling FPS player. I topped out at Diamond rank in competitive Overwatch back in the day, and these days I'm pleased to escape from Cryo Archive with my skin intact in Marathon. I'm certainly decent, but I'm nowhere near the esports pros. I absolutely suck at Valorant, for example.
For a regular player like me, I can't say that PureVector made much of a difference. Setting it up is easy enough; you just fire up the calibration tool in Aimlabs (the software itself is free) and go through four stages of aim training while the algorithm maps your performance. It then gives you a breakdown of the findings – it found that I tend to undershoot my targets by about 20% when aiming to the left, which was interesting – and then calibrates itself to compensate for your aim-related failings.
The calibration process produces a preset that sets sensitivity across eight primary directions, so my PureVector configuration included slightly elevated sensitivity for left, up-left, and down-left movements. The preset is saved directly to the mouse firmware itself, meaning that it'll be ready to use with any PC and doesn't require that you run any software in the background.
In fact, I'll take a quick aside here to say that beyond the initial Aimlabs calibration process, the Sabre V3 Pro doesn't demand that you download or run any software to use it. The recent introduction of the Corsair Web Hub has rendered the old iCue software largely unnecessary, letting you tweak your mouse settings from the comfort of your browser. It's great.
Anyway, back to PureVector. Did it actually improve my performance? Honestly, I don't think so. Sure, my performance in Aimlabs was a little better post-calibration, but in actual real-world gaming scenarios, I struggled to notice a difference even when I repeatedly switched PureVector on and off between matches.
I tested it across multiple games: The Finals, Marathon, Apex Legends, and Valorant (the latter of which I do admittedly suck at). I wasn't getting more crisp corner-peek headshots in Valorant, nor was I ranking higher on the postgame leaderboard in The Finals.
I think the problem stems from the fact that PureVector, at least in its current form, simply isn't doing enough. It measures your ability to shoot brightly-colored orbs while standing perfectly still in Aimlabs - but that's not what aim is really like in most shooters. In Apex Legends, I'm frequently aiming while running, jumping, or sliding; I need to account for bullet drop; I'm using a range of different guns that require subtly different recoil management. Oh, and my targets are usually moving unpredictably while shooting back at me. It's a wholly different experience compared to using a generic aim trainer, and I'm just not convinced that PureVector takes that into account.
Alright: enough about fancy aim-boosting tech. Let's talk about the physical mouse itself. Here, the newest Sabre is once again a mixed bag.
It's reasonably comfortable in the hand, and suitable for all grip types (though palm-grippers with particularly large hands might prefer the Asymmetric Ergo model, as opposed to my symmetrical review unit). The extremely low weight is great for fast flicks when aiming and helps reduce wrist strain during extended gaming sessions too.
Bundled in the box is a good-quality braided USB-A to USB-C cable and wireless receiver, which I found was responsive even when it wasn't immediately in front of the mouse. The receiver has a clip that lets you attach it to the edge of your mouse mat, and of course the cable can be used to charge the mouse (and use it in wired mode).
Under the hood, the two main buttons have optical switches, which are rated for more clicks and provide less input latency than traditional mechanical buttons. I found the actuation point a little high, but that's a personal gripe that probably won't bother most users. Click feedback is firm and tactile, which is good. The scroll wheel also feels quite robust, though the lack of a free-scroll option is yet another concession to keep the weight as low as possible.
The thumb buttons, however, feel a bit flimsy, and I couldn't shake the feeling that the entire mouse just isn't all that durable. The skates are also glued on, and I noticed that on my review model the front skate was slightly off-center. I wouldn't call the build quality bad, and I suspect that it's ultimately the price to pay for such a lightweight design, but I really have to question how long the Sabre V3 Pro would actually last under regular daily use.
There are absolutely no aesthetic frills to speak of, either. The usual RGB lighting is completely absent here, just one single power LED in front of the scroll wheel. Although there is some printed patterning on the left side of the mouse, it isn't actually textured like it is on many other Corsair mice, which feels like a missed opportunity, as it could've provided a bit of extra grip to the matte plastic casing without compromising on weight.
The good news is that despite it being so lightweight, Corsair didn't skimp on the Sabre V3 Pro's battery. It has an advertised battery life of 140 hours in the standard 1K polling rate mode, or 25 hours in 8K mode (though as I've said before in mouse reviews, 8K polling is a bit of a gimmick that most gamers simply don't need).
In my testing, I found that the battery life was indeed fantastic. I used it for more than a week without needing to charge it once, and at least three hours of that testing was using the 8K polling mode.
In short, the Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless is a good mouse, and if what you want is specifically the most lightweight, no-frills gaming mouse available, I might even call it a great mouse. But the high asking price and underwhelming PureVector software make it difficult to recommend wholeheartedly.
Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless review: Price & availability
- $179.99 / £159.99 / AU$289.99
- Available now worldwide
- Expensive for what it offers
The Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless has seen a hefty price increase over the previous V2 model, now costing an eye-watering $179.99 / £159.99 / AU$289.99. It's available directly from Corsair in the US and UK, while shoppers in some regions (including Australia) will have to go through third-party vendors.
The new price makes the Sabre V3 Pro one of the single most expensive mice that Corsair offers, and that's without factoring in the alternate magnesium alloy or carbon fiber chassis options, which are more expensive. At this price point, I'm inclined to say that there are better options elsewhere (and you can see my top recommendations further down this page). That being said, for users seeking the lightest mouse, this could be one to watch during sale events like Black Friday.
Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless review: Specs
| Connectivity | Wireless via dongle | 
| Battery life | Up to 140 hours | 
| Sensor | Corsair Marksman X | 
| Polling rate | 1K / 8K | 
| Maximum sensitivity (DPI) | 42,000 | 
| Programmable buttons | 5 | 
| Dimensions | 12.0 x 6.5 x 4.1 cm | 
| Weight | 37g | 
Should I buy the Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless?
Scorecard
| Value | High-end pricing for an honestly pretty basic gaming mouse with one fancy software feature that doesn't really do that much for the average PC gamer. | 2 / 5 | 
| Design | Comfortable and reasonably sized, usable by all grip types. Impressively light package weight, though this does make the chassis feel less durable than I'd like. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | Setup is quick and easy, battery life is great, and the 42K DPI sensor is accurate and responsive. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Final score | While it is impressively lightweight and PureVector might have potential in the future, it's very difficult to justify the asking price here right now. | 3.5 / 5 | 
Buy it if…
You want the lightest mouse
At just 37g of well-distributed weight, the Corsair Sabre V3 Pro is so light, you just might forget you're holding it.
You're an Aimlabs user
If you're committed to using Aimlabs or similar aim-training software, then getting on the PureVector bandwagon early could be a worthwhile move.
Don't buy it if…
You want plenty of inputs
The Sabre V3 Pro only has five programmable buttons, so PC gamers looking for lots of input options for MMO or MOBA games probably own't be satisfied.
You want great value for money
Yes, there are more expensive mice out there, but the price of the Sabre V3 Pro is simply too high for what it actually offers.
Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless review: Also consider
Razer DeathAdder V4 Pro
A high-end gaming mouse that sits close in price to the Corsair Sabre V3 Pro, the latest and greatest DeathAdder from Razer is, simply put, one of the best gaming mice on the market right now. Read our full Razer DeathAdder V4 Pro review. 
Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike
Another mouse that sits in the same price bracket as the Sabre V3 Pro, the Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike boasts a revolutionary haptic trigger system that makes it an excellent choice for any PC gamer who wants to fine-tune their mouse experience. Read our full Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike review.
How I tested the Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless
- Tested for nine days total
- Used for both work and gaming
- 8+ years of experience reviewing tech hardware
As usual for peripheral reviews, I swapped out my regular mouse (the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike) for the Corsair Sabre V3 Pro Ultralight Wireless and used it for a little over a week. During this time, I naturally used it for plenty of gaming, as well as my typical daily work and some personal projects.
I tested the Sabre V3 Pro in a range of games, including Warframe, Marathon, The Finals, Apex Legends, and Soulframe. I found it comfortable for lengthier gaming sessions, using my usual palm grip type.
I've been testing, evaluating, and reviewing all kinds of PC hardware for more than eight years, starting off at Maximum PC magazine before making the leap to digital journalism and joining the TechRadar team in 2021. I put all my knowledge and experience into every one of my reviews, so you can rest assured you're getting a comprehensive and bias-free product analysis.

Christian is TechRadar’s UK-based Computing Editor. He came to us from Maximum PC magazine, where he fell in love with computer hardware and building PCs. He was a regular fixture amongst our freelance review team before making the jump to TechRadar, and can usually be found drooling over the latest high-end graphics card or gaming laptop before looking at his bank account balance and crying.
Christian is a keen campaigner for LGBTQ+ rights and the owner of a charming rescue dog named Lucy, having adopted her after he beat cancer in 2021. She keeps him fit and healthy through a combination of face-licking and long walks, and only occasionally barks at him to demand treats when he’s trying to work from home.

articles.title: Dubai to bring together global startup and investment leaders at Doers Summit 2026
articles.text:
Dubai to bring together global startup and investment leaders at Doers Summit 2026
Press release:
Dubai will host the second Middle East edition of Doers Summit 2026 from 25-26 November at Dubai Silicon Oasis (DSO) - the specialised economic zone for knowledge and innovation - and a member of the Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (DIEZ).
The summit aims to bring together founders, scaleups, investors, corporates and ecosystem leaders from around the world to unlock new business connections, drive strategic partnerships and facilitate market-entry opportunities. The summit will reinforce Dubai's position as a global platform integrating innovation, capital and enterprise, connecting high-growth companies with regional and international growth opportunities.
Designed around the theme ‘Where Doers and Investors Build What’s Next’, the 2026 edition will feature high-growth technology companies and investment leaders from Europe, the GCC, Asia, Africa and emerging innovation hubs globally. Over three days, the event serves as a curated platform for companies exploring international expansion, investors seeking cross-border growth opportunities, and ecosystem leaders building new corridors between Dubai and the world's most dynamic innovation markets.
Building on the success of the inaugural 2025 Middle East edition, which brought together more than 4,000 attendees from across 115 countries, including founders, investors and ecosystem leaders, the inaugural event featured keynotes, panel discussions, investor meetings, workshops and curated networking sessions focused on scaling innovation and cross-border collaboration.
The 2026 edition further expands its scope and ambition, returning as a global platform with a strengthened focus and a more dynamic format designed to turn dialogue into impact. It also aims to reinforce Dubai's key role as a strategic gateway between Europe, the GCC, Asia and the Global South, while showcasing how Dubai Silicon Oasis and District IO enable technology companies to enter, scale and grow across regional markets.
The Doers Summit Dubai 2026 will go beyond highlighting the latest technology trends. It will focus instead on how technology is applied in real markets, how companies expand across regions, how partnerships are formed, and how founders and investors move from ideas to execution.
The summit will feature a restructured programme across two main stages, combined with interactive networking and engagement formats across the venue. Shifting away from passive conference formats, the summit will place greater emphasis on masterclasses, workshops, roundtables, curated networking sessions, ecosystem meetups, private discussions and experiential activations.
The content programme will balance inspirational future-focused conversations with practical discussions on company building, market entry and international growth. Core themes will include AI and frontier technologies, deeptech, climate and sustainability, longevity, fintech, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, mobility, robotics and future industries.
The summit will also feature CarryON MENA, an investor intelligence summit focused on the capital side of the ecosystem. CarryON MENA will bring together institutional investors, family offices, venture funds, growth investors and selected founders for private and curated discussions around direct investment opportunities, strategic partnerships, cross-border expansion and long-term value creation.
Confirmed founders and operators include Ahmet Bahadir Ozdemir, Co-Founder of Airalo, the world's largest eSIM marketplace, as well as H.E. Badr Jafar, UAE’s Special Envoy for Business and Philanthropy, and CEO of Crescent Enterprises, alongside Fares Akkad, Regional Director, MEA at Meta; Yousof Alsatom, Head of Bosch Innovation Campus at Bosch; and Peji Kanani, Regional Lead, Middle East & Africa at Carta - together with leaders from Miro, Gjirafa, and many others.
On the investor side, the event will host Abishek Nair, Head of Investment & New Ventures at Sharjah Asset Management; decision-makers from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Investment and IFC; Pedro Santos Vieira, Managing Partner at 500 Global; Raluca Ragab, Partner at Eurazeo; Rana Abdel Latif, Partner at Speedinvest; and Bilal Baloch, Partner at Shorooq Partners, among many others.
Badr Buhannad, Director General of Dubai Silicon Oasis: ‘Following last year's successful edition, which highlighted the growing importance of platforms that accelerate cross-border collaboration and knowledge exchange across innovation ecosystems, hosting Doers Summit Dubai 2026 reflects Dubai's ongoing commitment to shaping a global ecosystem where ideas are translated into impact. It also reflects Dubai Silicon Oasis' continued efforts to advance the Dubai Economic Agenda D33 by strengthening Dubai's position as a global hub for innovation, investment and enterprise, and enabling high-impact collaboration between founders, investors and ecosystem leaders from key international markets.’
Stylianos Lambrou, Founder and CEO of The Doers Company: ‘Doers Summit is built around people who turn ideas into companies, technologies into products and conversations into partnerships. The 2026 Dubai edition will be more global, more interactive and more focused on practical outcomes. It will not only look at what is next in technology, but in a true Doers spirit, at how founders, investors and corporates can actually build it, fund it and scale it across markets.’
About Doers Summit
Doers Summit is an international platform connecting founders, startups, scaleups, investors, corporates and ecosystem leaders across regions. Formerly known as Reflect Festival, the summit built a strong presence across Europe and expanded to Dubai to support cross-border collaboration, venture building, and investment and technology growth.
About Dubai Silicon Oasis
Dubai Silicon Oasis is a specialised economic zone for knowledge and innovation, and a member of the Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (DIEZ), which integrates and consolidates the products and services of three of Dubai's leading economic zones including Dubai Airport Freezone, Dubai Silicon Oasis and Dubai CommerCity. DIEZ supports technology companies, entrepreneurs and innovators through an integrated ecosystem designed to enable business growth, talent development, entrepreneurship and future-focused industries. www.diez.ae, www.dso.ae.

articles.title: Bajo esta apariencia cuqui y rechonchita, se esconde un auténtica máquina de matar. La buena noticia es que sabemos por qué
articles.text:
El domingo 11 de diciembre de 2016, hacia las once de la mañana, dos topillos rojos picoteaban semillas bajo un comedero de Joensuu, al este de Finlandia. Una idílica escena campestre (a 15 grados bajo cero). Entonces apareció un gavilán y, tras él, una urraca.
Se formó la gozadera: las dos aves se enzarzaron en una pelea y, en palabras del dueño, volaron las plumas por todo el jardín. Como daño colateral, uno de los topillos cayó a la nieve; pero ninguna se lo llevó.
Al topillo se lo comió el ave que menos esperábamos: un carbonero.
¿Y por qué nos sorprende un carbonero? Durante los siguientes 10 o 15 minutos, dos carboneros comunes estuvieron picando en la nuca del topillo, vaciaron los sesos del bicho y se fueron sin más.
Sami Majoinen, fotógrafo aficionado y vecino de Joensuu, los pilló infraganti y captó una foto del carbonero con una pata sobre el topillo que dio la vuelta al mundo.
Pero lo curioso es que no hay nada de sorprendente: Desde finales de los años 2000 sabemos que este pájaro con pinta de cuco es una auténtica máquina de matar. En la cueva de Istállós-kő, en los montes Bükk del noreste de Hungría, un equipo de Péter Estók y Björn Siemers, del Instituto Max Planck de Ornitología, vigiló la cueva unas 45 horas y observó 18 depredaciones. Cazaban murciélagos.
Otro ejemplo, entre 2007 y 2016, en dos parques nacionales del norte de los Países Bajos, aparecieron 88 papamoscas muertos. Los papamoscas son aves migratorias que van y vuelven de África. Cuando vuelven a Europa buscan 'casas' en las que pasar el verano y, a veces, esas casas ya estaban ocupadas. Según el estudio de Jelmer Samplonius y Christiaan Both, de los 88 papamoscas muertos, a 86 los había matado un carbonero.
¿Y por qué pasa todo esto? La respuesta es más sencilla de lo que podríamos pensar. Hablamos de un ave principalmente insectívora que basa su dieta en orugas, arañas y larvas, por un lado; semillas, frutos secos, bayas y brotes tiernos, por el otro. Si se pone a matar bichos, es o por competencia (el caso de los papamoscas) o por hambre (el caso de los murciélagos y los topillos).
Y es interesante porque hay una historia mucho más atractiva que la de un pájaro pisando un bicho: es la de qué va a pasar conforme el cambio climático empuje a condiciones extremas a cada vez más animales. Con el jabalí ha generado un sinfín de problemas, con el resto de especies está por ver.
Imagen | Patrice Bouchard
En Xataka | Lleva 50 años cruzando España con 2.500 ovejas. Tiene 64 años y un problema: nadie quiere heredar su trabajo

articles.title: Réserver un TGV dans l'application Uber, ce sera possible en France dès le 30 novembre
articles.text:
Uber lance Uber Trains en France dès le 30 novembre 2026. L'application permettra de réserver ses billets de train SNCF, OUIGO, Eurostar ou Renfe, avec 10 % du montant reversé en crédits Uber pour les réservations éligibles.
Après les VTC, les repas livrés et même les bateaux, Uber s'invite sur les rails. Oui, dès le lundi 30 novembre en France, Uber Trains permettra de réserver ses billets SNCF, OUIGO ou Eurostar dans l'application. Grâce à un partenariat avec la plateforme Omio, le service regroupe les offres des quatre compagnies ferroviaires et rend 10 % du montant des billets éligibles en crédits pour son lancement. Plus que jamais, Uber devient une application qui accompagne les voyageurs du quai de départ jusqu'à leur chambre d'hôtel.
Uber se met au train en France, et la SNCF n'est pas la seule compagnie à bord
Concrètement, Uber Trains fonctionne un peu comme un comparateur. On y trouve les TGV INOUI, les TER et Intercités de la SNCF, mais aussi les OUIGO, Eurostar, Trenitalia France, Renfe et Lyria. Au-delà de la France, l'utilisateur pourra envisager voyager jusqu'à Milan, Londres, Genève, Amsterdam ou Madrid, et même changer de compagnie en route, en faisant pourquoi pas un Paris-Lyon avec la SNCF, puis un Lyon-Milan avec Trenitalia, avec tous les billets rangés dans la même application.
Les habitués du train peuvent souffler, puisqu'on apprend que les cartes de fidélité s'enregistrent dans l'appli, quel que soit l'opérateur, et en plus, on garde ses avantages. Pour le lancement, Uber ajoute même une carotte. Chaque réservation éligible en France rapporte en effet 10 % de son montant en crédits Uber. Un billet à 50 euros donne donc 5 euros à dépenser plus tard en course ou sur Uber Eats, selon les conditions prévues. Ce bonus n'arrive que quelques jours seulement après l'intégration de Revolut Pay dans l'appli Uber, elle aussi accompagnée d'avantages fidélité.
L'atout principal de cette nouveauté, c'est clairement de pouvoir enchaîner les trajets sans changer d'application. Il est possible de réserver à l'avance la voiture qui vous mène à la gare, puis celle qui vous emmène à l'hôtel, à un rendez-vous ou en balade dans la ville à l'arrivée. « Le train vient naturellement compléter les services qu'ils utilisent pour rejoindre leur gare ou se déplacer à destination », explique Pablo del Olmo González, General Manager d'Uber France.
Du quai à l'hôtel, Uber agrandit son terrain de jeu
L'Hexagone n'est pas le premier pays concerné. Uber propose déjà la réservation de billets de train au Royaume-Uni et en Espagne, là aussi grâce à Omio. Chez nous, Uber et le train se connaissaient déjà. Depuis mars 2025, SNCF Connect permet de réserver une course Uber juste après l'achat d'un billet. Avec Uber Trains, c'est l'inverse, car on part de l'application Uber pour acheter son billet. L'argument compte, puisque l'application compte 2,5 millions d'utilisateurs en France, dans plusieurs dizaines de grandes villes. Uber décrit d'ailleurs le service comme un « point d'accès supplémentaire » à la réservation de billets de train. « Avec Uber Trains, nous franchissons une nouvelle étape », résume Pablo del Olmo González.
Uber Trains arrive juste après le partenariat avec ALL Accor, récemment déployé en France. En reliant les deux comptes, on gagne 1 point Reward par euro éligible dépensé en course (Berline, Comfort, Taxi, Van, Reserve) ou sur les commandes Uber Eats d'au moins 40 euros. Les points s'échangent ensuite contre des séjours à l'hôtel ou des expériences. Les abonnés Uber One gagnent 2 points par euro sur ces courses et des points dès 35 euros sur Uber Eats. Les abonnés annuels éligibles obtiennent en plus le statut Silver, avec accueil prioritaire, boisson de bienvenue et départ tardif, selon les conditions applicables. Attention, les deux offres ne se cumulent pas, donc il faut choisir entre ALL Accor et Flying Blue.
Uber met aussi en avant l'écologie, dans la lignée d'Uber Electric. Selon SNCF Voyageurs, prendre le train à grande vitesse en France réduit en moyenne de 90 % les émissions de gaz à effet de serre par voyageur et par kilomètre par rapport aux autres transports longue distance. L'objectif affiché par Pablo del Olmo González est que chacun passe « moins de temps à l'organisation de son voyage et plus de temps à en profiter ». Uber continue de tisser sa toile d'acteur majeur du transport en France, après s'être ouvert à la location de bateaux cette année et avoir lancé ses premiers robotaxis à Londres.

articles.title: À 800 €, cette excellente barre de son Samsung a de quoi transformer votre salon en salle de cinéma
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : La barre de son Samsung HW-Q990H notée 5/5 tombe à 800 € chez Boulanger et Darty
Fleuron de la gamme audio 2026 de Samsung, la HW-Q990H profite du Black Friday pour s'afficher à un tarif nettement plus séduisant. Avec ses enceintes arrière, son caisson de basses et ses prestations acoustiques de haut vol, cet ensemble home cinéma a de sérieux arguments à faire valoir.
Lancée en avril dernier à 1 499 €, la Samsung HW-Q990H voit son prix fondre à l'occasion du Black Friday. Elle est désormais proposée à 800 € chez Boulanger et Darty, soit une économie de 699 € par rapport à son tarif de lancement. Plus significative encore, cette offre représente une baisse de 10 % par rapport au prix moyen relevé ces 30 derniers jours (889,27 €).
Un ensemble home cinéma particulièrement convaincant
Avec ses 23 haut-parleurs répartis dans une configuration 11.1.4, la HW-Q990H ne joue pas dans la même cour que les barres de son traditionnelles. Ses deux satellites arrière participent activement à l'immersion, tandis que son caisson de basses, relativement compact, restitue les fréquences graves avec une remarquable efficacité.
Samsung HW-Q990H
Notre test ayant débouché sur une note de cinq étoiles, souligne notamment la précision de la spatialisation, la bonne restitution des voix et l'équilibre général de la signature sonore. Les amateurs de cinéma apprécieront tout particulièrement la capacité de l'ensemble à donner de l'ampleur aux bandes-son sans sacrifier la lisibilité des dialogues.
Les joueurs ne sont pas oubliés avec deux entrées HDMI 2.1 acceptant les signaux 4K à 120 Hz et le VRR. L'application SmartThings permet quant à elle d'affiner les réglages acoustiques.
Un tarif qui change la donne face au modèle précédent
La HW-Q990H demeure toutefois une évolution très timide de la HW-Q995F de 2025. Hormis la compatibilité avec le format Eclipsa Audio, les nouveautés logicielles présentent un intérêt assez limité. On regrette également un afficheur étriqué et des effets verticaux Dolby Atmos qui pourraient gagner en précision.
Si son prix de lancement rendait difficilement justifiable son achat face à sa devancière, la situation est bien différente à 800 €. Pour qui souhaite s'équiper d'un système home cinéma complet sans multiplier les câbles audio ni investir dans un amplificateur dédié, cette Samsung constitue désormais une proposition particulièrement attractive.

articles.title: Apple is readying MacBook Neo 2 for a spring 2027 launch
articles.text:
Bottom line: The entry-level MacBook Neo was a breath of fresh air for the industry as a whole, launching just ahead of a major leadership transition at Apple. The affordable laptop served as a wake-up call for traditional PC and Chromebook makers but as we wind down 2026, plans are already in place for a successor and that should be a surprise to absolutely nobody.
According to the well-connected Mark Gurman, Apple is putting Neo on an annual update cycle that doesn't sound much different than the MacBook Air and Pro lines. The next iteration, reportedly codenamed J701, is scheduled to debut in the spring of 2027 and will primarily focus on hardware upgrades and perhaps new colorways.
The first generation Neo is powered by Apple's own A18 Pro iPhone chip and for next year, we are told to expect a bump up to the A19 Pro SoC. As Gurman correctly highlights, that is not really going to be enough incentive for existing Neo owners to upgrade, but it does give Apple an opportunity to market the product to first time buyers for another year without sounding as if they are being sold dated technology.
Not much else is known about the next Neo at this stage, although Gurman did say he's heard of plans for fresh colorways annually. That would be in line with yearly iPhone updates, which typically introduce a new color or two while retiring an old one. Keep it fresh, right?
Gurman
With any luck, Apple will keep the Neo close to its debut price and maintain that entry point. Far too often, we've seen companies debut exciting new product lines at reasonable prices, only for the starting price to climb year after year. Take the Google Pixel, for example, or your pick of Chromebook. Granted, a slight price bump to account for the continued memory shortage wouldn't be unheard of (it has already happened once, back in June), but here's to hoping it doesn't become a regular occurrence.

articles.title: iPhone 17e (512 GB) surge em queda com cupom exclusivo na Black da Amazon
articles.text:
iPhone 17e (512 GB) surge em queda com cupom exclusivo na Black da Amazon
iPhone 17e (512 GB) com chip A19 de ponta e câmera de 48 MP alcança o menor preço que já vimos, com desconto de 38% no Pix com cupom exclusivo Amazon Prime
O iPhone 17e de 512 GB está saindo por R$ 4.630 no Pix com cupom 20BLACKPRIME exclusivo para assinantes do Amazon Prime. O celular da Apple, com chip A19 e câmera de 48 MP, alcança o menor preço já publicado pelo Achados, com desconto de 38% sobre o original de R$ 5.999 durante a Black November 2026.
Atual modelo acessível da Apple, o iPhone 17e entrega alto desempenho por meio do chip A19 e dos 8 GB de RAM, que dão conta de apps em multitarefa e funções do Apple Intelligence localmente. Os 512 GB de espaço interno dão e sobram para guardar fotos e vídeos.
Seu kit de câmeras inclui wide traseira de 48 MP com OIS e “zoom com qualidade óptica” de até 2x, que usa algoritmos nas aproximações, e frontal de 12 MP que tira ótimas selfies. Ambas filmam em 4K a 60 fps.
A tela Super Retina XDR OLED de 6,1″ com brilho de até 1.200 nits reproduz imagens com cores vibrantes e garante a visibilidade em qualquer ambiente. O vidro Ceramic Shield 2 protege-a em acidentes diversos.
O corpo de alumínio com design vintage do iPhone 17e possui certificação IP68, que adiciona proteção em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 4.005 mAh resiste a até um dia de uso, segundo a fabricante. O suporte ao MagSafe e carregamento rápido permite receber uma carga de 50% em apenas 30 minutos, ideal para usuários com agendas corridas.
O iPhone 17e de 512 GB (R$ 4.630 no Pix com cupom 20BLACKPRIME exclusivo Prime) foi atualizado para o iOS 27 e deve receber pelo menos mais cinco updates do sistema operacional. O celular da Apple possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, NFC e suporta eSIM.
Esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos para o iPhone 17e 512 GB. Nas outras 6 ofertas publicadas desde maio de 2026, o melhor foi R$ 4.799,08 (Magalu, 22/9/2026).
Lojas como a Amazon estão no clima da Black Friday 2026, que chega nesta sexta-feira (27): ofertas de gadgets com cupons e condições especiais vêm sendo oferecidas desde o início de novembro e continuarão vindo até o fim do mês.

articles.title: Valve Opens Nominations for 10th Anniversary Steam Awards With 3 New Categories
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 24th 2026
Valve Opens Nominations for 10th Anniversary Steam Awards With 3 New Categories
Valve has officially opened nominations for the 10th Anniversary Steam Awards, marking the special occasion with a new Hall of Fame awards category, which allows players to nominate a prior Game of the Year award winner as the best game of the last decade. That list includes Grand Theft Auto V, The Witcher III, PUBG: Battlegrounds, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Red Dead Redemption, Resident Evil Village, Elden Ring, Baldur's Gate III, Black Myth Wukong, and Hollow Knight: Silksong. 
The other categories are the standard fair of Game of the Year, VR Game of the Year, Labor of Love, Best Handheld Game, Better with Friends, Outstanding Visual Style, Best Soundtrack, Best Game You Suck At, Outstanding Story-Rich, and the Sit Back and Relax award. However, there are also a few newcomer categories that bring the total category count to 14: The "This Is My Job Now" award for real-world job simulators, the "Defies Description" award for games that mix genres and gameplay mechanics to the extent that they no longer conform to one specific genre, and the "Just Five More Minutes" award for games that suck players into a hole of "just one more level."Nominations for the 2026 Steam Awards is open until November 30, and players can nominate any game they've played that fits the bill and was released in 2026, or they can choose from a list of popular and recommended games. Official voting for the Steam Awards starts on December 17.
Source:

articles.title: Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling — UT Arlington shares real-world test that measured four servers sharing the same pool at SC26
articles.text:
Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling — UT Arlington shares real-world test that measured four servers sharing the same pool at SC26
The results land as memory makers push shared CXL pools as a home for AI’s KV cache.
Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware. In a presentation shared at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), they found that because the hardware doesn’t automatically keep shared data updated across servers, necessary software overhead adds a 3-5µ (microsecond) delay per lock, each time servers access the same data. These minute delays effectively cancel out the benefits — a finding that comes as CXL memory pools are being proposed as a potential AI KV cache solution.
Locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it. This way, no two servers overwrite the same data at the same time. Within a given server, the CPU’s hardware handles that handoff in a fraction of a microsecond, but across these servers, software is in charge of enforcement.
The setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box. The switch, which UT Arlington’s Peiran Du called “the only commercially available product we can use,” caps their setup at four servers. The catch is that there is no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations on “a real four-host CXL shared-memory system.”
This means no synced CPU caches and no hardware atomics between servers to build locks on, so software has to handle both. Writers publish their cached copy out to the pool and wait for it to finish, while readers throw out stale copies before reading, with the locks built from plain reads and writes, such as Lamport’s fast mutex. CXL 3.0 defines a hardware fix for the caches, called Back-Invalidate, but the researchers hadn’t received vendor confirmation that their platform supports it.
Aside from the lock acquisition penalty, which is “roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks,” there is a visibility cost: “one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs.” This is 0.94 µs, one way, compared to 1.91 µs for an RDMA write on their 400Gb/s InfiniBand, so the link isn’t the cause. A local compare-and-swap takes about 100 ns and, across servers, a lock’s median is 3.7 µs if uncontended, but 132 µs at the 95th percentile with several servers on one lock.
The result: breadth-first search (BFS), a standard graph algorithm and a common benchmark, “gains nothing from adding a second host,” and was actually slower on four servers than on one, at 0.74s versus 0.55s. This was mostly not from the locks and barriers, which were only about 3.5% of its runtime, but due to the repeated flushing of shared state at every level.
On the other hand, throughput for a hash table — using independent buckets and per-host allocators — grew almost linearly when adding hosts. Triangle counting, another standard graph benchmark, also had a runtime reduction of more than half when scaling from one to four hosts.
| Scaling on shared CXL memory (UT Arlington/Intel, 32 threads per server) |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Workload | One server | Four servers | Change | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Graph search (BFS) | 0.55 s | 0.74 s | About 35% slower | 
| Triangle counting | 2.43 s | 0.97 s | About 60% less time | 
| Hash table, 95% reads | 4.1M ops/s | 16.6M ops/s | About 4x throughput | 
Why it matters
Those costs matter, in part, because shared CXL pools are emerging as a new home for KV cache — an AI model’s stored record of a conversation’s state — once it outgrows GPU memory and a server’s own DRAM. The CXL Consortium’s SC26 session description says cloud providers and GPU makers “have highlighted CXL memory pooling as an effective approach for improving KV cache access.”
SK hynix, which makes CXL memory modules, showed a design that hands KV cache between GPU servers through a shared pool and claims 2.6x faster time to first token than standard RDMA setups. Its abstract also claims 3.0x lower P99 latency and 1.9x higher throughput. Micron, at SC26’s CXL Pavilion, showed its Abaco reference design of pooled CXL memory shared across rack servers and GPUs. It claimed 10x to 30x agentic AI gains, with famfs support for apps like Nvidia’s Dynamo.
The need is real, even if efficiency gains have led to less cache needed per token. Vikram Sharma Mailthody of Nvidia Research said at SC26’s Emerging Storage panel that his own analysis of open models on Hugging Face shows KV per token falling “by 50% every twelve months” with “up to 78 times reduction so far,” giving the example that 128K context took “about 64 gigabytes” three years ago and now takes less than one. But context lengths are heading toward millions of tokens, and “the product of those two will keep increasing,” he said.
Agents also add to the demand. Earlier in the conference, a workshop talk by Argonne National Laboratory and RIT researchers, based on public AI serving traces, showed that a “session calls again ~2 min later, once its tools return: a 160 GiB recency cache keeps 1% of its context,” needing the GPU to recompute the rest, or about 99%. Recomputation is significantly slower and more demanding, and memory is needed to cache more.
That makes it a capacity problem more than a speed problem. “Memory capacity is becoming a dominant factor. Memory latencies have not been seen as a primary problem yet,” Mailthody said. An agent’s context only has to survive a gap of a couple of minutes. It’s also ideal for any KV cache solution to be as inexpensive as possible, and given that a 128GB DIMM costs more than four times that of a 64GB DIMM last year. According to Intel’s Anil Godbole on SC26’s CXL panel, being able to add capacity past the DIMM slot limit — including reusing DDR4 — bolsters the case for CXL even further.
It doesn’t hurt that the KV cache handoff is write-once, read-many, which is the type of pattern that actually scaled in testing, although UT Arlington did not specifically test KV cache. Researchers behind OCEAN, a CXL emulator, backed this idea in the same paper session as UT Arlington, saying that software coherence is fine for read-heavy work, with hardware essential as writes climb. Its abstract reports that hardware coherence, at least in emulation, can give an 11x improvement at full coverage on Tigon database workloads.
Limitations still exist, which is why SK hynix, for one, is relying on “novel locking and coherence protocols” for its design. Hardware isn’t quite there yet, and Back-Invalidate might “be pretty costly,” Du said, suggesting that both hardware and software coherence may be required.
Micron, which built prototype KV cache sharing into Nvidia’s Dynamo, noted two primary failure cases in a CXL Consortium presentation last month: where the writer’s data never reaches the pool, and where the reader never sees the updates. The first can be fixed by producers flushing before blocks are published, so unflushed blocks can never be found. The second is fixed with a consumer flush, that is, invalidation of their cached lines, before reading. These are the fixes and costs that UT Arlington was measuring.
Micron cut its flushing cost by flushing each slot only once, which works because KV cache is content-addressed — a slot in the pool that hasn’t changed stays coherent after its first flush. Micron’s presentation also notes that neither failure causes a crash. Instead, the read returns plausible-looking data, and the output is wrong in subtle ways, with the wrong tokens on some requests under cache pressure.
Working against CXL as a solution is the fact that the memory pooling only reaches within a rack today, Godbole said; it doesn’t span a full data center. Marvell and Penguin Solutions, in collaboration and in addition to others like Lightelligence, have shown or announced memory expansion and pooling over optical links, which could stretch pooling past a single rack. CXL is also “not the protocol to ferry such big data,” Godbole added, as it’s built for smaller reads and writes, 64 bytes at a time, closer to how a CPU uses RAM. For bulk transfers, he said, RDMA is more efficient.
A research system called Beluga, in a paper published on arXiv a year ago, had KV cache in “a commercial CXL switch-based memory pool” with time to first token cut by 89.6% and throughput raised 7.35x compared with an RDMA-based setup once its cache was filled. This suggests some optimization could improve the usefulness of the technology, too.
CXL is clearly a hit or miss with how it is actually used being a main concern, with “a gap between the [CXL] spec and the implementation from different vendors,” according to UT Arlington’s Jia Rao. SK hynix’s second-generation CMM-DDR5, at 256GB and using CXL 3.2, has only been shown, and the device its KV cache design uses to select what to send is still what the company’s Younghoon Min called a “research prototype.” These are early times, and the enterprise landscape is simultaneously changing quickly.
On paper, shared CXL pools do fit the KV handoff idea, but until a commercial switch ships with confirmed coherence across servers, the best we have is KV cache numbers from vendor demos and research prototypes. Back-Invalidate should cut the software overhead UT Arlington measured, but Du expects it to add delays of its own; production systems would likely need a combination of hardware coherence and software approaches like Micron’s.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft s’apprête à supprimer ces deux fonctions « obsolètes »
articles.text:
Microsoft continue sa chasse aux fonctionnalités logicielles qu’elle considère comme obsolètes. La firme de Redmond s’apprête à amputer Windows 11 de deux de ses fonctionnalités : elle vient d’annoncer la mise au rebut du protocole MTP sur Bluetooth, qui permet de partager des fichiers sans fil, mais aussi de son application Family Safety pour Windows.
Ces deux outils, qui ne recevront plus aucune mise à jour de développement, devraient finir par disparaître dans une prochaine mise à jour du système d’exploitation.
Windows 11 ne pourra bientôt plus transférer de fichiers par Bluetooth
Microsoft vient de mettre à jour sa page dédiée aux fonctionnalités en fin de vie. L’entreprise vient ainsi d’officialiser la mise au rebut de la fonctionnalité MTP (pour Media Transfer Protocol) via Bluetooth. Cela signifie concrètement que vous ne pourrez bientôt plus transférer aucun fichier en utilisant la connexion Bluetooth de votre PC avec un autre appareil.
La fin du MTP via Bluetooth n’a rien de très étonnant. Cette fonctionnalité, aujourd’hui très peu utilisée, est bien plus lente qu’une connexion filaire ou qu’une connexion réseau pour transférer des documents d’un appareil externe vers votre PC. Microsoft n’entend toutefois pas vous laisser sans solution alternative. La firme de Redmond suggère ainsi d’utiliser le MTP via un câble USB, ou d’utiliser une application passant par le réseau.
C’est le cas, par exemple avec Mobile Connecté / Lien avec Windows, une application native de Microsoft qui permet d’afficher le contenu de votre smartphone directement dans l’Explorateur de fichiers de Windows 11.
Mais bien d’autres solutions existent. Vous pouvez par exemple privilégier la solution Nearby Share de Google qui permet de transférer des fichiers entre un smartphone Android et votre PC, ou encore opter pour une application comme LocalSend qui a l’avantage de proposer une solution universelle pour transférer des fichiers entre tous vos appareils à travers un réseau local, aussi simplement que le AirDrop d’Apple.
Pour l’heure Microsoft n’a pas précisé quand le protocole MTP via Bluetooth serait définitivement supprimé de son système d’exploitation. La firme a simplement indiqué qu’il « pourrait être supprimé dans une version ultérieure de Windows ».
La gestion du contrôle parental ne doit plus passer par votre PC
Microsoft a réservé le même sort à son application Family Safety. Le module de contrôle parental, qui permet de gérer les demandes d’autorisation sur une machine utilisée par vos enfants depuis votre PC, est à présent déconseillé par Microsoft. L’entreprise a indiqué que l’application « devrait être supprimée de Windows dans une prochaine version du système d’exploitation ».
Les utilisateurs de Family Safety devront donc se tourner vers les alternatives restantes, à savoir utiliser l’interface Web depuis leur navigateur Web habituel, ou gérer les demandes liées au contrôle parental depuis l’application mobile pour Android ou iOS.
Là encore, il ne s’agit pas d’une suppression immédiate de Family Safety pour Windows. Microsoft va simplement cesser de la mettre à jour et, si elle reste pour l’instant utilisable, elle pourrait disparaître dans une prochaine mise à jour de Windows 11.
