articles.title: Como escolher o notebook ideal para reuniões e videoconferências
articles.text:
Resumo IA
- O notebook ideal para reuniões e videoconferências precisa ter bom processamento, autonomia suficiente e boa câmera embutida.
- Recursos extras como otimização de áudio e vídeo são importantes para garantir a qualidade das chamadas.
- Os notebooks Dell 14 e Dell 15 são opções interessantes, com processadores Intel Core recentes, memória RAM de até 16 GB e recursos de otimização de áudio e vídeo.
Escolher seu próximo notebook para reuniões e videoconferências pode ser mais fácil do que você imagina. Atualmente já é possível encontrar computadores que misturam portabilidade com capacidade suficiente para realizar as principais tarefas do dia a dia, incluindo chamadas de trabalho.
Por padrão, modelos do tipo precisam contar com características como bom processamento e autonomia suficiente para passar algumas horas em ligação, além de uma boa câmera embutida. Mas alguns recursos extras podem ser interessantes, como suporte a otimização de áudio e vídeo.
Outra característica importante é o tamanho de tela, que pode ajudar bastante a seguir com suas tarefas sem precisar se desligar das chamadas. Para isso, notebooks com 14 ou 15 polegadas podem ser ideais para garantir a portabilidade necessária sem deixar sua produtividade de lado.
O que o notebook ideal para reuniões e videoconferências precisa ter
Na hora de comprar seu novo notebook pensando em participar de reuniões do trabalho, da faculdade ou da escola, algumas características específicas podem fazer diferença. Por isso, é importante conhecer bem os fatores que vão garantir ligações sem engasgos, travamentos e outros problemas na captação de áudio ou vídeo. Para comprar seu novo computador, vale prestar atenção em:
- Design: modelo precisa combinar portabilidade com dois outros fatores: tamanho de tela e a presença de uma boa câmera.
- Desempenho: o processamento do computador precisa dar conta das chamadas sem travamentos.
- Bateria: uma boa autonomia vai garantir que você participe de reuniões em qualquer lugar, mesmo sem ter uma tomada por perto.
- Recursos extras: ferramentas de otimização de áudio e vídeo são essenciais para diminuir ruídos, editar o fundo das chamadas e mais.
- Conectividade: é importante contar com uma boa oferta de entradas para conectar fones e os padrões mais recentes de Wi-Fi e Bluetooth.
Design e tamanho de tela
A escolha de um notebook para reuniões passa, necessariamente, por um modelo com boa câmera disponível – de preferência com gravação em Full HD. Além disso, a tela precisa ter um tamanho suficiente para dar conta de tarefas, apresentações e outras atividades durante as chamadas. Dessa forma, modelos com 14 ou 15 polegadas disponíveis prometem ser ideais.
Ainda no design, é importante falar de conectividade. Muitos computadores mais recentes costumam trazer apenas entradas USB-C, limitando o uso de fones à conexão Bluetooth, por exemplo. Portanto, uma dica é procurar por uma variedade maior de interfaces, como USB padrão (tipo A) e plug de 3,5 mm para utilizar fones com fio sem problemas.
Por fim, mas não menos importante, vale ficar de olho nos detalhes de tamanho e peso do notebook para transportar em qualquer bolsa ou mochila. Uma espessura reduzida pode parecer detalhe, mas faz diferença na hora de abrir seu computador no café para uma reunião, por exemplo. Da mesma forma, ter bordas ultrafinas para aproveitar ao máximo o espaço de tela também é um fator que vai além do charme do modelo.
Desempenho e bateria
Para ter uma garantia de horas rodando aplicativos de videoconferência, é essencial buscar modelos com boa autonomia. Sem uma bateria suficiente, você pode acabar refém de uma tomada na hora de participar de reuniões importantes. Por isso, notebooks com recursos de recarga rápida como o ExpressCharge da Dell e algumas horas de uso disponíveis devem funcionar muito bem em uma rotina agitada.
Já no desempenho, é importante buscar processadores mais recentes. Um Intel Core 5, por exemplo, já deve ser suficiente dar conta de tarefas de produtividade e rodar os principais apps de vídeo sem problemas. Isso, claro, aliado a uma memória RAM de ao menos 8 GB e armazenamento em SSD para abrir rapidamente seu sistema operacional e navegar por aplicativos, planilhas e mais.
E os recursos extras?
Pode parecer pouco, mas ter um computador atual pode garantir ferramentas importantes para chamadas de vídeo. Otimização de áudio, redução de ruídos, edição de fundo, entre outros recursos vão fazer diferença na qualidade da sua chamada.
Em uma reunião de negócios, por exemplo, aparências contam bastante – e uma ligação com a voz clara e sem ruídos externos pode mudar os rumos da conversa para melhor. Da mesma forma, não travar na hora de apresentar um trabalho da faculdade também pode ajudar na avaliação final do professor.
Conheça o Dell 14
Considerando os aspectos mais importantes para um notebook voltado para reuniões e videoconferências, o Dell 14 vendido no Brasil aparece como uma alternativa interessante de custo-benefício. Com processadores Intel Core mais recentes, é possível escolher versões com Core 5 ou Core 7, ambas com promessa de boa fluidez e gráficos embutidos que devem ser suficientes para suas chamadas e apresentações.
O Dell 14 também traz memória RAM de 8 a 16 GB, armazenamento de até 1 TB em SSD e recursos como o Express Charge para recarga rápida, redução de ruídos na captação de áudio, câmera com resolução Full HD, entre outros.
Conheça mais do Dell 14 no site oficial da Dell.
Dell 15
Uma opção semelhante para quem deseja maior espaço de tela é o Dell 15. O computador também oferece RAM a partir de 8 GB, chips Intel Core 5 ou Core 7, além de recursos de otimização de áudio e vídeo. Com design elegante na cor preta, o notebook não deixa a portabilidade de lado mesmo com um display grande o suficiente para realizar suas tarefas durante as chamadas de vídeo.
Conheça o Dell 15 em detalhes no site oficial da Dell.

articles.title: OpenAI and Cisco team up to stop AI-generated security threats before they get too big
articles.text:
OpenAI and Cisco team up to stop AI-generated security threats before they get too big
Shirudo is a new AI-powered open source runtime
- OpenAI and Cisco released Shirudo, an open source tool that uses AI and eBPF to shield Linux systems from known vulnerabilities before patches are deployed
- The platform creates temporary protections that block exploit behavior while allowing legitimate workloads to continue running
- Developers say Shirudo can help reduce the risk from n-day vulnerabilities by providing automated, verifiable defenses during the patching window
OpenAI and Cisco want to make n-day vulnerabilities on Linux a thing of the past with Shirudo (Japanese for ‘shield’) a new tool which is being open sourced so the wider cybersecurity community can inspect it and contribute if they want.
Security vulnerabilities generally fall into two broad categories: zero-day flaws, and n-day flaws. Zero-days are flaws unknown to the vendor and as such have no official patch or fix. They’re called “zero-day” because the vendors have had zero days to fix the issue before threat actors started exploiting it. Following the same logic, n-day flaws are those that are known to the vendor but have not yet been patched.
This puts software users in a tricky position: do they turn off vulnerable services to protect the wider infrastructure (and thus hurt their bottom line and their reputation), or do they keep the services running in anticipation of a patch, and risk being exposed and exploited? It is this security limbo that Cisco and OpenAI are trying to solve.
How Shirudo works
“Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks,” OpenAI said in an announcement. “Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.”
Shirudo, which is powered by AI apparently does just that - protects Linux systems while IT teams roll out patches. Teams can set up a temporary safeguard (called shield), and test to see if it blocks behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while allowing legitimate requests through. After approval, the shield gets deployed and the service can continue unabated.
OpenAI said Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. That way, users can monitor for suspicious activity and apply targeted protections to otherwise running systems. eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, and security teams can monitor how a proposed shield affects applications before even enforcing it.
OpenAI also said Shirudo was designed to give AI agents “programmable controls” to investigate vulnerabilities, build targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads, while security teams get to control what gets deployed. All shields are cryptographically signed and verified through Linux’s eBPF verifier, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Finally, OpenAI said the verification is backed by hardware: “Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.”
How to get started with Shirudo
The two companies shared a technical walkthrough from the Linux Plumbers Conference, showing how to apply the shield and verify it on the target host. They also demonstrated how Shirudo helped protect a running Elasticsearch application against the Java4Shell vulnerability by adding an input check to Java's Base64 decoder, blocking malicious input without interrupting the service.
“Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable,” OpenAI and Cisco said in the announcement post. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.”
Shirudo is an open-source tool, allowing developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators to inspect the code, test it, and contribute at will. It is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.
Those interested in testing out Shirudo should follow the VM quickstart to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

articles.title: The Kobo Libra Colour got me back into reading after many years
articles.text:
I used to love reading.
Since I was late to getting a smartphone, my introverted self passed many a long bus ride to school with my nose in a book. But like many, I fear, my easily distracted self became addicted to tech. Not for a lack of interest — I just simply found it hard to focus on reading anymore. I’ve read the odd book over the past number of years, like the memoirs from Canadian Simu Liu and Nintendo legend Reggie Fils-Aimé, but not much more.
But at the end of this summer, I started getting back into reading more — fittingly enough, by using technology. Meeting both of these interests halfway, I took on the opportunity to review a Kobo Libra Colour. And so, as I’ve been using it on-and-off over the past few months, I’ve been finding myself falling back in love with reading. What’s more, some of its unique tech-powered features have enhanced that experience.
First and foremost: the slim form factor. It can’t be overstated just how much I love the 200g weight and size of the 7-inch tablet. As someone who travels often for work, my bags are often stuffed with my laptop, a gaming handheld, snacks, cables and clothes, among other things. And so, having something so compact is truly wonderful.
This is especially true on flights. I’ve had a few to Europe this year, which, naturally, go for 7-plus hours from Toronto. At the same time, the little table you get on the seat in front of you is rather tiny. But with the Libra Colour and its foldable case, I can easily put it on the table alongside other things, like a drink and my phone. (The only downside with the tan case I received with the Kobo is that it’s dirtied fairly easily on my travels.)
But before I go further, I should stress that there were some growing pains. For one, I found the touchscreen a bit finicky. At times, I thought it had actually frozen, only to realize it simply didn’t register my input and I had to use my nails or a stylus. Further, the setup process was decidedly laborious, with the QR code not showing up at first and then the loading process being somewhat slow from there.
But once I was past those pain points, I had a blast going through the storefront to search for books. For a while, I’ve been interested in checking out Dune and Neuromancer, the former due to Canadian Denis Villenueve’s grand cinematic trilogy and the latter since it’s the pioneering cyberpunk work from American-Canadian author William Gibson. Finding and buying these books was satisfyingly quick, as was Michael Mann’s Heat 2, which I’ve wanted to read as a big movie buff, or even something as niche as James Mielke’s biography of legendary Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu.
That said, I quickly realized, to my frustration, that some books weren’t available when I searched, like Dungeon Crawler Carl. After a quick Google search on my phone, I realized it was only on Amazon Kindle. I wasn’t exactly surprised, mind you, as exclusivity defines so much of the entertainment industry, especially in the gaming space, which is my bread and butter. But it was a good early reminder to expect the same in the ebook space — something that wouldn’t really be an issue when buying a paperback or hardcover copy.
But of course, the most important thing is the actual experience of reading itself, and on that front, I love what the Kobo offers. Right away, I was pleased by the variety of lighting options which made it perfect for my red-eye European flight. That, coupled with the compact form factor, made it easy to use, especially as I would inevitably keep shifting in my claustrophobic seat in a futile effort to get comfortable.
I also loved the built-in features to enhance the reading experience. As I started Neuromancer, I was delighted to discover I could click on a word to get a dictionary definition of it. Footnotes are also embedded into the text so you can click on them to see more. Getting all of this within the Kobo, rather than having to break immersion and check my phone, was a game-changer for me. (For instance, one fun fact is that the Vancouver-based Gibson, as he explains in his foreword, wasn’t aware at the time of writing that the book ended up being translated into Chinese, but the footnote confirms, as of May 13, 2018, that Chinese has been added.)
Meanwhile, I appreciated how the Kobo would not only keep track of my reading progress, but also tell me how much I had left in a given chapter. As someone who likes to leave off in a clean spot when putting a piece of media down, knowing that I only had X number of pages left, without having to physically leaf ahead and potentially spoil myself, was really handy.
All of these are welcome features that kept me locked in. And the fact that the ebook has a crazy long battery life when not in use meant that I could come back weeks later and it still had a decent amount of juice is fantastic. So many times I’d go on a trip with several devices and forget to charge one of them, so knowing the Kobo has ample battery in case of such situations is great for peace of mind during travels.
The only thing that hasn’t kept me locked in, honestly, is me. Indeed, I haven’t used the Kobo as much as I had been planning to when I received it during the summer, but that’s not a reflection of the product itself. Part of that comes down to not travelling nearly as much as I did last year — a conscious choice to avoid the U.S. when possible. I’ve also been rather swamped the past couple of months with some big features and approximately 87,000 game releases, including a little title called GTA VI, as part of my duties as a juror for The Game Awards.
But if anything, the fact that I’m still thinking of the Kobo and looking forward to getting back to reading is a testament to how much I’ve enjoyed my time with the device. And given that I’ll undoubtedly be burned out on games come the holidays, I’m excited to pick it back up and catch up on some books. Neuromancer awaits.
The Kobo Libra Colour normally retails for $289.99 but is on sale for $259.99 for Black Friday.

articles.title: Why AI Struggles To Reuse Chip Designs
articles.text:
AI can accelerate derivative designs, but physical constraints and incomplete data limit how much can be automated.
Key Takeaways:
- AI can accelerate derivative chip design, but those derivatives may not be physically viable or cost-effective.
- AI-assisted reuse depends on the availability of accurate design data, engineering knowledge, and proven methodologies.
- End-to-end automation is limited by gaps in multi-physics simulation, implementation, and verification.
Chipmakers are seeing mixed results when they apply AI to derivative and new chip designs, finding that AI-generated solutions can be substantially different and more costly than expected, and that AI-driven designs introduce new manufacturing and verification challenges.
Several key problems have emerged when incorporating AI in chip design. Among them:
- The data needed to ensure that follow-on designs will function as expected may not be complete because some of that data resides in other companies, such as foundries, OSATs, and various equipment and process providers;
- Integrating rapidly evolving AI capabilities into established EDA flows remains challenging, especially where predictability, traceability, and silicon-proven results are required.
- Many organizations have customized tools for their own chips, markets, and expertise, and AI tools have not yet adapted to those changes.
“There’s the engineer in me that says if AI can take us to brave new worlds where humans haven’t yet gone, that’s an exciting thing,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA. “But I’ve seen it run into problems. For example, I had a low-pass filter, which we call a pixelated model, and it looks like a QR code in the middle. There’s a high-frequency part running at about 2 GHz. If I want to change it to 2.5 GHz, a human would look it up in a textbook. There are traditional ways to do it, and they would create something that any other human would recognize. AI looks at this, says, ‘I don’t understand your textbook, so I’m going to just turn on and off any single part of this grid, and I’ll come up with something.’ It does sort of work, but there are constraints. Is this manufacturable? Is this cost-effective? Did I learn anything out of this? Yes, AI solved a problem for me, but as a human, I had intuition about what worked at 2 GHz. Now, if I want to shift to 2.5 GHz, that same intuition will change the design.”
Instead of making an incremental change to account for a new spec, AI may come up with something completely different, with no correlation between versions, Kamdar explained. “There’s a cost of letting AI do all of these things.”
Reusing designs across multiple generations of chips has long been the go-to strategy as a way of amortizing non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs and reducing development time. Using AI agents to come up with derivatives adds a whole different way of looking at the problem. AI agents can assess existing architectures and RTL to identify potential bottlenecks, explore design modifications, optimize EDA tool settings, and automate portions of verification and debugging. And they can orchestrate workflows across multiple tools, reducing the manual effort required to adapt existing IP to new specifications.
But the resulting AI-generated design is not necessarily ready to be implemented in a follow-on chip. Engineers must determine whether proposed changes are physically feasible, manufacturable, cost-effective, and compatible with the new design’s requirements. That, in turn, will determine where AI can and cannot be used, and where EDA tools need to evolve in order to close that gap.
Software reuse easier than hardware reuse
Despite AI’s promise, a lot of human effort is still needed in today’s designs. Working with natural language interfaces is a big plus, but minor differences in queries can result in very different answers.
“We were rapidly adapting the automotive solution to robotics because there’s a lot of commonality,” said Baaziz Achour, CTO of Qualcomm. [1] “Many of the key functions are similar, such as perception, path planning, and foundational technologies like sensor fusion, object recognition, location, and control. We were able to take the full automotive solution and apply it to robotics. We have very effective solutions for scaling the software. However, hardware IP scaling and SoC integration still require significant human effort.”
Those differences can also be significant across domains. for example, developers may increase the number of cores in an NPU and use tools to analyze bottlenecks as application workloads shift. But this type of scaling is very different with mobile multimedia, such as a camera, Achour explained. “Across a lot of this AI spectrum of products, the basic camera and display blocks are similar, but the requirements are very different in camera count, speed, and power.”
Fig. 1: Designers can use tools to adapt common IP, but there is still a non-recurring engineering cost for SoC implementation. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
While designers can leverage core IP blocks, such as an image signal processor, every processing core, camera, and display across these devices must meet diverse requirements and cost targets. “Currently, we often create separate architectures and hardware design variants for each case,” said Achour. “Can EDA help us build one flexible architecture that adapts to these diverse requirements instead of manually customizing for each time?”
The answer? Maybe. Ensuring that a chip design will function flawlessly requires an ecosystem. Automating some steps in the design flow can help, but how much automation and which steps are still being explored. Nevertheless, there are plenty of places where engineers would welcome more flexibility and automation, such as iteratively tuning EDA tools to meet design targets.
“Three months were spent in recipe tuning of EDA tools,” said Achour. “Neither the RTL nor the floorplan were changed in these iterations, so this is a huge source of inefficiency. EDA tool companies have AI-aided fine-tuning, but that consumes a lot of compute. Further innovation is needed for this.”
Fig. 2: EDA tools to help designers reuse IP need to account for area, thermal, PDN, and much more. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
The overall goal for engineers is to reduce runtime and compute, shortening time to market, increasing coverage and improving confidence at sign-off, and enabling engineers to be more productive. “We need innovation in GenAI, including GenAI that can create design input for the EDA tools, like a human designer, to drive fast convergence, and agents that can orchestrate design flows to reduce human effort for iteratively running tools to refine and optimize the design,” said Achour. “These are critical technologies to rapidly adapt common hardware to evolving AI product demand. We need innovation in AI for SoC design.”
Capturing IP data and design knowledge
Before AI can effectively help engineers adapt existing designs to new requirements, it needs access to accurate, organized information about the IP already available, including its configurations, constraints, dependencies, and previous implementations. Capturing and managing that information, along with the engineering knowledge and methodologies used to develop it, is essential to making AI-assisted derivative design scalable.
To help solve these challenges, established EDA vendors and startups are releasing physics-based, assistive AI co-pilot technology to speed up design exploration, PPA optimization, RTL generation, and verification.
However, before deploying an AI tool to create a brand-new design or a derivative design from existing IP, engineering teams must first collect the knowledge already inside the organization. After that, IP lifecycle management software is needed to connect engineering data, automate workflows, improve traceability, and make valuable IP easier to find and reuse.
“How do you pull different IPs, and where is information about that IP?” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You could have information that says this IP works great for certain power levels. If you are developing an earbud, the available power may be much lower, so you know which IP will not be suitable. You have to look for a different source of IP from the finished product. You can create a software bill of materials (SBOM) or hardware bill of materials (HBOM) that lists all the IP you used, and you can confirm whether that was the latest and greatest version of the IP. Were there other variants of the IP? There are all kinds of different ways to do IP management.”
Teams also need a way to share the AI prompts, skills, and workflows they develop so that everyone can benefit from communal wisdom. “We invested in a platform and innovation store that allows our people to share prompts, plugins, check-ins, and solutions across teams,” said Ram Narayan, senior director of engineering at Arm. [2] “That was done primarily with the vision that teams can share skills and upskill themselves through that exchange. They can use the platform to upskill teams across the company, as well. This is an opportunity to bring people together around common ways of working and common learnings, which may have been lost over the years because we have acquisitions of groups, and groups going off and doing things differently. This is a real opportunity to enable these practices.”
An organization’s specific workflows need to be captured to get the best results from agentic AI-based design exploration tools.
“A company’s methodology is as important as the design, and the methodology they have used for the last 20 years to be able to tape out their chip has brought a lot of learning,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents. “For example, ‘Use this cell/ don’t use this cell. Optimize for PPA that way. Don’t do this. Don’t do that. Or, do this.’ When you are in the ECO stage, and you have crosstalk, you can talk to the customer, and they say, ‘Oh, for crosstalk at this modem company, I have a very specific way of solving it. I have done the same thing for the last 10 years, and I am able to solve the crosstalk.’ That’s what we call the ontology.”
This is a very promising use case for agentic AI. A common approach from EDA tool providers today is to have an agentic collaboration platform sit with the customer, allowing sharing between users while also feeding data, methodology information, and design information back into agentic workflows so they can do the best possible job and deliver the best possible outcome. In ChipAgent’s approach, all proprietary customer data stays on-prem. “This belongs to the customer,” Rahim noted. “It is not something that comes back to us.”
Automating interconnect design
While organizations wrestle with how to apply AI, they also are leveraging improvements in algorithmic optimization, software-driven simulation, and deterministic EDA. This is especially important when it comes to data movement, which is one of the key performance bottlenecks, along with moving data in and out of memories and processors. A tiled, algorithmic fabric is easier to scale up or down for derivatives than crossbars.
“For our switch customers who have been working with crossbars in the past, and have had deep, lived experience over decades, it is still a very hands-on experience with hand-coding RTL to build huge custom networks, and almost hand-wiring things,” said Saurabh Gayen, chief solutions architect at Baya Systems. “They say, ‘When this wire comes in, it’s going to come in here, then this other data is going to come from there, and we’re going to make it like an arbiter. This is a painstaking process where the whole design just gets bigger and more difficult by an n-squared factor. This is super painful for engineers, companies, and project managers, as well. It’s an incredible source of risk for them, because it’s iterative. It’s manual. They don’t know if they’re going to find surprises later.”
Massive parallelism and other techniques have transformed what previously looked like a complex engineering project into a very manageable math problem. “Suddenly, this becomes an algorithmic construct that says mathematically we will give you the exact performance properties you need,” Gayen explained. “This will create, literally, a grid of identical tiles. Top-down, you get that guarantee that it meets the performance needs ahead of time. Then in terms of implementation, when it’s the physical design, you actually build it and harden those designs, then figure out how to put it within a chip.”
In today’s landscape, a software-first approach is needed to build hardware, adapt it to new use cases and better products, and reduce customer cost, pain, engineering effort, and time to tape out. “It’s all built step by step,” Gayen observed. “For example, when I came in, we already had a really good software-defined flow, which is new for hardware. People don’t like writing software. They like getting their hands dirty and writing RTL. Having that software perspective of coming in and generating RTL is something that unlocks a different type of thinking and allows breakthroughs like this to happen. Companies are happy, and the engineers are happy because they don’t have to do the painstaking manual work anymore.”
Multi-physics optimization limits
However, for design exploration or reusing IP, no tool yet optimizes timing, IR, and thermal together at the RTL or architecture level.
“Today, we don’t have anything that helps the RTL designer all the way,” said Vinay Patwardhan, senior director, product management at Cadence. [3] “We have something that can help customers from the netlist stage. We have a vision for going all the way to architectural, but right now it’s either timing-based improvement, IR-based improvement, or thermal-based improvement — not all three together as a multi-physics problem. If you want improvement at the RTL stage, you have to incorporate all of them into the source code, which isn’t available because thermal analysis works on layout layers. IR needs the locations of the power sources. At the RTL stage, there is no physical awareness of any of this, so it is a difficult problem. However, if we can find correct ways to model and abstract all those effects at that early stage, then it will be possible. There is some work going on in that phase, but to answer clearly, we don’t have anything in the RTL today. We can optimize the netlist continuously with feedback.”
Tool providers are addressing the challenge from many angles. For example, ChipAgents developed Build-A-Chip-Bench to evaluate AI agents from workload spec and RTL generation through synthesis, physical implementation, and layout verification.
Fig. 3: Key steps from workload specification to GDS. Dashed arrows show problems found downstream that send the agent back to revise an earlier step. Source: ChipAgents
While these advances show AI’s potential to automate increasingly complex design workflows, generating a design is only part of the challenge. Each stage of implementation introduces physical constraints and interdependencies that can affect decisions made earlier in the process. Changes intended to improve one aspect of a design may create problems elsewhere, requiring tools to account for the interactions among electrical, thermal, mechanical, and other physical effects.
The need for agentic tools to be grounded in fundamental physics is one reason why end-to-end solutions are still under development.
“The limiting problems are no longer inside the chip,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO of Vinci. “They’re physical problems that live at the boundaries — heat moving from die to package to board to enclosure, thermo-mechanical stress across heterogeneous material stacks, power density interacting with cooling strategy at the system level. The physical world doesn’t respect the organizational boundaries the industry has drawn around it, and neither do the failures.”
Others agree. “EDA tools must expand beyond single-die optimization to system-level design, including multi-die integration, packaging, and software-hardware co-design, evolving toward intent-centric platforms rather than collections of disconnected point tools,” said Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing at Arteris. “One major gap is verification, where rising design complexity continues to outpace engineering productivity despite significant AI advances.”
These challenges become even more complex as designs move beyond the chip and package to the board level, where reused IP and previously verified components must operate within new electrical and physical environments. While reusing proven designs can reduce engineering effort, changes in placement, connectivity, and surrounding circuitry can introduce interactions that were not present in the original implementation. This makes verification a critical part of derivative design, even when the underlying components have already been validated.
Verification at the board level
As with SoC IP data management, a robust data management foundation enables teams to reuse known good blocks on the board.
“They verified them in the past, and they could say, ‘This block doesn’t need to be verified,'” said David Wiens, product marketing manager at Siemens EDA. “If they use that block more than once, they only need to verify it once. But in reality, blocks of data and blocks of designs can and will behave differently depending on what’s around them. It’s a step toward simpler verification, but you still have to be careful. You have this one circuit, and you place it on the top layer of the design, but whatever’s running underneath it that’s native to that, that’s custom to that design and may in fact interact with it. You could put a shield around it if you wanted to really trust it and really make sure that it’s not impacted. But particularly with signal integrity, that’s a bit of a scary proposition to say, ‘I’m just going to trust that it’s more than likely to pass by itself.’ It’s a question of what it interacts with on the board.”
Fig. 4: Data management is a key component of using AI tools to speed up any part of the design flow. Source: Siemens EDA
Agentic AI tools can now shrink verification time. Siemens reported that its HyperLynx Agentic Toolkit reduced the design analysis for 112 high-speed channels from several weeks to a couple hours. “In a manual process, engineers would first need to figure out the signaling protocol,” Wiens explained. “What SerDes protocol is it using? I’ve got to dig up the manual, which can be hundreds of pages long. I’ve got to find the rules within that, and the conditions to set up my simulator. Then I’ve got to push the button and wait for it, and then when I get it back, I’ve got to visualize. I’ve got to look at the results one waveform at a time. Did it pass? Did it fail? And if not, I’ve got to figure out why, and I’ve got to iterate.”
With new agentic solutions, the AI can inspect the database itself. “It can identify potential issues off the bat before it even simulates,” he said. “Then it automates the workflow. That’s a big thing because it’s part of what democratizes the tool. Specialists understand both the workflow and the results. Democratizing that automation, simplifying it, means anybody can push the button. With visualization, when you’ve got a ton of data, you don’t want to look at it one at a time. We can use AI to take that data and visualize it to produce different types of results that aren’t just simple waveforms. The AI can diagnose where the problem is. ‘This eye [diagram] is failing. Here’s where I think the problem is, and here’s what we recommend you do next.’ It takes the engineers through that entire path.”
The speedup doesn’t come only from AI and software capabilities. “It’s about leveraging hardware horsepower, GPU horsepower, CPU cluster horsepower,” said Wiens. “That’s what gets us the speed. But there are also areas of AI that help us explore the design space faster without brute-force simulation. Agentic AI accelerates the steps, mostly through smarter execution, and then delivers trusted outcomes because it’s physics-based. It’s leveraging known good simulation engines, and IP can be managed in a safe way on-prem.”
Leveraging GPUs and CPUs comes with computational costs, a concern raised by Qualcomm’s Achour. Moreover, engineers still must manually implement many of the changes recommended by agentic AI tools.
“What engineers do next is go back to the design, the actual layout or schematic, and make the changes that were recommended,” said Wiens. “Today, that’s still largely a manual process. Watch this space. Automating the actual place and route and things like that is a lot harder than automating workflow.”
What AI still can’t automate
AI-based design tools are advancing rapidly, with vendors introducing new capabilities for RTL generation, design exploration, physical optimization, and verification. These advances are reducing engineering effort in individual stages of the design process, but efficiently adapting existing hardware IP to new applications remains a much broader challenge.
Making derivative chip design more scalable will require more than increasingly capable AI models. Design teams need organized, accessible IP data; reusable engineering methodologies; tools that can evaluate architectural and physical trade-offs; and verification workflows that account for changes in configuration, implementation, and operating environment. Agentic AI may help connect and automate these processes, but the underlying tools must still produce results grounded in physical reality.
At the most fundamental level, many AI tools are text-based LLMs. “They are really, really good at predicting the next word, the next phrase, the next line, then the next paragraph, and that means AI can be used to write text-based chip design specs or chip design documents like RTL design,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “AI can be used to write verification scripts that will test RTL and prove it’s good RTL or not, or find flaws in it. AI can read a long series of debug logs that could be gigabytes long, and humans will take forever to go through that. AI can quickly say, ‘Hey, did you go to line 79? That’s where I see a major issue.’ Largely, that’s what AI is helping with. There are so many other aspects of chip design that are not text-based, not suitable for words, and they still need humans actively.”
For chip architects and design teams, the opportunity is not simply to generate new designs faster, but to reduce the engineering effort required to turn proven IP into new products. Achieving that goal will depend on how effectively AI-driven automation can work with established EDA tools, engineering knowledge, and physics-based verification to identify what can be reused, determine what must change, and validate the resulting design. The real measure of AI’s success in derivative chip design will not be how quickly it generates new RTL, but how reliably it can help engineers transform existing IP into verified, physically viable designs with less manual effort.
References to DAC presentations
Related Articles

Can LLMs turn a specification into a set of formal properties that can be used to verify an implementation? The answer is getting closer to being yes, but with caveats.

Technology is only useful if it improves an existing methodology. Property generation is still refining that goal, but in the long term it could be very useful.

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups
articles.text:
Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.
Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.
The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.
The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.
Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

articles.title: GTA 6 hace historia en PS5 y se convierte en el lanzamiento más exitoso de PlayStation
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 no para de crecer. A pocos días de que llegara al mercado, el juego de Rockstar Games batió todos los récords de ventas, preventas y ya superó en ganancias a la taquilla de las películas más exitosas de Hollywood. Ahora, GTA 6 logró convertirse en el lanzamiento más exitoso de la historia de PlayStation, impulsando la venta de consolas.
De acuerdo con el blog oficial de PlayStation, más de 39 millones de usuarios han jugado GTA 6 en PS5 desde su lanzamiento. El juego también estableció un récord por el mayor número de jugadores simultáneos que ha tenido un solo título en las consolas PlayStation, superando incluso los récords en otros títulos multijugador o free-to-play, que normalmente lideran en este apartado.
Según Sony, los jugadores de GTA 6 en PS5 acumularon más de 683 millones de horas de juego entre el día de estreno y el 22 de noviembre. Cada uno ha pasado una media de 17,4 horas explorando el estado de Leonida durante los primeros días desde su lanzamiento.
Estas cifras superan a cualquier otro juego de consola en los últimos años, incluyendo aquellos de los estudios first party de Sony. Si bien no hay datos oficiales, juegos como Marvel's Spider-Man 2 o God of War Ragnarök tuvieron un lanzamiento importante, aunque no al nivel de GTA 6. Otro juego que podría colarse en la comparativa es Fortnite, que se convirtió en un fenómeno cultural entre 2018 y 2019, registrando millones de jugadores concurrentes.
GTA 6 también ha impulsado las ventas de consolas PS5
Además de los récords en horas de juego, Sony también registró un aumento en las ventas de hardware. La compañía afirmó que GTA 6 generó el mayor número de nuevas PS5 conectadas en un solo día desde el lanzamiento de la consola, excluyendo los periodos habituales de compras de fin de año. El juego de Rockstar Games fue el primer título ejecutado en el 70% de las nuevas PS5 activadas durante este período.
Las cifras podrían sonar escandalosas para alguien que no ha seguido el fenómeno de Rockstar Games. Desde los primeros rumores que anticipaban su llegada, la mayoría de jugadores sabía que GTA 6 representaría un momento clave en la industria de videojuegos.
Grand Theft Auto 6 superó los 32 millones de reservas, algo que no había logrado ningún otro juego o producto de entretenimiento. No obstante, la situación se volvió aún más espectacular en el lanzamiento, generando 3.790 millones de dólares en ventas durante las primeras 24 horas. Esto representa más de 4,6 veces lo que obtuvo GTA V durante su día de estreno, o 5,2 veces lo que generó Red Dead Redemption 2 en su primer fin de semana.
Fuera de los récords comerciales, GTA 6 también ha cosechado elogios de la crítica especializada. Hace unos días se reportó que el juego alcanzó el 99 en Metacritic, una calificación que mantenía The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time desde 1998. La mayoría coincide en que Rockstar Games ha logrado su cometido, convirtiendo a GTA 6 en uno de los juegos más importantes de la generación.
El estudio todavía tiene trabajo por delante, con una versión de PC que se estrenará durante el primer trimestre de 2027. También está pendiente el multijugador de GTA 6, que intentará superar lo que ya consiguió GTA Online.

articles.title: I tried ChatGPT Space, OpenAI’s answer to Google Docs — and liked it until I had to go back to chat to make a presentation
articles.text:
ChatGPT is giving Plus users a Google Docs-style workspace for interactive pages and presentations — and some pages can even update themselves
Space replaces Library in the sidebar and gives pages, slides, images, and uploaded files a new home
If you’ve logged in to ChatGPT recently and you’ve got a Plus account, you might have noticed a small change in your sidebar. OpenAI is rolling out a feature called Space, a workspace for building pages and presentations. It replaces the old Library option, but it takes a bit of getting used to.
It’s quite hard to get your head around what Space actually is. For starters, OpenAI calls the overall feature Space and the individual collections inside it spaces. That’s needlessly confusing when you’re using it for the first time. It also sounds a lot like Projects, Canvas, or ChatGPT Work, and OpenAI hasn’t made the distinction between them particularly intuitive.
I think the easiest way to understand it is that a ChatGPT conversation is something you have with AI. A space is something you make with AI, then keep using.
Say you ask ChatGPT to help plan a vacation. A chat can give you an itinerary. In a space, you could turn that itinerary into an interactive travel planner that you can come back to, update as your plans change, and share with other people.
What Space actually is
The best way to think of Space is as a cross between Google Drive, Google Docs, and a lightweight website builder, all living inside ChatGPT.
There are three levels.
- Space — the overall area. The new home for your documents, presentations, images, and uploaded files.
- A space — a collection. You could create a space called “Japan holiday” to keep related pages and files together.
- A page — the content you work on. An itinerary, a budget, a packing list, or an interactive guide that you can edit yourself or ask ChatGPT to update.
Once you’ve created a page, you can write directly in it or ask ChatGPT to make changes, including adding charts and interactive content. You can also invite collaborators to edit and comment on a page. They can use ChatGPT to help make changes, too.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Perhaps the most interesting thing is that OpenAI says pages and slides can update automatically using connected apps and tools. One example it gives is a project plan that reflects decisions made in Slack. That’s potentially the biggest departure from an ordinary AI-generated document.
Space is rolling out to Plus users aged 18 and over, so it might take a while to appear in your sidebar. To open a shared page, recipients need an eligible paid ChatGPT account. There are no public sharing links for pages. Slides are rolling out separately, and Sheets are listed as coming soon.
Testing it out
To try it out, I created a space called “My holiday planner.” Space was the second option down in my left-hand sidebar, so it was easy to find. I wanted a page with a three-day Tokyo itinerary, an interactive packing checklist, and a budget I could update as I spent money. Initially, I thought the only way I could create it with a prompt was to start a new chat and ask ChatGPT to add the page to my space, but later I noticed that if I created a new page inside my space, there was a chat option right down in the bottom right corner of the screen. I found that hard to notice, and I can imagine a lot of people missing it.
Once the page was there, I could edit it directly inside my Space to update my budget. I could also invite other Plus users to edit it using the email address associated with their ChatGPT account.
When I opened Slides from Space, it felt a lot like Google Slides. I could start from scratch or pick a template. I wanted ChatGPT to turn the itinerary I’d already made into a presentation, and I could just ask Chat to do that for me. It worked really well.
Currently, Space feels like OpenAI’s take on Google Docs. What makes it interesting is how easily ChatGPT can turn something you’ve already made into something else using its generative AI ability.
What Space means for ChatGPT
Having Google Docs-like functionality inside ChatGPT is interesting, and it makes me wonder what OpenAI's long game is here.
My guess is that OpenAI wants ChatGPT to be where you keep working after it’s given you an answer. If it can build a holiday planner, let you share it with the people you’re traveling with, and turn the itinerary into a presentation, there’s less reason to copy the whole thing into Google Docs in the first place.
What gives OpenAI the edge over Google Docs is its integrated generative AI ability that links to your existing history and projects in ChatGPT, but even if you don't want to use that, I can still see myself opening ChatGPT for the same reason I open Google Docs today.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Graham is the Senior Editor for AI at TechRadar. With over 25 years of experience in both online and print journalism, Graham has worked for various market-leading tech brands including Computeractive, PC Pro, iMore, MacFormat, Mac|Life, Maximum PC, and more. He specializes in reporting on everything to do with AI and has appeared on BBC TV shows like BBC One Breakfast and on Radio 4 commenting on the latest trends in tech. Graham has an honors degree in Computer Science and spends his spare time podcasting and blogging.

articles.title: South African township delivery startup Gobuddy gets $121k working capital facility
articles.text:
South African logistics startup Gobuddy has secured a ZAR2 million (US$121,000) working capital facility from Anglo American’s Impact Finance Network (IFN) to scale its township delivery model.
Founded by Leon Strumpher during the COVID-19 pandemic, Gobuddy tackles the last-mile e-commerce gap in South Africa’s townships. Traditional couriers often avoid them because of safety risks, long distances and high costs.
The startup first matched parcels with people’s existing commutes, but its data showed that women made up 60 per cent of registered transporters and were less likely than men to own a vehicle, which limited how much they could earn. Gobuddy responded by building a network of community micro-hubs. Couriers drop parcels at local collection points, and vetted residents then deliver them on foot within their own neighbourhoods.
“You don’t need a vehicle. You can walk,” Strumpher said.
Gobuddy now runs 50 micro-hubs in areas such as Soweto, Thembisa, Umlazi, Chatsworth and Motherwell, which together have an estimated 12 million residents. Transporters are recruited and verified through the SA Youth platform, and deliveries are monitored with a tracking system the company spent three years building. Each drop pays around ZAR50 (US$3).
Gobuddy joined IFN in 2024 and received business coaching and investor-readiness support. The new revolving facility will cover the gap between the startup’s weekly payments to transporters and the weeks or months its delivery partners take to pay.
“This facility gives us the working capital to meet our commitments to transporters on time, while allowing us to take on more delivery contracts and grow the business,” said Strumpher.
Gobuddy plans to bring more courier and retail partners onto its platform. It aims to create delivery jobs for 5,000 women over the next three years.

articles.title: Jensen Huang revient à la tête de Nvidia : comment expliquer ce retournement de situation ?
articles.text:
Ce lundi 23 novembre, nous avons assisté à un rebondissement assez inattendu : Jensen Huang a récupéré son poste de PDG au sein de Nvidia, alors qu’il avait remis sa démission 11 jours auparavant à la suite d’affaires extraconjugales, notamment avec Alice Huang, suspectée par Washington d’être une espionne au service de la Chine. Mais comment expliquer ce retour alors que le conseil d’administration de l’entreprise avait clairement annoncé que cela n’arriverait pas, tout en entamant les démarches pour trouver un remplaçant ? Si nous ne savons pas exactement ce qu’il s’est passé en coulisse, plusieurs éléments permettent d’expliquer la situation.
Donald Trump a soutenu le retour de Jensen Huang
Cela n’est pas un secret : Jensen Huang et Donald Trump affichent une certaine complicité. Nvidia a par exemple donné 25 millions de dollars (environ 23 millions d’euros) pour financer la construction de la salle de bal de la Maison-Blanche (Apple et Google ont également fait un don de plus de 20 millions de dollars). En septembre dernier, en pleine conférence, Donald Trump a appelé Jensen pour rappeler une nouvelle fois sa volonté de ne pas freiner la course à l’intelligence artificielle. Les deux hommes avaient alors montré leur plein accord.
Et nous n’allons pas parler des termes utilisés par Trump pour qualifier Jensen Huang : « une légende », « un génie », « Le meilleur atout pour l’entreprise [Nvidia], mais aussi pour les États-Unis. », etc. Bref, Donald Trump avait tout intérêt à garder Jensen, un de ses alliés, à la tête de Nvidia. Le président américain a d’ailleurs salué le conseil d’administration de Nvidia pour sa « décision juste et appropriée » de rétablir Jensen Huang à la tête de l’entreprise. Il reste à voir dans quelle mesure Donald Trump à joué un rôle dans cette réintégration.
Selon Trump, Jensen Huang ne représenterait aucun risque pour la sécurité nationale
Donald Trump a également précisé un point : le PDG de Nvidia ne représenterait aucun risque pour la sécurité nationale. Le président américain a expliqué : « Le gouvernement des États-Unis n’a aucune raison de croire que le retour de Jensen chez NVIDIA présente un quelconque risque pour la sécurité nationale ». Il précise ensuite : « le procureur général des États-Unis a confirmé que le gouvernement américain ne dispose d’aucune preuve indiquant qu’il aurait commis des actes illégaux ».
De son côté, Nvidia a expliqué que « le conseil d’administration a consulté de hauts responsables du gouvernement américain » et qu’il est dorénavant « persuadé que la réintégration de M. Huang ne présente aucun risque pour la sécurité nationale ». Rappelons que Washington envisage de nouvelles restrictions sur les exportations de puces Nvidia vers la Chine, tandis que certains démocrates ont d’ores et déjà annoncé leur intention de mener une enquête approfondie sur l’affaire Jensen Huang.
Nvidia, une entreprise trop importante pour être fragilisée
Bien entendu, il n’est pas seulement question d’une amitié entre Jensen Huang et Donald Trump. Pour rappel, Nvidia est l’une des entreprises qui génèrent le plus de bénéfices au monde, sans parler de son rôle majeur dans la course à l’intelligence artificielle. Et comme le souligne Le Figaro, l’affaire Jensen Huang a donné au cours et à la capitalisation de Nvidia des allures de montagnes russes.
Lorsque Jensen Huang a reconnu son infidélité et que le conseil d’administration a ouvert une enquête, l’action de Nvidia a chuté de 4,3 %. À l’annonce de son retour au poste de PDG, le titre a bondi de 31,5 % en une seule séance, une réaction qui souligne clairement l’importance de Jensen Huang dans la confiance accordée à Nvidia par les marchés.
De multiples pressions pour demander le retour de Jensen Huang
Enfin, nous pouvons noter les multiples appels à réintégrer Jensen Huang en tant que PDG de Nvidia. La Silicon Valley s’est mobilisée en faveur de Jensen Huang. Des employés de Nvidia ont réclamé son retour, tandis que 157 000 personnes, parmi lesquelles Elon Musk, ont également pris position en sa faveur.
Quoi qu’il en soit, nous pensions que la démission de Jensen Huang marquerait la fin d’une ère dans le secteur de la tech. Elle ne constituera finalement qu’un épisode, certes très mouvementé. Du moins, pour l’instant. Au vu des innombrables péripéties de cette affaire, nous ne sommes pas à l’abri de nouvelles révélations.

articles.title: Remate final del Black Friday de Leroy Merlin con descuentos de hasta el 50 % en electrodomésticos, calefacción y más
articles.text:
Que el Black Friday está tocando a su fin es un hecho; que todavía quedan muchas ofertas interesantes para aprovechar, también. Una de las tiendas que está rematando actualmente esta promo es Leroy Merlin, que tiene actualmente descuentos de hasta el 50 % en un montón de dispositivos y productos diferentes. Aunque eso sí: solo hasta el 30 de noviembre.
Árbol de Navidad Patterson verde iluminado y decorado de 180 cm de alto 140 luces LED
Ahora mismo, no es complicado encontrar buenos descuentos en electrodomésticos, dispositivos para combatir el frío o incluso árboles de Navidad. Nosotros os dejamos a continuación una selección de las cinco ofertas de Leroy Merlin que más nos gustan:
- Pack de 2 enchufes inteligentes Shelly por 16,99 euros, un pack de enchufes para controlar tus dispositivos desde el móvil.
- Árbol de Navidad Patterson por 64,50 euros, árbol de Navidad de 180 centímetros que ya viene decorado e iluminado.
- Emisor térmico cerámico Ceramic por 255 euros, con 2.000 W y control desde el móvil.
- Estufa de pellets con kit de instalación y WiFi por 899 euros, con clasificación energética A+ y kit de instalación incluido.
- Microondas con grill Balay por 250,95 euros, un microondas integrable con 20 litros de capacidad y grill de 1.000 W.
Pack de 2 enchufes inteligentes Shelly
Este pack de enchufes Shelly, que incluye dos unidades, es perfecto para controlar cualquier dispositivo de forma remota. Por ejemplo, los podemos utilizar para encender (o apagar) algo que tengamos conectado sin necesidad de estar cerca. Funciona mediante WiFi y son compatibles con Matter, lo que hace que se puedan integrar en diferentes sistemas de domótica. Cada enchufe soporta hasta 3.000 W, incorporan protección frente a sobrecalentamiento y el pack cuesta 16,99 euros.
Pack 2 enchufes inteligente SHELLY plug M gen3 blanco
Árbol de Navidad Patterson
Aunque todavía estamos en noviembre, Navidad está a la vuelta de la esquina. Si estás buscando un árbol, este modelo Patterson es una buena opción por sus dimensiones especialmente (mide 180 centímetros), pero también porque ya incorpora iluminación LED: concretamente, 140 luces multicolor y con función de temporizador, por lo que no tienes que estar pendiente de encenderlas y apagarlas cada día. Está disponible por 64,50 euros, un descuentazo frente a su precio habitual (que es de 129 euros).
Árbol de Navidad Patterson verde iluminado y decorado de 180 cm de alto 140 luces LED
Emisor térmico cerámico Ceramic
Si buscas calentar una habitación de hasta 18 metros cuadrados, este emisor térmico de Purline es una buena opción. Tiene una potencia de 2.000 W y su núcleo cerámico le ayuda a acumular calor y a liberarlo de forma progresiva para lograr una temperatura agradable en toda la estancia. Además, como incorpora conectividad WiFi, podremos controlar varias de sus funciones a través del móvil. Está disponible por 255 euros.
Emisor térmico cerámico Ceramic de 2000 w
Estufa de pellets con kit de instalación y WiFi
Si necesitas calentar una estancia mucho más grande, entonces es mejor apostar directamente por esta estufa de pellets. Está pensada para superficies de entre 50 y 100 metros cuadrados, contando además con clasificación energética A+. Incorpora un depósito de 15 kg para los pellets y conectividad WiFi. Además, incluye kit de instalación y cuesta 899 euros frente a los 975 euros que cuesta habitualmente.
Estufa de Pellets Kit de Instalacion + Wifi incluido | 9 kW A+, Alto Rendimiento
Microondas con grill Balay
Para terminar, tenemos este microondas con grill Balay. Es una opción especialmente recomendable para los que busquen un modelo integrable que no ocupe espacio sobre la encimera. Cuenta con una capacidad de 20 litros, una potencia de 800 W para el microondas y de 1.000 W para el grill. Presenta un acabado en negro y acero que encaja muy bien en prácticamente cualquier cocina y está disponible por 250,95 euros.

articles.title: A medida que Xbox cumple 25 años, la CEO Asha Sharma dice: 'Pronto una sola persona podrá ejercer capacidades que antes requerían naciones enteras'.
articles.text:
Cuando Microsoft lanzó Microsoft Adventure en 1979, la empresa apenas tenía 13 empleados y uno de ellos, Gordon Letwin, se encargó de adaptar aquel juego de aventuras de texto. Casi medio siglo después, hay videojuegos que necesitan cientos de desarrolladores y presupuestos de cientos de millones de dólares. Asha Sharma ha recuperado esa diferencia con motivo del 25 aniversario de Xbox, aunque no precisamente para celebrar lo mucho que ha crecido la industria: la CEO considera que desarrollar grandes juegos se ha vuelto demasiado caro y arriesgado.
En una carta publicada en Xbox Wire, Sharma reconoce que muchas ideas nunca llegan a convertirse en videojuegos y que otros proyectos terminan lejos de lo que sus creadores habían imaginado. Durante décadas, explica, la ambición de un estudio dependía del dinero, las personas y los recursos que podía reunir. Ahora cree que esa relación está empezando a romperse, hasta el punto de que “una sola persona pronto podrá disponer de capacidades que antes requerían naciones enteras”.
Xbox quiere que los equipos pequeños puedan hacer juegos mucho más grandes
La directiva va incluso más allá y asegura que un grupo reducido de desarrolladores podrá crear mundos que actualmente necesitan cientos de trabajadores y cientos de millones de dólares. Para explicar hasta dónde puede llegar ese cambio utiliza Microsoft Flight Simulator, cuya primera entrega apareció en 1982. Sharma imagina que los grandes estudios podrán desarrollar proyectos tan alejados de los juegos actuales como lo está Flight Simulator 2024 de aquella primera versión.
Aunque sus palabras apuntan hacia las posibilidades de la inteligencia artificial generativa, Sharma no menciona expresamente la IA en su carta. No es la primera vez que habla de cambios importantes en la creación de videojuegos sin utilizar ese término: en octubre ya había presentado Xbox Labs, un experimento relacionado con nuevas formas de desarrollar y modificar juegos.
La carta también recupera otra cifra del aniversario. Microsoft todavía cuenta con 111 trabajadores de Xbox y sus estudios que llevan al menos 25 años en la compañía. Son empleados que han vivido desde el lanzamiento de la primera consola, en noviembre de 2001, hasta una etapa en la que su máxima responsable plantea que los próximos grandes videojuegos podrían salir de equipos mucho más pequeños.

articles.title: Moins de 3 secondes de 0 à 100 km/h et faux son de 6 cylindres : la Porsche 718 Boxster électrique promet des sensations fortes
articles.text:
Le Boxster électrique se fait attendre. Après les nombreux bruits de couloir, Michael Leiters, président du directoire de Porsche, avait confirmé en août l’arrivée de la 718 électrique, puis la marque a annoncé le 7 octobre que les prochains 718 Boxster et Cayman abandonneraient définitivement l’essence.
Sauf qu’il manquait encore du concret, et Porsche a enfin donné quelques os à ronger ce mardi 24 novembre 2026 dans un communiqué. Ce sera la première sportive deux portes 100 % électrique de la marque. Le communiqué ne dit rien du Cayman, pourtant lui aussi confirmé en version électrique.
Une architecture spéciale pour la 718 électrique
Porsche a surtout travaillé l’emplacement de la batterie, qui fonctionne en 800 volts. Sur la plupart des voitures électriques, elle est posée sous le plancher. Sur la 718, elle se loge juste derrière les sièges, à la place de l’ancien moteur thermique. Porsche appelle cette architecture « E-Core ». Selon Porsche, elle permet de garder une position de conduite basse et une répartition des masses identique à celle d’une sportive à moteur central, avec 40 % sur l’avant et 60 % sur l’arrière.
Le châssis reprend aussi beaucoup de pièces de la 911, comme la direction, dérivée de la version Carrera GTS, ou le différentiel piloté « PTV+ » qui répartit la force entre les roues arrière pour mieux tourner. Pour la première fois sur un Boxster, des roues arrière directrices font leur apparition. La 718 électrique ne devrait donc pas avoir de mal à enchaîner les virages.
Plus vif qu’un Spyder RS, mais plus lourd
Au rayon des performances, Porsche annonce moins de 3 secondes pour abattre le 0 à 100 km/h, avec les seules roues arrière motrices. À titre comparatif, le 718 Spyder RS, le Boxster thermique le plus radical avec son six-cylindres de 500 ch, met 3,4 secondes. Comme Porsche promet la 718 la plus puissante de l’histoire, la version électrique devrait donc dépasser les 500 ch. En revanche, la vitesse de pointe s’arrête à « plus de 250 km/h », alors qu’un 718 Boxster GTS 4.0 en boîte PDK atteint 288 km/h et le Spyder RS 308 km/h.
Pour le poids, Porsche se contente d’annoncer un total « comparable à celui des modèles 911 Cabriolet actuels équipés du groupe motopropulseur T-Hybrid », le système hybride de la 911. Or, une 911 Carrera GTS Cabriolet pèse 1 675 kg à vide, soit 240 kg de plus qu’un Boxster GTS 4.0 PDK (1 435 kg). Les chiffres qui comptent pour une voiture électrique manquent toujours à l’appel : capacité de la batterie, autonomie et temps de recharge.
Une boîte PDK virtuelle et un six-cylindres reproduit
Tous les Boxster électriques auront de série le système E-Shift. Un bouton active une boîte PDK virtuelle à sept rapports, du nom de la boîte à double embrayage des Porsche thermiques, avec des passages automatiques ou manuels via des palettes. La voiture diffuse alors le son d’un six-cylindres à plat, inspiré du Boxster GTS de génération 981 (celle qui précédait la 718).
Porsche assure que les performances ne changent pas, que le mode soit activé ou non, grâce à un surplus de couple au moment des changements de rapport. Quand le E-Shift n’est pas activé, les palettes servent à choisir entre trois niveaux de récupération d’énergie.
Le reste des détails suivra lorsque Porsche présentera le 718 Boxster 100 % électrique au premier trimestre 2027. La production se fera dans son usine historique de Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen.

articles.title: 60 Millions de consommateurs : le patron de Free va reprendre le magazine... qui compare ses forfaits !
articles.text:
L'État a validé l'offre de NJJ Médias, la holding de Xavier Niel, pour reprendre le mensuel édité par l'Institut national de la consommation. Une majorité des salariés seront conservés, mais pas tous, et l'indépendance éditoriale du titre reste en question.
Les forfaits de Free figurent depuis des années dans les comparatifs de 60 Millions de consommateurs. Le fondateur de l’opérateur est désormais en passe de devenir le propriétaire du mensuel. Lundi 23 novembre, le ministère de l’Économie a confirmé à l’AFP avoir retenu l’offre de NJJ Médias, la holding de Xavier Niel.
L’emploi a pesé dans le choix de Bercy
Le magazine a été mis en vente après la dissolution de son éditeur public, l’Institut national de la consommation (INC), placé en liquidation le 31 mars. La loi de finances pour 2026 avait prévu la cession éventuelle de son activité de presse à un acteur privé. Trois candidats se sont manifestés, dont NJJ Médias et Que Choisir Ensemble, l’ancienne UFC-Que Choisir, qui édite le magazine concurrent Que Choisir.
Bercy juge l’offre de NJJ Médias la plus favorable à l’emploi et met en avant le projet présenté pour assurer la pérennité du titre. La Commission des participations et des transferts (CPT) doit encore publier son avis sur la valeur des actifs concernés. La cession doit être autorisée par un arrêté du ministre chargé de la consommation.
Le plan de sauvegarde de l’emploi prévoit le départ de 20 salariés de l’INC. Les 29 personnes reprises travaillent notamment à la rédaction et dans les services techniques. Bien que la CFDT a signé l’accord collectif, le SNME-CFDT juge toutefois le dispositif déséquilibré et critique notamment les conditions d’indemnisation des salariés les plus anciens.
L’indépendance des comparatifs en question
À ces départs s’ajoute, selon le syndicat, la décision de l’État de licencier les 22 journalistes pigistes qui contribuent régulièrement au titre. Le SNME-CFDT craint que l’équipe ne puisse plus produire le mensuel, alimenter le site et préparer les hors-série dans les mêmes conditions.
Le syndicat souligne que l’INC a renoué avec les bénéfices en 2025. L’institut a dégagé 236 000 euros de bénéfice pour 11,9 millions d’euros de chiffre d’affaires, après une perte de 719 000 euros l’année précédente. Le magazine comptait alors plus de 71 000 abonnés et vendait environ 20 000 exemplaires en kiosque par numéro.
Dès septembre, des élus, des associations et des syndicats ont alerté sur le risque de conflit d’intérêts. Xavier Niel contrôle le groupe Iliad, maison mère de Free, dont les offres sont régulièrement évaluées par le mensuel. La sénatrice Michelle Gréaume a demandé au gouvernement de préciser les garanties dont disposerait la rédaction pour enquêter sur les entreprises dans lesquelles le repreneur a des intérêts. Les modalités de cette protection restent à préciser publiquement.
Si le prochain comparatif de forfaits mobiles ou de box Internet tourne au désavantage de Free, le mensuel pourra-t-il encore le dire aussi librement qu’avant ?

articles.title: 100 euros de moins pour cette unité centrale dédiée au gaming (Ryzen 7, RTX 5060) pendant le Black Friday
articles.text:
Pourquoi ne pas profiter du Black Friday pour donner un coup de neuf à votre configuration gaming ? Avec l’inflation des prix des composants, c’est le moment de faire des économies sur votre nouvelle installation. Sur le site de Cybertek, le Black Cyber est actuellement disponible avec une réduction de 100 euros. De quoi jouer aux jeux récents en 1080p, quitte à baisser quelques réglages sur les titres les plus gourmands.
Que retenir du Cybertek Black Cyber ?
- L’AMD Ryzen 7 5700X et 16 Go de RAM
- La Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060
- L’unité centrale et son verre transparent avec plusieurs LED personnalisables
Grâce à cette offre, le Cybertek Black Cyber passe de 1 199,99 euros à 1 099,99 euros sur le site de la marque.
Une unité centrale polyvalente
Le Cybertek Black Cyber est une unité centrale pensée pour le gaming, avec un AMD Ryzen 7 5700X et 16 Go de RAM. Associés à la Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 (8 Go), ils permettent de jouer confortablement en Full HD, et même en QHD sur de nombreux jeux en activant le DLSS.
Sécurisez vos achats durant Black Friday avec la meilleure offre de l’année. Dénichez les bonnes affaires, Bitdefender s’occupe des arnaques.
Cette carte graphique est compatible avec le DLSS 5 qui offre une touche de réalisme appréciable sur certains titres. C’est notamment le cas sur NBA 2K27, ce qui donne l’impression de se plonger dans un vrai match de basket.
En dehors du jeu, cette unité centrale peut aussi servir au montage vidéo ou à la 3D sous Blender, pour des projets pas trop lourds. Les 16 Go de RAM suffisent pour le multitâche du quotidien. Petit bémol, ils tiennent sur une seule barrette (1 x 16 Go) : la mémoire ne profite donc pas du double canal, plus rapide pour le processeur. L’autre point faible est le SSD de 512 Go, vite rempli si vous installez plusieurs gros jeux et quelques projets vidéo.
Une unité centrale qui se fond dans le setup
Pour combler ce manque d’espace, vous pourrez vous appuyer sur la connectique complète de ce Cybertek Black Cyber. On retrouve un total de huit ports USB répartis à l’avant et à l’arrière de la tour. Ainsi, vous pourrez connecter un disque dur externe. Côté refroidissement, le processeur est placé sous un watercooling de 240 mm (le Serenity 240 de M.RED), de quoi le garder au frais pendant les longues sessions.
Pour relier la tour à l’écran, branchez-vous sur les sorties de la RTX 5060 et non sur le HDMI et le DisplayPort de la carte mère : le Ryzen 7 5700X n’a pas de partie graphique intégrée, ces deux ports ne servent donc à rien ici. Côté audio, on trouve une prise casque et une prise micro en façade, plus trois jacks à l’arrière.
Le Cybertek Black Cyber est aussi une unité centrale réussie visuellement. Comme beaucoup de ses camarades, il possède une vitre qui permet de voir son intérieur. Des zones lumineuses sont disséminées à plusieurs endroits et vous pourrez les personnaliser.
Pour accompagner ce Cybertek Black Cyber d’un excellent écran gaming, vous pourrez découvrir les meilleures références du moment dans ce guide.
