articles.title: Kenya can fine Meta about six seconds of revenue over its AI glasses
articles.text:
In a statement to Kenya’s data protection regulator on October 21, Joy Kalekye, a Kenyan student, recounts an encounter she had long since forgotten. A man approached her, asked a few personal questions and left. She never saw him take out a phone, a camera or any other recording device. At the time, she had no reason to think her privacy had been violated. Eleven months later, she would find out just how wrong she was.
In March 2025, Kalekye was waiting for a friend near a petrol station in Ngara, a busy Nairobi neighbourhood known for its bus stops and wholesale stalls. A man wearing dark glasses approached her and asked her name, age, and whether she lived with her parents or with her husband. She took his number but declined his suggestion to meet at a nearby lodging. Then she forgot about him. Eleven months later, a friend called to tell her she was trending.
Kalekye’s statement forms part of an investigation by Kenya’s Office of the Data Protection Commissioner into Meta Platforms and two companies in its AI outsourcing chain. They are Samasource Kenya EPZ Limited, which employed Nairobi workers to label footage from Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, and its US parent, Samasource Impact Sourcing, Inc. Both operate under the Sama name, an outsourcing business that supplies human workers to label data and review content for AI systems.
The statement became public on November 16, alongside a sharply worded open letter from The Oversight Lab, a Kenyan legal advocacy group that takes on technology companies over their treatment of workers and their impact on the public. The group had petitioned the data regulator to investigate Meta’s glasses and the handling of footage they capture.
Kenya has spent seven years building a legal framework to hold big tech accountable for harm caused on its soil. Yet when it comes to enforcement, the companies easiest to reach are often the ones least able to pay.
Sama, the most accessible respondent in this case, is already on its way out. Its US parent said it was winding down and liquidating its assets, as TIME first reported.
Kenya’s Data Protection Act caps penalties for breaches at KES 5 million ($38,000) or 1% of annual turnover, whichever is lower. For Meta, it would mean a fine of just under $40,000. The company reported revenue of over $200 billion in 2025, meaning the penalty would amount to roughly six seconds of its annual revenue.
Who is speaking?
The Oversight Lab is not a neutral observer in this case. Its executive director, Mercy Mutemi, also runs Nzili & Sumbi Advocates, the law firm representing 185 former Facebook moderators in their case against Meta and Sama.
The group has also taken the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill to court alongside the Africa Tech Workers Movement. It was among the groups that asked the regulator to investigate Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses. It is a campaigner, a petitioner and a litigant in the same fight.
One example is its assertion that Meta “now owns” Remotasks, an online platform that hired gig workers to label images, videos and other data used to train AI systems. Meta actually bought a 49% stake in Scale AI, Remotasks’ parent company. Remotasks also stopped operating in Kenya in March 2024.
Two flows of data, and only one points at Meta
The investigation follows two paths, as revealed by footage from Meta’s glasses. One leads to Nairobi’s AI data labelling workers. The other leads to social media, where private moments can become public entertainment. The regulator is looking at both, but the people involved are different.
On the first path, footage travels from the glasses to Meta’s servers and eventually to annotation companies. In February, Sama workers told Swedish journalists they had labelled clips showing people undressing, using the toilet, and having sex. If the regulator finds that Meta breached Kenyan data protection law in processing this footage, the company could face direct scrutiny over how it collected, stored, and shared the material.
Kalekye’s case followed a different path because her statement provides no indication that her footage went through Sama or was reviewed by an annotator. Instead, a man filmed her and posted the video online. Kenyan social media users then picked it up and circulated it across TikTok, Instagram, X, Facebook, and YouTube.
One of those who reposted the clip was a 22-year-old aspiring content creator. He told the BBC that his upload attracted more than a million views in two hours. The BBC also reported that the man who filmed Kalekye had not been traced. Kenya’s Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), which probes criminal cases, has warned that people who circulated the footage could face prosecution.
This leaves an awkward picture of accountability, where Meta made the glasses, but the people most exposed to prosecution in Kalekye’s case are the Kenyans who shared the video for views. The man who recorded her remains missing, and the company behind the device is another step removed from the investigation.
The vendor takes the hit, again
When former Facebook moderators sued Meta and Sama in 2023, Sama dropped its content moderation contract and the work moved to Majorel, another business process outsourcing (BPO) company. Meta’s regional moderation operations later surfaced in Accra, Ghana, where moderators sued the company over the psychological toll of reviewing graphic content. Teleperformance, a Paris-based BPO corporation, now owns Majorel.
In 2026, the fallout came much faster. Swedish journalists published their investigation into the use of Kenyan workers to review footage from Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses in late February. The data protection regulator confirmed its investigation on March 31. By mid-April, Sama was laying off more than 1,100 workers after Meta ended its contract. Meta said Sama had failed to meet its standards, although Sama disputes that account, saying it was never told that it had failed any of them.
The Oversight Lab blames Meta’s departure for Sama’s collapse. Sama’s own account is different. Sama told its creditors that falling revenue, increased competition and the cost of defending class-action lawsuits cost its business. The financial position it disclosed was bleak, with about $1 million in assets against $17 million in liabilities.
The companies leave, but the liability stays
According to the petitioners challenging it, the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill would make outsourcing firms alone liable for technology workers hired through them, even where the client company supplies the tools, directs the work and takes the benefit.
The Oversight Lab describes the clause as immunity from prosecution, which overstates it; the provision governs civil claims and does not expressly bar workers from suing the companies that hire the outsourcers. Sama’s books show what it could mean in practice. Under the clause, a worker’s claim would land on a company holding about $1 million in assets against $17 million in liabilities, while its former client booked $201 billion in revenue in 2025.
The ODPC has imposed the full $38,000 before, in its first penalty notice, against smartphone manufacturer OPPO in 2022, and a ruling against Meta would count for more than the cash.
The Court of Appeal has already held that Meta can be sued in Kenya. A finding that Meta, as data controller, unlawfully processed footage in Nairobi would hand the former moderators’ lawyers, and whoever sues next, an official record to build on.
The student is asking for less than the campaigners who carried her evidence to the regulator. She wants rules on wearing recording devices in public places, recording lights that people can actually see, and on having her video taken down. She is not seeking compensation from Meta.
Even that modest request is proving hard to meet. Sama has shut down in Kenya, and its parent company is selling off what remains, while the man who filmed her has not been located. The one party still standing is Meta, whose AI runs the glasses, and its business is growing.

articles.title: Entrará en vigor: el Gobierno aprueba que los autónomos declaren el IVA una vez al año si facturan menos de 85.000 euros
articles.text:
Los autónomos que facturen menos de 85.000 euros al año podrán dejar de hacer la declaración trimestral del impuesto sobre el valor añadido (IVA). El Consejo de Ministros ha aprobado un régimen voluntario que la sustituye por una declaración anual. El paquete también incluye descuentos en el impuesto sobre la renta de las personas físicas (IRPF) y cambios en los pagos por adelantado que los trabajadores por cuenta propia ingresan a Hacienda.
Después de la reunión del Ejecutivo, el ministro de Hacienda, Arcadi España, ha presentado las medidas. En la nota sobre las medidas para los autónomos, el ministerio cuantifica la rebaja fiscal en 465 millones de euros. Los cálculos que ha presentado España dicen que son beneficiados 2,6 millones de contribuyentes. A la rebaja fiscal suma un efecto distinto: hasta 1.800 millones de impuestos que podrán aplazarse con las simplificaciones y los cambios en los pagos fraccionados.
Una declaración anual, con pagos de abril, julio y octubre
El nuevo régimen del IVA permitirá cambiar las cuatro autoliquidaciones trimestrales por una única declaración anual. En el transcurso del ejercicio se producirán tres pagos a cuenta, en los meses de abril, julio y octubre. La Agencia Tributaria calculará cada uno, dividiendo entre cuatro la cuota de la autoliquidación anual del ejercicio anterior, y pondrá esa información a disposición del contribuyente.
El sistema, según Hacienda, puede beneficiar a unos 1,1 millones de autónomos y permitir que estos tengan en caja 577 millones de euros más. Es una previsión de liquidez: el impuesto continuará existiendo y se tendrá que liquidar.
Este cambio hay que diferenciarlo bien del IVA franquiciado que se plantea para los pequeños comercios. El acuerdo adoptado cambia la forma de declaración y pago a cuenta del impuesto; no introduce una exención general para los que facturen menos de 85.000 euros.
Más deducción del impuesto sobre la renta y cambios en los pagos por adelantado
A los tributantes en estimación directa simplificada, la reforma aprobada eleva del 5 al 10 por ciento el porcentaje de gastos y provisiones de difícil justificación, y el límite anual sube de 2.000 a 3.000 euros. La mejora se aplicará para el ejercicio 2026. El Ministerio de Hacienda calcula que beneficiará a 1,6 millones de trabajadores autónomos, lo que supondrá un ahorro conjunto de 362 millones de euros en este aspecto. Ese tope es el importe que se puede deducir, no un reembolso automático de 3.000 euros.
A los que tributan por módulos, la reducción del rendimiento neto pasa del 5 % al 10 % en 2026, un 15 % en las actividades agrícolas. Según los cálculos del ministerio, un millón de contribuyentes se verán favorecidos por la mejora en módulos. El paquete también amplía hasta 2027 los límites para permanecer en el sistema de módulos.
De otra manera, cambian los pagos fraccionados del IRPF. El ejemplo puesto por Hacienda es el de un autónomo en estimación directa que facture menos de 85.000 euros y cuya declaración de 2025 haya sido negativa porque pagó por adelantado más de lo que le correspondía pagar. Bajo ese supuesto, señala, podría dejar de hacer pagos fraccionados en 2027.
Para los que deban seguir haciéndolos y facturen menos de 250.000 euros, el tipo anunciado baja del 20 % al 19 %. También se contempla una alternativa de cálculo que tenga como referencia el rendimiento neto de 2025. Con esta opción, la Agencia Tributaria realizará los cálculos de los pagos y el contribuyente podrá domiciliarlos, sin necesidad de presentar las declaraciones trimestrales del IRPF correspondientes.
Hacienda estima que la exención de los pagos fraccionados, la reducción del tipo y el nuevo cálculo permitirán diferir hasta 1.200 millones de euros. Esa cantidad corresponde a impuestos cuyo pago se difiere y que afectan a la disponibilidad de dinero durante el ejercicio.
El paquete también incluye el aplazamiento de Verifactu, el sistema de facturación verificable, hasta octubre de 2028. El Boletín Oficial del Estado, al publicar el real decreto-ley, deberá especificar la fecha de entrada en vigor y las condiciones de aplicación de cada uno de los cambios.

articles.title: Nvidia engineer who quit over Jensen Huang's departure admits he "may have moved too quickly" after CEO's return
articles.text:
Facepalm: Never act too hastily, especially in the fast-moving world of corporate tech. An Nvidia robotics engineer who just quit the company in protest over Jensen Huang's departure has admitted he "may have moved too quickly." Now that the CEO is back in the top position, Darrell Dai says he's open to exploring the possibility of returning – assuming Nvidia wants him back.
Dai was one of the many Nvidia employees aghast at Huang's departure. He wrote in a November 15 post that he was disappointed with how the situation has been handled and the lack of transparency from the company. The engineer also praised Huang's long-term vision, early investments in CUDA and AI, commitment to robotics, and the engineering culture he fostered.
Dai also admitted that Huang's leadership and the culture he helped create were key reasons why he stayed at Nvidia, and that his boss' departure prompted his decision to leave.
 – Darrell Dai (@darrell_dai) November 21, 2026
But yesterday brought the surprise news that Huang had been reinstated as CEO by the board, just a week after its chair said there were no plans to do so. Nvidia said the decision followed input from senior US officials, who reportedly confirmed that his return posed no national security risk.
It's also left Dai wishing he hadn't been so quick to leave the company. In his most recent post, he writes, "Looking back, I may have moved too quickly, and I don't want to rush into another major decision."
 – Darrell Dai (@darrell_dai) November 23, 2026
Dai suggests he would be open to coming back to Nvidia. Given that he left in support of Huang, most comments suggest that Nvidia refusing to bring Dai back would be a bit hypocritical on the company's part. It would probably generate more bad publicity that Nvidia doesn't need right now, too.
November has turned out to be a month to remember for Nvidia. After the first reports of Huang's extramarital affair with Alice Huang, who is alleged to have been spying for China, revelations of other affairs surfaced, including one with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. With the board under pressure and lawsuits being filed, Huang resigned as CEO of the company he co-founded in 1993.
Given his importance to the AI industry and, by extension, the US and global economies, a lot of people wanted Huang back. More than 150,000 people signed a petition demanding he be reinstated. Many signatories are Nvidia shareholders and employees – and this is despite reports that Huang berated his workers for years, once threatening to rip off the top of an employee's head and urinate on their brain. One assumes Dai was never on the receiving end of one of these outbursts.

articles.title: Precios personalizados: cómo las tiendas usan tus datos para cobrar distinto y qué hacer antes del Black Friday
articles.text:
Dos personas pueden ver precios distintos por el mismo producto en una tienda en línea porque el vendedor usa información sobre cada una, como su ubicación o lo que compró antes, esta práctica se llama precio personalizado y en Black Friday es algo a lo que los usuarios deben estar atentos.
La profesora Pnina Feldman, de la Escuela de Negocios Darden de la Universidad de Virginia, la distingue del precio dinámico. En el dinámico, el valor cambia según la oferta y la demanda, pero todos ven el mismo precio en el mismo momento. En el personalizado, el precio depende de quién compra.
Según Feldman, los vendedores pueden apoyarse en la ubicación, el historial de compras, la navegación y el dispositivo que se usa. Un informe preliminar de la Comisión Federal de Comercio (FTC), la agencia que vigila la competencia y protege al consumidor en Estados Unidos, añadió otro dato: incluso los movimientos del ratón en una página.
Qué están investigando los autoridades
El 28 de octubre, la FTC ordenó a nueve empresas que entreguen información sobre cómo usan datos personales para fijar precios: JetBlue, Delta, United, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Walmart y Target, según informó The Record. Tienen 45 días para responder y rl organismo publicará después un estudio.
El presidente de la FTC, Andrew Ferguson, dijo que la agencia quiere examinar la “metodología opaca” con que algunas compañías podrían decidir cuánto paga cada cliente. La orden no afirma que esas empresas cobren precios individuales: busca averiguar si lo hacen.
El 19 de agosto, la FTC había publicado un borrador de política para consulta pública. Sostiene que, cuando el consumidor espera ver el mismo precio que cualquiera, el vendedor debe avisar de forma clara que el precio es personalizado, en qué se basa y qué datos usó. La agencia advierte que no hacerlo probablemente sea una práctica engañosa.
Casos documentados y límites de la evidencia
Feldman recuerda que el mecanismo está documentado en algunos casos. El año pasado, Consumer Reports y el grupo Groundwork Collaborative pidieron a voluntarios comprar en Instacart al mismo tiempo y en las mismas tiendas. Cerca de tres cuartas partes de los artículos aparecieron con más de un precio, con diferencias de hasta el 23%.
Instacart respondió que eran pruebas aleatorias de precios, que no usaban datos personales y que ya las suspendió. Feldman aclara que la medida en que los comercios fijan precios individuales se desconoce. Lo mejor documentado, dice, es el reparto de ofertas distintas entre clientes.
Un informe de agosto del Centro de Información sobre Privacidad Electrónica (EPIC) y la Federación de Consumidores de Estados Unidos recopila casos públicos y señala que las empresas suelen negar o dar por terminadas esas prácticas. Los autores indican que la falta de transparencia impide confirmar esas afirmaciones. También informa que en 2026 se aprobaron leyes sobre el tema en Connecticut, Maryland y Nueva Jersey.
Qué puede hacer un comprador
Los consejos de Feldman apuntan a la comparación. Primero, mirar el historial de precios del producto en lugar de fiarse del tamaño del descuento: “en oferta” no siempre significa buen precio. Segundo, comparar entre varios comercios. Tercero, aprovechar las tiendas que devuelven la diferencia si el precio baja después o si otro comercio vende más barato.
La organización Consumers’ Checkbook siguió a 25 cadenas en 2025 y halló que 21 anunciaban precios “de oferta” más de la mitad del tiempo. El grupo británico Which? vigiló 175 productos durante un año: el 83% costó lo mismo o menos en otro momento que durante el Black Friday.
El informe de EPIC menciona un caso que circuló en redes: la respuesta del servicio al cliente de JetBlue a un usuario que se quejaba del precio le sugería borrar el historial del navegador o usar el modo incógnito. El texto lo cita como indicio, no como prueba de que ese método sirva ni de que la aerolínea personalice tarifas.
Los programas de fidelidad son otra vía de recolección de datos: el mismo informe explica que algunas empresas los usan para repartir descuentos distintos según la disposición estimada a pagar de cada cliente. Comprar sin iniciar sesión o sin la aplicación de la tienda reduce la información que el comercio recibe, aunque ninguna de las fuentes consultadas mide cuánto cambia el precio por ello.
Las empresas notificadas por la FTC tienen 45 días desde el 28 de octubre para entregar la información. Antes de eso llegan el Black Friday, el 27 de noviembre, y el Cyber Monday, el 30 de noviembre.

articles.title: Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X's playbook with cashtags
articles.text:
It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.
While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.
The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.
In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.
The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.
Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

articles.title: AI Can Read The Code, But Can It Understand The Chip?
articles.text:
Frontier models are improving design automation, but layouts, waveforms, and other semiconductor-specific data presents challenges that general-purpose AI has yet to fully overcome.
Key Takeaways:
- Agentic AI could dramatically increase chip design productivity, but multiplying autonomous workloads will place unprecedented demands on EDA data management systems, compute resources, and network infrastructure.
- Fragmented design data, inconsistent data quality, and strict IP security requirements are major obstacles to deploying AI at scale, making data governance, accessibility, and traceability increasingly critical.
- Frontier AI models are becoming more capable of automating traditional EDA workflows, but achieving deeper optimization of chip layouts, waveforms, and other domain-specific data may require specialized models and hybrid AI architectures.
Experts at the Table: Agentic AI promises to close the chip design productivity gap, but the explosion of autonomous workloads is exposing fundamental limitations in how EDA data is stored, accessed, secured, and managed. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss this at the 2026 Design Automation Conference with Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at Cadence; Simon Rance, general manager, IP and Data Management Business at Keysight EDA; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI and Solido at Siemens EDA; Ramesh Narayanaswamy, scientist at Synopsys; and Dean Drako, CEO of IC Manage. What follows are excerpts of that discussion.
L-R: Cadence’s Alpert; Keysight EDA’s Rance; Siemens EDA’s Balasubramanian; Synopsys’ Narayanaswamy; IC Manage’s Drako.
SE: What are the biggest challenges your customers are dealing with for implementing AI in EDA data management?
Drako: The biggest problem facing large customers with globally distributed design systems is continuing to scale to larger, more complicated designs and to reuse IP. Right now, designs are a giant assembly of IP components that need to be assembled, verified, and put together. With AI coming into the equation, those customers want clean databases that the AI can use. They want easy access for the AI to get to that IP, leverage it, and manage the complexity the AI introduces in running more jobs faster. That puts a bigger load on the design management system and the distribution of that data.
Alpert: There’s a huge productivity gap, so they need AI. It’s not like, ‘Oh, it would be nice, so we’re more productive.’ They’re desperate because the gap between designs and our ability to improve keeps growing, even though EDA always improves year over year. Hopefully agentic AI will narrow the gap. In terms of deploying it, part of the biggest challenge is that there’s so much noise. There are so many options — internal/ external models, startups. How do they figure out what to do to make a production-worthy AI flow? That’s probably a real challenge for them.
Balasubramanian: What we are seeing right now is there’s so much AI stuff, both in terms of terms and nomenclature and what people think they can do and cannot do with AI. In the last couple of years, top customers have at least figured out what to do and what not to do at a high level, but the key challenge I see is that many new factors are coming into play. What they’re worried about right now is the quality they’re seeing. They want to have a deterministic flow. They also want to make sure that they are not overkilling in terms of their token budgets and compute infrastructure to get those same answers fast — correct answers. So there’s quite a bit of nuance in how they’re deploying, and it’s really based on where they are focusing and what problem they’re solving. And they are getting to a point where they know what to solve. It’s not like this push-button flow for the entire problem, where you push a button and say I want a chip for this case. They are becoming more realistic. And another point is there are so many variables. Every customer wants to do everything, but then they get stuck in this loophole about what is the right thing to do.
Narayanaswamy: In dealing with customers, we see they’re looking to close the productivity gap. There are all these magic numbers, like we are 2× short of the number of designers people want for all these new design starts people want. On the data management side, we see a couple of flavors of issues. One is, ‘Where the heck is my data going?’ Because you license IP, can you train with that licensed IP? Probably not. But somebody needs to govern that. Or even, ‘Under what contract are you handing that to an LLM?’
Drako: An LLM might go and use something that you didn’t know it used.
Narayanaswamy: If you don’t have an enterprise account with Anthropic and you don’t click the right button, everything you’re doing is there, and Anthropic will train with what they want. So the governance is one. The second is the internal things we build out of this. So you have agentic memory. That sounds good. It helps the flow, but what did you stick in it? And when I am transitioning from, say, when this chip is done, or this block is done, to the next design, what do I carry forward? Historically, we haven’t saved reproducible stuff. But now, there’s a whole new set of things. And the third thing is that models are, in some ways, horrible at dealing with the volume of data. You say I have a waveform database. The model is smart enough to take that waveform database and turn it into text. But that waveform database was like a terabyte of stuff, and you just spent how many tokens going there? You need to provide something where the model can query what it needs or the abstraction it needs. I’ve even seen where, if you give a model enough time, it starts writing a little MCP server. It goes and finds the API from somewhere. So it’s doing all these sub-optimal things, and I don’t think our customers can afford this stuff anymore at scale. Those are things we are looking to solve.
Rance: Our customers have been using our solutions for almost 30 years now, and they’re realizing they’re sitting on a treasure trove of data to leverage for AI. But the challenges that they’re finding are that data is all over the place. What’s the quality of that data? How can we trust that data? And then, how can we govern and secure that data so it doesn’t get released to an LLM, flawed, or to the wrong people? Data management has been seen as a necessity, but it’s just about managing the data. Now it’s, ‘How do you help us find that data, organize it, secure it, and control it so our AI isn’t leaking any of our IP?’ And, ‘How can AI can leverage that and help with better reuse of IP?’ That’s been a challenge for 20 years or so. Solutions like IC Manage, ours, Perforce, and others help with IP reuse, but how it’s packaged and how reusable it is are always a challenge. In the AI era, there’s a lot more automation that can be wrapped around that to help with real IP reuse, but it comes back to those foundational pillars that our customers are seeing in that challenge — quality, trust, and how we cover and trace it.
SE: Scaling was mentioned right off the bat. What does this mean for EDA data management today?
Drako: An engineering project to design a chip may be 10 engineers, 100 engineers, or 1,000 engineers. But what we want, to overcome the productivity issues that everyone’s bringing up, is to use agents to augment those engineers. So maybe have those engineers, instead of operating in 10 workspaces in one workspace each, have 10 or 20 agents that each of them is directing. They get parallelism with all these agents doing work, and they’re more like the director of the orchestra, and so their productivity goes up. To do that, those agents need workspaces. They’re checking stuff out of the version control system or out of the design management system, they’re doing work on it, and then they’re checking it back in, and so you’ve just 10× or 20×’d the load on your design management system, your network file system (NFS), and you’ve 10× or 20×’d the number of licenses you need to buy from Cadence or Siemens or Synopsys or Keysight, or whoever, because you know that that much more is going on. So there’s a scaling issue. We focused on scaling the design management piece, which we’ve always been very strong at. But if you go and say, I’ve got 1,000 engineers, which used to have 1,000 workspaces that you’re managing and updating on an hourly basis, now I’ve got 25,000. The scaling problem is quite large, so that’s one aspect. Then we’ve done a lot of work on the NFS component. NFS is a great solution, but everything has to go over the network. It’s very inefficient. It’s a very chatty protocol, so it’s slow. That means all our customers are constantly fighting speed issues with the file system and the servers. When you want to launch a regression run, and it’s going to launch at 10 p.m. when everybody’s out, but it’s going to launch on 5,000 servers, you’ve got to get all 5,000 servers to have the same data so that you can run all those regression tests. That’s a huge load on the file systems. We had one customer who would launch the regressions every night, and the elevator would stop running because they’d somehow hooked the elevator into the local network, so nobody could leave. So we introduced what is essentially an NFS booster to help with that problem. And then you’ve also got scaling of CAD. If you think about it, there’s a small organization of CAD and IT guys supporting 100 or 1000 engineers. Now they’ve got to support 100,000 engineers plus 10,000 agents, who are also trying to use that same infrastructure to get work done.
Narayanaswamy: An interesting side of scaling the business is also velocity. We were running some experiments, and somebody said, “Look, we run these 20 epochs, but it’s actually over 20 nightly runs. Suddenly, those 20 epochs are happening in 8 hours. So you grab the LSF queue, and your agent is hanging on to it. So the bursty workload is one thing. Predictability is another.
Drako: One of the things customers are very concerned about, and is a big focus, is security. Inside of [our technology], there are a lot of security components to limit access, often for government contracts, often for locations in other countries where they don’t want them to have full access to everything in the design. There are lots of very practical reasons that aren’t really obvious when you just think about it, and so all of those security components, security restrictions, or security controls are going to be critical in the AI execution as well because the AI can get a little rambunctious and actually kind of start creating things like you mentioned and try to get to things. We’ve seen a bunch of stories in the press about AI going rogue and digging into places it shouldn’t. With those security issues, oftentimes there’s security by obscurity, or mediocre security constraints, or people haven’t thought through the security a whole lot. There’s going to be a lot more in the data management world around security with AI in the game, because AI doesn’t necessarily have the same conscience that an employee might, and it isn’t bound by the same laws.
Narayanaswamy: That’s why we’re going around doing secure sandboxes. The more conscious customer is really saying, ‘There’s an LLM call. I need to know what access that sub-agent is going to have.’ It needs to be bounded. Most customers have gotten smarter. They used to do the air gap themselves.
Balasubramanian: One customer said, ‘Every prompt is an IP that I’m giving away. If I’m trying to say, ‘Do this in a way that does this,’ that’s the way I’m actually designing or doing something. I’m actually giving advice, so we really are planning to go for air-gapped on-prem.’ I would say everyone is thinking about it right now.
Alpert: That trend’s reversing now. A year and a half ago, all customers were saying, ‘Oh yeah, only air-gapped on-prem. We need to use open-source models.’ But frontier models like Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini have gotten so good that people don’t want to sacrifice quality. They’re figuring out how they can use these and connect with them. I’d say more customers are on that side of the fence now, but maybe they’re also making special deals where they can host it themselves.
Drako: Customers are figuring it out. Because it’s all new, there’s a big strategy question: ‘Do I go and invest in my own AI models and train them on my designs?’ These are all LLMs, and they do very well when it’s language. If I’m looking at Verilog, they’ll do well. If I’m looking at a waveform file, they don’t understand it, so they convert it to text. If I’m looking at layout, they don’t understand it. They’ve never been trained on it. They’ve never seen it, and it’s not words. There’s a big question of who’s going to create AI models that are trained on it and understand it. Is that going to be the EDA companies, or the Nvidias and AMDs who are going to go do that? They don’t know right now. Everybody’s trying to figure it out.
Rance: We’re seeing a bit of a hybrid of that, where we’re training our own models, but then we’re creating the infrastructure to provide to them. So they can add and create their own models in conjunction with that, and get a lot more value when they combine our EDA tools with the models and the data. Then they’re using the environment to train and create their surrogate models, put that into the workflow, and build trust between the two. ‘This is what it’s doing. It’s contained to that, secured. We don’t have to worry about it going rogue.’ They’re doing it in small phases and rolling it out, but they’re creating agentic workflows that are very tightly constrained right now to prevent leakage.
Narayanaswamy: In terms of the modeling, Chuck makes an important point. When you need reasoning, if you don’t use a frontier model, you may be applying the wrong tool. But for the more domain-specific stuff, there’s this hybrid where you could have sub-domain models, even some very specialized things. Models seem terrible at things like assertions, which are very specialized temporal assertions that reason over time. And you could say, ‘Let’s have a model that is quite good at assertions — but for reasoning.’ That is the tension. Maybe folks like Anthropic need to come to the table and provide a level of trust. It’s a ‘trust me’ business with all of them. Something has to change there.
Alpert: When it comes to training models, the problem with that is like, ‘Okay, let me pick a model to train. It’s probably open-source, which means it’s probably already behind the frontier models. Now I’m going to work on that for three to four months and deploy it to the customer. But now it’s probably a year behind because some new model will come out. That means the training we’ve done has to be good enough to pass. That’s a tough, tough game, and it’s a cat-and-mouse game. It’s like, ‘I train on this model, but now I have to retrain on some new model.’ The danger is that the frontier models will just obliterate what we’ve trained. That’s happened before. Will it continue to happen? I don’t know. Maybe they’re stuck in a place. Then three months from now, it’s like, ‘Oh, there’s a model that’s pretty good at that and understands it.’
Balasubramanian: The frontier models are getting better, but one thing they still lack is enterprise data. They just don’t have access to it. On the front-end side, they can probably get away with it, but not on the RTL generation side.
Drako: They don’t need it. There’s enough RTL code out there publicly that they can get. They can do it, but there are not a whole lot of layouts in the public world.
Alpert: Here’s where I’ll disagree. We can now do skills. We can now give expertise to LLMs, so you could say a lot of people who do place-and-route actually never look at it. They’re just command-line junkies, and they get reports and the like.
Drako: That’s if you’re using the tool. But that’s the command-line interface, the log files, the human interface. The LLM can plug in and do what the human did on the tool. But if you actually want to get AI in the tool, and the results aren’t a log file, you want to look at the layout and say, ‘Oh, that’s not the layout I want.’
Alpert: It’s one thing to say we’re trying to make humans more productive, so we can now automate the job they did with the stuff with the command line. What you’re saying is that you think we could reach a higher level of PPA.
Drako: You’ve just got to differentiate those two piles.
Alpert: So as we’ve been saying about closing the design productivity gap, that’s not needed. You don’t need trained models. But if you want to reach that next level, then now it’s time for some real creativity. What’s going to be really interesting is how we as an industry, for example, write a new place-and-route tool that’s truly agentic, image-based, and all that.
Drako: It will eventually happen. It’s inevitable.
Alpert: But quantum computing is a matter of time, and I’ve been hearing about it for 30 years. I’ll be retired by the time it comes out.
SE: Quantum is 5 to 10 years out.
Alpert: Quantum might be available today, but when is more than 1% of semiconductor revenue going to go to quantum? That’s my bar. Like, is that 5 years, 10 years, 20 years? I don’t know.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: GTA 6 : Rockstar a caché un très gros secret qui vient d’être découvert par les joueurs
articles.text:
Un portail caché dans GTA 6 qui permet de replonger dans le Vice City de 2002. Et, au bout de la quête, Jason, l’un des deux héros du jeu, repart avec la chemise hawaïenne de Tommy Vercetti et sa moto.
Pour les puristes prêts à retourner chaque mètre carré de Leonida, le studio a dissimulé un véritable voyage dans le temps, pensé comme un hommage à GTA Vice City.
Un portail secret caché derrière un code de triche de 2002 sur GTA 6
On doit la découverte au youtubeur australien Memeio, qui vient de mettre en lumière un easter egg de GTA 6 de grande ampleur La quête cachée commence dans la tour radio Badger R&D, à Key Lento, où un interrupteur affiche le logo du Malibu Club sur une télévision. Il faut ensuite activer, dans l’ordre, douze sous-stations électriques réparties sur la carte, sans voyage rapide ni changement de personnage. Les lettres peintes sur leurs murs forment « LIFEISPASSINGMEBY », le code de triche de GTA Vice City qui accélérait l’horloge du jeu. Un SMS envoie alors le joueur au réacteur 2 de la centrale de Turtle Head, à visiter entre 19 h et 6 h. Oui, le voyage dans le temps se mérite.
Un portail violet y apparaît. En le traversant, Jason quitte les graphismes réalistes de GTA 6 pour les personnages anguleux et les textures d’époque de la PlayStation 2. Il se retrouve dans le célèbre Malibu Club, recréé tel qu’il apparaissait il y a vingt-quatre ans. La nostalgie est là.
Danny Dyer reprend le rôle de Kent Paul
Tommy Vercetti n’apparaît pas en personne : seules sa chemise et sa moto reviennent, en guise de récompenses. Ray Liotta, qui lui prêtait sa voix, est mort en mai 2022. Pour la voix d’époque, Rockstar Games a rappelé l’acteur Danny Dyer, qui reprend le rôle de Kent Paul, l’impresario britannique survolté de Vice City.
Pour tenter l’aventure, il faut avoir atteint le chapitre 3 de l’histoire, qui ouvre toute la carte de Leonida.

articles.title: 12 startups named winners at 2026 South African Startup Awards
articles.text:
Twelve startups, including Community Wolf, WaFunda and VezoPay, have been named winners at the 2026 South African Startup Awards.
Run by Startup Club ZA and now in its fourth year, the South African Startup Awards held its awards ceremony at the Homecoming Centre in Cape Town’s District Six last week, attended by around 250 founders, investors and ecosystem players and livestreamed nationally.
This year’s awards drew 179 entries this year, with 51 finalists across 12 categories. Winners were chosen through a combination of 9,000 public votes cast over five days and scoring by a 24-strong judging panel that included the founders of iKhokha, Retail Capital, OrderIn and Payfast.
Community Wolf, which builds safety products that turn ground-level observations into usable intelligence, won the AI & Big Data category, while smart metering and energy trading startup Switch Energy took Climate & Sustainability. VezoPay, which makes battery-free payment wearables, won Consumertech, and AI-native energy management platform Tavas won Deeptech.
WhatsApp-based back-to-school concierge Zumii won Digital Commerce, learning resources provider Edufern took Edtech, and WaFunda – which helps graduates unlock qualifications withheld over unpaid fees through income share agreements – won Fintech.
Skills simulation platform LEVRA won Future of Work, clinical platform GreenNotes took Healthtech, and AskMandla, a WhatsApp service that helps households employ domestic workers legally, won the Informal Market category. CitiPods, which operates rest hubs for delivery riders and outdoor workers, won Mobility & Logistics, while mobile 3D mammography provider Radhiant Diagnostic Imaging was named People’s Choice.
“This year we saw a massive uptake in public participation, with public votes more than doubling, alongside a strong field of entries and real buy-in from key stakeholders across the country’s startup and venture capital ecosystem,” said Mathew Marsden, founder of Startup Club ZA.
The awards were presented in partnership with FNB, RMB, E Squared Investments, Canva Africa and the Western Cape Government, among others.

articles.title: Cet ordinateur Asus noté 4,5/5 perd 522,67 € pendant le Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : L'ordinateur Portable Asus ProArt P16 (RTX Spark 20c) 64 Go / 1 To à 4 239,99 € (-11%)
À l'occasion du Black Friday, l'Asus ProArt P16 (RTX Spark 20c) passe à 4 239,99 € chez Fnac.com, soit une baisse d'environ 11 % et 522,67 € d'économie. Efficace pour les calculs d'intelligence artificielle grâce à sa puce dédiée et doté d'un écran Oled très bien calibré, cet ordinateur portable affiche une note actuelle de 4,5/5 sur notre banc d'essai.
L'Asus ProArt P16 (RTX Spark 20c) s'adresse aux créateurs de contenu qui recherchent une machine dédiée à l'intelligence artificielle locale. Le constructeur intègre un écran tactile de 16 pouces dans un châssis fin, tout en misant sur une puce novatrice pour exécuter des calculs lourds. Cet ordinateur portable avait convaincu notre laboratoire lors de son passage sur notre banc de test.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, l'appareil descend à 4 239,99 € chez Fnac.com, soit environ 11 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (4 762,66 €). Cela représente une économie de 522,67 €.
Un écran OLED précis et une fiche technique calibrée pour l'IA
Pour afficher vos projets créatifs avec une grande exactitude colorimétrique, la dalle OLED tactile de 16 pouces propose une définition de 2880 x 1800 pixels. L'ordinateur portable s'appuie également sur 64 Go de mémoire vive pour soutenir l'exécution des modèles d'intelligence artificielle sans saturer le système. Tous les détails sur son ergonomie sont disponibles dans notre test complet.
Asus ProArt P16 (RTX Spark 20c)
Points forts
- Dalle bien calibrée.
- Performance en IA.
- Finition du châssis.
- Connectique complète.
- Slot M.2 disponible.
Points faibles
- Dalle brillante.
- Wifi 7 bridé.
- Bruyant en charge.
- Autonomie en charge.
- Écosystème ARM perfectible.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Une connectique généreuse avec quelques contreparties thermiques
L'Asus ProArt P16 simplifie le branchement de vos périphériques de travail grâce à la présence de trois ports USB-C et d'un lecteur de carte SD intégré. En contrepartie, la dalle brillante capte facilement la lumière directe, tandis que le refroidissement se montre bruyant lors des calculs intensifs. Ces concessions limitent son intérêt pour travailler en extérieur sous un fort éclairage, mais elles ne gênent pas un usage posé en intérieur.
Apple MacBook Pro 14 (M5 Pro) : l'autre option face au Asus ProArt P16 (RTX Spark 20c)
L'Apple MacBook Pro 14 (M5 Pro) repose sur un écran mini-led très bien calibré et assure une autonomie solide pour les créateurs qui se déplacent souvent. À l'inverse, l'Asus ProArt P16 conserve l'avantage d'une dalle OLED tactile plus spacieuse de 16 pouces et d'une mémoire unifiée de 64 Go conçue pour l'intelligence artificielle locale sous Windows.
Le MacBook Pro 14 est actuellement noté 5/5 contre 4,5/5 pour le PC d'Asus, tout en coûtant 1 640,99 € de moins que l'Asus ProArt P16 à son tarif remisé.
Apple MacBook Pro 14 (M5 Pro)
Points forts
- Design et finitions irréprochables.
- Clavier et pavé tactile.
- Écran mini-led bien calibré.
- Sonorisation impressionnante.
- SSD rapide.
- Wifi (presque) 7 et Bluetooth 6.
Points faibles
- Évolutivité et réparabilité réduites à néant.
- Verre nanotexturé en option.

articles.title: Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures
articles.text:
Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures
- Date:
  November 23, 2026
- Source:
  Universiteit van Amsterdam
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed remarkable materials that can crawl, walk, and dig using their own internal energy, potentially paving the way for a new generation of autonomous soft robots. They also discovered that making individual components more active can paradoxically make the entire material less responsive, challenging a long-standing principle of engineering.
- Share:
Most materials simply react when something pushes, pulls, or bends them. But a very different category of matter can draw on its own energy to change shape and respond to outside forces in surprising ways. Known as active matter, these unusual materials are attracting growing scientific interest. Now, physicists from the universities of Amsterdam, New South Wales, and Cambridge have uncovered remarkable new behaviors that could change how future machines and robots are designed.
Everyday materials such as metal, concrete, glass, and rubber are generally considered passive. They can stretch, bend, shift, or change shape when forces act on them, but the energy needed to produce those changes comes from outside the material.
Active matter works differently. It contains an internal source of energy that allows it to respond to its surroundings in ways ordinary materials cannot. Many examples occur naturally in living systems. A flock of birds, for instance, can move together as a coordinated group, adjusting its behavior in response to wind, changes in the landscape, available food, or a suitable place to rest.
Scientists can also recreate some of these remarkable properties in the laboratory. Researchers from the University of Amsterdam (The Netherlands), the University of Cambridge (UK), and the University of New South Wales (Sydney, Australia) have spent several years developing active materials from surprisingly simple components, including miniature motors, rods, and rubber bands. Their experiments have revealed unusual mechanical behaviors with potentially valuable applications, leading to two recently accepted scientific papers.
Scientists Create Materials That Can Crawl, Walk, and Dig
One of the discoveries involves two familiar mechanical behaviors known as buckling and snapping.
Imagine squeezing a paper ticket between your fingers. As the pressure increases, the ticket becomes unstable and bends to one side. If you then press against the curved surface, it initially pushes back before suddenly flipping in the opposite direction.
This is how ordinary passive materials behave. External forces supply the energy needed for the ticket to buckle and snap, and each action occurs only once in response to the applied force.
The researchers discovered that adding internal activity can fundamentally transform this behavior. They assembled a series of connected rods into a flexible chain, placing small motors at the joints where neighboring rods meet. These motors created interactions that were not symmetrical. Moving one rod could affect its neighbor in a different way than moving that neighbor would affect the original rod (by rotating over a different angle, for example).
The result was striking. When external forces acted on these active chains, they still bent and snapped, but the movement no longer had to end after a single event. Instead, the structures could repeatedly buckle and snap, producing ongoing oscillations.
The underlying physics involves a transformation of the system's critical point, where snapping normally takes place, into what researchers call a critical exceptional point. This unusual behavior makes it possible for the chains to generate movements resembling crawling, walking, and even digging.
The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, with Sami Al-Izzi of the University of New South Wales and Yao Du of the University of Amsterdam serving as joint first authors. One of the team's buckling chains was also featured on the journal's cover.
Beyond revealing unexpected physics, the discovery points toward a promising approach to building materials capable of performing multiple tasks autonomously. Such structures could be especially useful in flexible, "soft" robots, potentially allowing their bodies to produce complex movements without relying on a centralized control system.
Active Matter Challenges a Fundamental Engineering Principle
A separate investigation by the same international research team uncovered another surprising property of active materials, this time challenging a principle widely used in engineering.
Whether designing large bridges or tiny nanomechanical devices, engineers depend on established rules that connect the properties of individual components to the behavior of an entire structure.
One such rule is Le Chatelier's Principle. In the mechanical context described by the researchers, it suggests that changes made to individual parts of a system should produce corresponding changes in the overall structure. For example, making a structure's individual components stiffer would generally be expected to increase the stiffness of the entire assembly.
But the researchers found that active matter does not always follow this expectation. In some cases, increasing the activity of individual components can actually reduce the activity of the material as a whole.
To investigate this counterintuitive effect, the scientists built another structure using motors and rods. Rather than arranging the components in a chain, they connected them into a flat, two-dimensional network resembling a lattice. They then examined how the elastic behavior of the entire structure changed depending on the properties of its individual elements.
Their experiments revealed that the overall response depended on more than simply how active each component was. What mattered was whether the active elements formed connected pathways capable of transmitting mechanical responses throughout the structure.
Why More Activity Can Produce Less Response
The researchers identified a process called percolation as the key to understanding this unexpected behavior.
A useful comparison is the movement of water through ground coffee. If the coffee grounds are packed too tightly, water cannot easily travel through the entire layer. The arrangement of the grounds determines whether the water can find a continuous path.
Something similar happens inside active materials. If too many of the interconnected components have relatively low activity, they can prevent elastic responses from spreading through the structure. Even when other components are extremely active, their influence may not extend across the entire material.
This explains why making some parts more active does not necessarily produce a more active structure overall. The way the components are connected and distributed can be just as important as their individual properties.
The second study, led by first author Jack Binysh from Corentin Coulais's research group at the University of Amsterdam, was published in Physical Review X.
The researchers believe that this unexpected departure from Le Chatelier's Principle could have important implications for understanding and designing systems built from active microscopic structures. These include biological gels, epithelial monolayers, which are sheets of closely connected cells, and neuromorphic networks that mimic aspects of biological information processing.
Together, the findings reveal how dramatically materials can behave when their internal components actively consume energy and interact in unconventional ways. The discoveries could influence research across physics, soft matter science, mechanical engineering, the life sciences, and robotics, while opening new possibilities for creating adaptable materials and smarter robotic systems.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universiteit van Amsterdam. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Sami C. Al-Izzi, Yao Du, Jonas Veenstra, Richard G. Morris, Anton Souslov, Andreas Carlson, Corentin Coulais, Jack Binysh. Nonreciprocal buckling makes active filaments polyfunctional. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (11) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2531723123
- Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, Anton Souslov. More is Less in Unpercolated Active Solids. Physical Review X, 2026; 16 (2) DOI: 10.1103/flhb-kjyd

articles.title: Es oficial, el Gobierno amplía hasta las 20 semanas los permisos por nacimiento y a 10 días los permisos por duelo
articles.text:
Se vuelve a ampliar el permiso por nacimiento y cuidado del menor. Aunque esta vez la nueva semana no tenemos que descontarla en los primeros meses de vida del bebé. El Consejo de Ministros ha aprobado que ahora cada progenitor tenga 20 semanas (antes eran 19) de permiso retribuido. También beneficiará a familias monoparentales, que pasarán de 32 a 34 semanas.
Lo ha anunciado la Seguridad Social como un derecho personal e intransferible. Es decir que cada progenitor tiene el suyo propio. Y no pueden transferir sus semanas al otro.
Este cambio se produce tras la ampliación de julio de 2025, donde se pasó de 16 a 19 semanas (en esa ocasión se separaron en 17 para disfrutar en el primer año y otras 2 que pueden guardarse hasta los 8 años). Ahora se añade una nueva semana en este segundo caso.
Tres semanas que podrán reservarse para más adelante
El cambio es en el reparto. Se mantienen las 17 para disfrutar en el primer año. En cuanto al periodo flexible, pasa de dos a tres semanas. Estas tres semanas pueden disfrutarse de manera continuada o discontinua hasta los 8 años de edad (como explican desde el Ministerio de Trabajo en la comunicación oficial sobre los nuevos permisos).
En el caso de las familias monoparentales pasa de cuatro a seis semanas. De ahí que haya un aumento de dos semanas (de 32 a 34). También afecta a los permisos por adopción, guarda con fines de adopción y acogimiento.
Desde la Seguridad Social indican que entrará en vigor desde que se publique en el Boletín Oficial del Estado. Con respecto a qué partos puede aplicarse la ampliación (algo que aún no está concretado), habrá que consultar en el texto publicado las fechas y eventuales disposiciones transitorias.

articles.title: ShinyHunters claims to return after FBI arrests, uses old PGP keys as proof
articles.text:
The ShinyHunters extortion gang claims to have returned in posts on a new data leak site after a series of arrests over the past two months targeting alleged members.
The new Tor site, launched on November 23, contains messages in both Russian and English announcing the group's return, distancing itself from alleged impostors, and denouncing a former member who was reportedly arrested and is cooperating with law enforcement.
The site also includes two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys dating back to 2020, including one previously used to authenticate communications with BleepingComputer in August 2025.
BleepingComputer confirmed that both messages were signed using known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang, confirming that the new operators have access to private signing keys historically used by the group.
However, these keys do not confirm whether the individuals behind the new operation are the same people who previously controlled the group, as the keys have circulated among numerous people.
The announcement follows a series of law enforcement operations targeting alleged ShinyHunters members after the group claimed to have breached FBI systems in September using an Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability.
Later that month, Dutch police confirmed the arrest of a 24-year-old Amsterdam man suspected of involvement with ShinyHunters, who was identified in media reports as Pepijn van der Stap, previously known online as Umbreon.
In early October, another alleged ShinyHunters member known as Rey or Saif was reportedly detained in Jordan and is cooperating with law enforcement. Around the same time, Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested in Pennsylvania in an extortion investigation reportedly linked to ShinyHunters.
After the arrests, ShinyHunters' main representative, who had regularly communicated with BleepingComputer and other media outlets, abruptly stopped responding, and their Telegram account was deleted. Soon after, the group's data leak site went offline.
In the new statement, the purported ShinyHunters operators say they are returning after months of rumors and misinformation circulated about the group.
"We’re finally back. A lot has happened recently, and there’s still plenty going on right now," reads the English announcement.
"To be honest, there’s just too much nonsense going on. Everyone’s telling different stories, but no one is really explaining what’s been happening over the last few months."
The operators of the new data leak site say they will communicate exclusively through the Exploit hacking forum account, which they claim to have controlled since 2020, and through the new Tor site.
The statement also addresses the reported arrest of a hacker and ShinyHunters member known as Rey, Dedale, or Saif, who was reportedly detained in Jordan in late September.
According to the announcement, Rey previously collaborated with ShinyHunters but began operating independently, creating Telegram channels without the group's approval.
"As far as we know, he has already been arrested and is now "actively cooperating" with the authorities," reads the English message.
"We already rotated the PGP key that Rey used for DLS, since it has most likely been compromised."
The message also mocks two other individuals reportedly tied to the ShinyHunters investigation, Umbreon and Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky, referring to their arrests.
"It was a pleasure working with you. And it’s truly a shame that our guys got caught because of such silly mistakes, ones that could easily have been avoided if you fools hadn’t gotten involved with the wrong people," reads the post.
The operators say they plan to launch a new CDN for hosting stolen data and will no longer use any of the existing backup servers.
Old PGP keys used to authenticate new site
To attempt to prove their legitimacy, the operators published two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys created in January and August 2020.
The keys have the following fingerprints:
- ShinyHunters RaidForums PGP key: 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3
- ShinyHunters Empire Market PGP key: 828537C15F43F135A8317153CD16A1660CC7CE51
BleepingComputer verified that both messages were signed using these known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang.
PGP uses a pair of cryptographic keys: a public key that anyone can access and use to verify a message or data, and a private key used to create signatures. The private key must be kept secret to prevent others from impersonating the key's owner.
BleepingComputer previously verified a message received from ShinyHunters on August 26, 2025, using the 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3 public key.
Successful verification of the November message with that same public key shows that whoever signed it had access to the same private signing key used in the earlier communications, linking it to the ShinyHunters operation behind the widespread data theft attacks in 2026.
However, both historical keys were revoked in March 2026, when ShinyHunters announced a replacement PGP key with the fingerprint F4953411767DE71BEDCDABCB76F4E26F7A20978A.
At the time, the group used both 2020 keys to authenticate the replacement and stated that the older keys would no longer be used for communications.
Despite this, the November 23 announcement once again uses the two revoked 2020 keys to authenticate another new PGP key, 27DA9D5B183247CADFC322880ABC63E30F73822E.
However, none of the November messages examined by BleepingComputer were signed using the March 2026 replacement key, leaving it unclear whether the new operators also have access to that private key.
Because it was rumored that numerous people had the original 2020 keys, these unfortunately do not prove with certainty that the ShinyHunters group has returned or that the brand has not been revived by imposters.

articles.title: « BYD travaille avec la France » : Emmanuel Macron évoque une usine de voitures en Moselle
articles.text:
Inaugurée par Jacques Chirac et Helmut Kohl pour fabriquer la Smart, l’usine de Hambach en est déjà à sa deuxième vie. La troisième pourrait être chinoise, et Emmanuel Macron n’a pas attendu la fin des tractations pour s’en féliciter. « BYD travaille avec la France à une implantation industrielle en Moselle ! », a écrit le président sur X. Il y voit le fruit direct de sa politique économique et de son action européenne sur l’automobile. Rendez-vous est donné au sommet Choose France du 18 janvier pour les détails, le dernier de son mandat avant son départ de l’Élysée en mai.
Le tweet ne nomme pas le site, mais les deux industriels l’ont fait le même jour. BYD et Ineos Automotive confirment des négociations exclusives pour la cession de Hambach, sous réserve de consulter les représentants du personnel.
Ineos, qui a racheté l’ancienne « Smartville » à Mercedes fin 2020, y assemble depuis 2022 son 4×4 Grenadier. Le groupe britannique compte pourtant transférer cette production dès 2028 aux États-Unis, où il réalise 70 % de ses ventes. Comme on le détaillait dans notre article sur le rachat de l’ancienne usine Smart, Hambach deviendrait la deuxième usine européenne de BYD, après celle de Szeged en Hongrie. Ce choix d’un site existant prolonge un virage amorcé quand BYD a revu sa stratégie de production en Europe.
Votre production solaire dépasse votre consommation ? Stockez le surplus au lieu de le revendre à bas prix. Le SolarFlow 2400 AC+ se branche sur votre installation existante, 100 % plug-and-play, et s’amortit plus vite grâce au Black Friday.
    Pour aller plus loin
BYD veut racheter l’ancienne usine Smart pour fabriquer ses voitures en France
            
    Pour aller plus loin
BYD change finalement de stratégie pour produire ses voitures électriques en Europe
            
Une victoire revendiquée avant la signature
Rien n’est signé, et l’opération consiste à reprendre un site existant. Le lien de cause à effet revendiqué par Emmanuel Macron mérite aussi d’être nuancé.
Depuis fin 2024, l’Union européenne surtaxe les voitures électriques fabriquées en Chine, ce qui pousse les constructeurs chinois à produire sur place. BYD a en plus besoin de capacités, maintenant que les marques chinoises dépassent les japonaises en Europe. Au Mondial de l’Auto, en octobre, l’Élysée disait vouloir éviter les « usines tournevis », où l’on visse en Europe le dernier boulon de pièces venues de Chine. Ce virage stratégique de BYD ne vaudra donc quelque chose que si les batteries et les composants suivent.
    Pour aller plus loin
Voitures chinoises : elles dépassent désormais les marques japonaises en Europe
            
Le communiqué du constructeur reste très vague. Stella Li, vice-présidente exécutive de BYD, assure que « notre engagement envers l’Europe s’inscrit dans le long terme ».
Aucun modèle, aucune date de démarrage ni aucun engagement chiffré sur les effectifs n’ont été annoncés. Ineos indique de son côté que le Grenadier resterait assemblé à Hambach « à moyen terme », d’où une possible cohabitation de deux constructeurs sur le site.
Le contexte complet se trouve dans notre décryptage du dossier Hambach. Quant à la poussée des voitures chinoises sur le marché européen, elle explique pourquoi BYD cherche des chaînes de montage à l’intérieur de l’Union européenne.
Il y a une ironie certaine à voir l’ancienne usine de la Smart, dont la production est partie en Chine dans la coentreprise de Mercedes et Geely, accueillir à son tour un constructeur chinois. Pour les salariés de Hambach, l’essentiel est ailleurs, dans le nombre de postes que BYD gardera vraiment. On le saura peut-être le 18 janvier, à condition que l’annonce présidentielle ne précède pas une fois de plus la signature.
