articles.title: He vivido en el futuro de la IA para todos gracias al MSI EdgeMesa con la RTX Spark de Nvidia y 128 GB de memoria
articles.text:
Probar el nuevo MSI EdgeMesa con la Nvidia RTX Spark ha sido como volver a los inicios de Internet en casa. Los recuerdos del módem “bipeando” tras un grito a mi madre para que dejara de hablar por teléfono y no ocupara la línea, el alto coste de cualquier conexión por corta que fuera y luego la rápida evolución a ADSL, fibra, Internet en el teléfono con coste por consumo y finalmente conexión invisible casi con cualquier dispositivo de casa. Estos sentimientos son un calco de lo que creo que va a llegar con la IA ... pero en este caso de manera explosiva.
El miniPC MSI EdgeMesa es un equipo listo para sacar de su caja y empezar a ejecutar modelos de IA en local que actualmente no caben en cualquier PC con gráfica dedicada. Hemos pasado dos semanas disfrutando de modelos de 120.000 millones de parámetros sintiendo que era como el que abre un procesador de textos cada mañana para escribir. O un navegador para contestar correos. Así de cerca he vivido en el futuro de la IA. Y os lo voy a contar.
Ficha técnica del MSI EdgeMesa N1X
|  | MSI EdgeMesa N1X | 
|---|---|
| Procesador | Nvidia RTX Spark N1X con CPU de 20 núcleos a 4 GHz TDP 140W | 
| Gráficos | Nvidia Blackwell RTX con 6.144 núcleos | 
| Memoria | 64 / 128 GB memoria unificada LPDDR5X Hasta 270 GB/s de ancho de banda | 
| Almacenamiento | Hasta 4 TB PCIe GEN5x4 NVMe | 
| puertos | 3 x USB-C 3.2 GEN 2X2 (20G) 1 x USB-C (alimentación) 1 x HDMI 2.1 Ranura Kensignton | 
| Conectividad | Wi-Fi 7 10G RTL8127-CG | 
| DImensiones y peso | 152 x 147 x 53 mm 1,32 kg | 
| Sistema operativo | Windows 11 Pro | 
| Precio | Desde 4.849 euros | 
MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ X-004DE AI Desktop NVIDIA RTX Spark Grace mit Blackwell RTX 6144 Core GPU und 64 GB RAM - 1 TB SSD Windows 11 Pro Premium
Estamos cada vez más cerca de una IA “de verdad” en el PC
Llevamos ya unos cuantos años usando equipos portátiles y de sobremesa que tiran de las siglas IA para llamar la atención. Pero todo ha sido un engaño. O al menos un trampantojo. Botones dedicados, resúmenes automáticos, transcripción, traducción ... asuntos menores para lo que las grandes compañías nos han estado poniendo como anzuelo estos dos años últimos con sus modelos frontera.
Con el MSI EdgeMesa N1x que hemos probado en Xataka, la pregunta de “IA en el ordenador, ¿y eso, para qué?” cambia de sentido. Ya no queremos una tecla dedicada ni un botón o icono en la barra o menú. Queremos algo resolutivo. Y potente. Y capaz. Y caro. Porque tener un MSI EdgeMesa con NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X sale por, mínimo, casi 5.000 euros en su versión con “solo” 64 GB de memoria unificada.
Decimos “solo” porque con la IA local, los modelos viven y mueren por la memoria. Por eso este tipo de miniPC con RTX Spark tienen ahora mismo un mercado potencial todavía enfocado en el profesional al que un desembolso de casi 5.000 euros le renta. Pero tengo claro que este tipo de equipos debe y va a ser el futuro de la IA local en el hogar junto con la propuesta que Apple y sus chips M llevan años maquinando.
El modelo que hemos analizado en Xataka disfruta de la máxima memoria a la que podemos optar ahora mismo con Nvidia Spark N1X: 128 GB. Así que no se trataba en esta prueba de ver si este bicho nos daba para abrir un documento o jugar a muchos fps. El objetivo era exprimir esta pequeña caja con modelos de 120.000 millones de parámetros, veer cuánto tardaba en responder al pasarle un libro entero en PDF, su consumo o si nuestro agente de programación favorito podía trabajar durante horas sin que el equipo acabara por derretirse. Y tenemos las respuestas a nuestras dudas.
NVIDIA RTX Spark: una forma distinta de pensar el PC
La razón de ser del MSI EdgeMesa N1x es claramente el SoC RTX Spark de NVIDIA. Tras su estreno en portátiles como el ASUS proArt P16 que analizamos recientemente, ya tenemos una gran oleada de equipos de sobremesa de estilo especialmente compacto que nos irán sonando cada vez más.
A modo de recordatorio, el RTX Spark encapsula juntos un procesador ARM de 20 núcleos y una GPU Blackwell de 6.144 núcleos. Y como lleva años haciendo Apple con sus chips M, les hace compartir una sola memoria. Esa memoria unificada de NVIDIA no tiene sentido sola. Hay todo un ecosistema que la apoya y gestiona, desde CUDA a los modelos para ejecutar de manera local y que ya vienen pensados para este tipo de equipos.
A la hora de ejecutar modelos locales de IA, usar memoria compartida tiene una consecuencia práctica que lo es todo. Imagina una tarjeta gráfica de consumo de gama alta con 32 GB de VRAM como la bestial RTX 5090 en la que queremos cargar un modelo local. Si éste no cabe, la prueba se acaba en ese mismo momento.
Con la RTX Spark, la GPU tiene una cantidad mucho mayor de memoria disponible. En nuestro caso, con 128 GB de memoria iniciada, por defecto la GPU dispone de 62 GB pero podemos gestionarla manualmente para ofrecerle hasta 96 GB. Dependerá del uso que hagamos del equipo, pero incluso en ese escenario extremo tenemos todavía 30 GB de RAM para Windows. Justo, pero suficiente.
Y todo esto es un miniPC
Cuando uno lee la ficha técnica del MSI EdgeMesa N1x, especialmente a nivel de potencia, seguramente nos vendría a la mente la imagen de un enorme sobremesa de consumo desmesurado. Nada más lejos de la realidad.
El MSI EdgeMesa es en realidad un miniPC como pocos hemos visto nunca desde hace tiempo. Diseño minimalista en metal, muy compacto, de poco peso pero con una fuente de alimentación casi tan grande como el propio sobremesa. Basta esconderla bien gracias a su generosa longitud de cable para que no desentone.
A nivel de diseño, casi todo ha sido pensado para que parezca pequeño pero sin obviar que la refrigeración es crítica. Hay elementos de disipación del calor en el frontal, la parte inferior y por supuesto la trasera. Y como ya veremos, nunca parece suficiente para cuando tenemos NVIDIA Spark a todo rendimiento.
Ser un equipo tan compacto limita por ejemplo la conectividad. Todo queda aglutinado en la parte trasera, donde además de un conector Kensington, contamos con el botón de encendido, cuatro puertos USB-C (uno ocupado ya para alimentación y tres más DisplayPort), un HDMI y un puerto Ethernet 10G. Curiosamente este puerto es el que más nos hemos alegrado de tener porque aquí, descargar decenas de GB es el día a día.
Por eso es también tan importante que la capacidad del almacenamiento interno parta de 1 TB, aunque la versión que nosotros hemos probado disfrutaba de 4 TB. Rapidísimos, por cierto, como no podía ser de otra forma.
Con estas credenciales, las pruebas habituales de rendimiento nos han dado cifras especialmente destacadas. Tanto a nivel de rendimiento de la CPU como de la GPU. Tenemos por ejemplo más de 3.400 puntos en Steel Nomad, 2.508 y 22.690 en GeekBench 7 así como 550 y 7.200 puntos en Cinebench 2026.
Poniendo a prueba el límite de los 128 GB de memoria unificada
Se vienen unos años en que, al igual que para el gran público ya no es tan misterioso el valor/rol de la memoria RAM en su ordenador o smartphone, la memoria unificada y cómo funcionan los modelos de lenguaje pasarán a formar parte de conversaciones de bar. Bueno, igual no tanto. Acuérdate de esto en la próxima cena de Navidad con tu cuñado/a.
Para ponernos en contexto y de forma general, cuando un modelo local lee el texto que le hemos proporcionado, la potencia de cálculo lo es casi todo. Sin embargo, cuando se pone a escribir la respuesta palabra a palabra, lo que manda es la memoria. Generar cada token requiere leer el modelo completo que estamos usando, es decir, el equipo debe leer todos los pesos del modelo desde la memoria donde esté cargado y llevarlo a los núcleos de cálculo. Es así de manera general, luego veremos los “trucos” a los que podemos optar.
Si nuestro modelo ocupa 16 GB y la memoria tiene una capacidad de lectura de 270 GB/s, ya tenemos el número máximo de tokens por segundo con el que vamos a poder trabajar. En nuestras pruebas, los datos teóricos del MSI con NVIDIA Spark se cumplen en los test con menos de un 10% de desviación. El verdadero cuello de botella es el ancho de banda, que en nuestro equipo es de 270 GB/s.
Para corroborarlo, pusimos a trabajar el miniPC de MSI con modelos de diferente tamaño. El de referencia para nuestros test, el Qwen3.8-27B cuantizado a 4 bits, nos ofreció una media de 16,8 tok/s, siendo el máximo teórico que podíamos conseguir de 17 tokens por segundo. Con modelos de 54 GB y con uno de 40 GB (70B) las cifras de tokens/s bajaron a 5 y 6,6 respectivamente.
Como veremos más adelante en detalle, hay “trucos” que rompen esta regla, como los modelos MoE (mezcla de expertos). En estos forks solo se activan una parte de los parámetros para cada token. Así, un modelo MoE de 120.000 millones de parámetros podría ir cuatro veces más rápido que un modelo denso de 27.000 millones. Con esta idea es con la que nos interesa jugar en el MSI EdgeMesa para sacarle todo el partido.
Pero, dado que este miniPC con NVIDIA Spark nos permite jugar con la cantidad de memoria asignada a la GPU, ¿qué ocurre si le asignamos hasta 96 GB que es lo máximo que permite NVIDIA? Pues básicamente que podemos cargar modelos más grandes, pero no hace nada más rápido.
Así hemos puesto a prueba el NVIDA Spark del MSI EdgeMesa N1X con 128 GB
Para las pruebas de rendimiento con LLM locales en el MSI EdegMesa con NVIDIA Spark con 128 GB de memoria unificada hemos seguido un procedimiento sistemático. En todos los test hemos usado llama.cpp b12503 con CUDA 13.5 y modelos verificados con SHA256 con la huella publicada.
Cada prueba la repetimos tres veces, con enfriamiento entre una y otra. Luego cogimos como datos la media de las tres. Además, nos aseguramos de que nada más estuviera usando la GPU. Por último, recogimos en cada prueba datos de temperatura y potencia de la CPU.
En lo que respecto a los tokens, medimos tres cosas a la vez: velocidad de lectura, de escritura y de tiempo hasta la primera palabra.
La primera prueba de las posibilidades de este MSI EdgeMesa la realizamos con el modelo de referencia para este equipo: Qwen3.8-27B en Q4_K_M. Con él, el equipo lee a más de 1.100 tokens/s y escribe a 16,8 tok/s. Esta velocidad de escritura es cómoda para un usuario pues le permite leer a la vez que se va produciendo ... pero para un agente es muy lenta si tiene que encadenar docenas de peticiones.
Hay que indicar que este resultado lo obtuvimos sin aplicar ningún tipo de técnica de decodificación especulativa. Más adelante veremos cómo podemos mejorar estos resultados de manera muy significativa.
Con el mismo tipo de pruebas pusimos a prueba otros modelos de diferentes características y posibilidades. Estos fueron los resultados obtenidos:
Aquí ya podemos comprobar que los modelos MoE, como adelantamos, son los ganadores en este equipo. Tenemos por ejemplo un gpt-oss-120b, con 120.000 millones de parámetros, que es capaz de escribir a 66 tok/s, cuatro veces más rápido que un 27B denso y casi diez veces más rápido que el 70B.
Esta tabla es una lectura inicial sobre este equipo de MSI y NVIDIA Spark en general: no es un miniPC para correr modelos densos enormes sino para disfrutar de la ejecución rápida de modelos grandes que deben leer poco.
Otro aporte tiene que ver con el consumo. En nuestras mediciones con diferentes modelos, el chip se mantiene la mayor parte del tiempo con un consumo de entre 40 y 55 W durante la escritura, con una temperatura que no pasa de 67 grados centígrados. Y hay detalles importantes como que el modelo que menos consume es justo el más pesado ya que al tener que leer 51 GB por palabra, la GPU no “gasta” al tener que estar esperando a la memoria.
Pero cuidado con este dato, porque no se traslada directamente a un gasto menor, ya que aunque al trabajar con este modelo se consume menos vatios por segundo, al ir más lento generando tokens, tarda mucho más tiempo en acabar la tarea y al final, supondría un gasto de energía total mayor.
Si hay tantos modelos es por algo
Basta echar un vistazo a Huggingface para darse cuenta de que si hay tal cantidad de modelos disponibles es por algo. Muchos de ellos son modificaciones a base de técnicas y atajos para mejorar su desempeño. Depende de lo que queramos hallar, así debemos buscar.
Como dijimos anteriormente, con el modelo de referencia Qwen3.8-27B la velocidad de generación de tokens en nuestros test no alcanzó los 17 tok/s. Sin embargo, si recurrimos a la especulación integrada (MTP en nuestro caso), todo mejora de manera muy sustancial.
Un ejemplo claro: Qwen3.8-27B en NVFP4, al activar la predicción multi-token con 4 borradores conseguimos que la escritura de apenas 14,4 tok/s suba hasta 27,2 tok/s. Eso es una mejora de casi el doble.
En los modelos de lenguaje el tamaño manda, y los MoE mandan más
Con el MSI EdgeMesa y su NVIDIA Spark, entender las diferencias entre modelos y sus versiones es la base para optimizar el rendimiento. Y la elección de modelos MoE es la clave con este equipo pues son los grandes ganadores de nuestras pruebas.
Otro ejemplo de configuración resultante de nuestras pruebas es la elección del Qwen3.8-Flash-Next de 87 GB. Este es un MoE enorme que cuando teníamos asignada 62 GB de memoria a la GPU no podía ni cargarse. Sin embargo, hacer el esfuerzo de darle espacio y asignar a la GPU 96 GB de la memoria compartida consigue que este modelo alcance los 37 tok/s, más del doble de lo que medimos con el 27B denso, que pesa prácticamente seis veces menos. En este caso sí que tiene todo el sentido subir el reparto de memoria.
¿Se pierde calidad al comprimir?
Dentro de nuestra batería de pruebas quisimos comprobar cómo afecta a los resultados el hecho de optar por modelos comprimidos. Sin esta técnica, no podríamos ejecutar muchos modelos que nos interesa poder usar.
Al cuantizar un modelo, reducimos su tamaño y con ello conseguimos subir la velocidad pero a coste de perder algo de calidad. ¿Pero esa pérdida de calidad al “comprimir” el modelo afecta suficiente como para dejarlos de lado?
Para salir de dudas pasamos baterías de 100 problemas del test matemático GSM8K a cada versión de los modelos que teníamos en nuestro banco de pruebas.
Mirando los resultados, comprobamos que, por ejemplo, el modelo Qwen3.8-27B en Q4, en NVFP4, en Q8 y en BF16 acierta lo mismo, un 96 %. Esto significa que la versión de 51 GB y la de 15 GB tienen la misma eficacia en sus soluciones y sin embargo con el modelo de 15 GB conseguiríamos escribir tokens hasta tres veces más rápido.
Cierto es que son solo 100 preguntas y que habrá que valorar la precisión que necesitamos para la tarea que estemos realizando en cada momento, pero la tendencia es favorable al potencial uso de este MSI EdgeMesa y la NVIDIA Spark.
El contexto largo: ahí está el verdadero límite de este MSI
Aunque la velocidad de generación de tokens es bastante similar en modelos con diferentes contextos, no ocurre lo mismo con el primer token. Esto afecta a las tareas que le pediríamos pues si en vez de pasarle como entrada un par de párrafos, le pedimos al modelo que lea un libro entero, pasaríamos de unos segundos en empezar a generar tokens a varios minutos.
Para comprobar cómo afecta el contexto a este equipo de MSI usamos de nuevo el modelo Qwen3.8-27B pero en este caso con DFlash 2, una técnica de decodificación especulativa muy eficaz.
Esta prueba nos sirvió además para aceptar que DFlash permite a los modelos locales mejorar su escritura de tokens entre 2 y 2,5 veces ... y que los contextos largos apenas le afectan.
En esta prueba pudimos además comparar los resultados con los que obtuvimos en nuestro análisis del ASUS ProArt P16 también con NVIDIA Spark aunque con solo 64 GB de memoria unificada, de la cual podían usar como máximo 48 GB para la GPU.
Con nuestro equipo, el primer token lo conseguimos más rápido en todos los casos, con una media de entre un 30 y 35% menos. Aquí juega el mayor margen de consumo que nos proporciona tener NVIDIA Spark en un equipo de sobremesa y no en un portátil.
Optar por un modelo de sobremesa como este MSI EdgeMesa tiene otra clara ventaja frente a un portátil: su posible uso como servidor para equipos. Simulamos lo que sería trabajar con varios usuarios a la vez por medio de 8 conversaciones simultáneas. El servidor llegó a 67 tok/s en conjunto, lo que significa que cada usuario pierde algo de velocidad individual al obtener sus respuestas y tarda más segundos en conseguir su primera palabra por parte del modelo. Pero son diferencias asumibles para un equipo de trabajo pequeño que quiera compartir un modelo local.
Un equipo ideal para generar sin parar imagen, vídeo y audio
Tras poner a prueba modelos de lenguaje, al MSI EngeMesa le tocaban el reto de trabajar durante horas generando imagen vídeo y audio. Para las pruebas usamos ConfyUI y diferentes flujos de trabajo automatizados para medir consumo y velocidad de generación de los diferentes tipos de contenido. Las pruebas las repetimos con diferentes modelos de referencia.
En este caso concreto, las mediciones de realizaron con la asignación de 96 GB a la GPU.
En base a los resultados de nuestras pruebas, el MSI EdgeMesa es un equipo perfectamente capaz para la generación de imágenes y audio. E incluso para vídeo siempre dependiendo del proyecto final que queramos conseguir.
Con NVIDA Spark en este miniPC conseguimos generar imágenes en tres segundos con un consumo de apenas 54W. Y para vídeo, 5 segundos de vídeo a 720p con audio con un modelo de 22.000 millones de parámetros paró el cronómetro en menos de un minuto.
Si somos de trabajar mucho con audio, por ejemplo para transcripciones, NVIDIA Spark consigue que tardemos menos de un minuto en transcribir una hora de grabación.
Además de nuestras propias pruebas, también conseguimos números con benchmarks como MLPerf Client, el cual mide FLUX.2 Klein a 41,4 imágenes por minuto, eso sí, usando su configuración propia, con otro motor y otro flujo. En nuestro caso las condiciones de la prueba las marcamos nosotros para comparar entre modelos.
Otras pruebas que realizamos fueron las de búsqueda semántica (7.758 tok/s con Qwen3-Embedding de 0,6B, 2.790 con el de 4B) y visión, en la que el modelo debía describir una imagen. Con el modelo QWEN 3.8 27B tardamos entre 4,5 y 6,3 segundos, y con Gemma 4 12B entre 3 y 4.
Un equipo que es una estupenda casa para nuestros agentes
Disponer de un sobremesa compacto y de relativo bajo consumo es una invitación a que sea usado como servidor para pequeños equipos o como puerto base de nuestro agentes. Además, este MSI EdgeCube es silencioso. Bueno, relativamente. Cuando está trabajando a máxima potencia se puede escuchar algo de ruido de fondo, pero es prácticamente irrelevante.
En cuanto al calor, basta echar un vistazo al diseño para comprobar que MSI no ha escatimado en salidas de aire, como ya mencionamos. Y sobre todo en la parte trasera, se produce calentamiento si tenemos algo colocado ahí. Hay que tenerlo en cuenta cuando pensemos dónde irá colocado ya que es importante que esa parte trasera no esté completamente pegada a paredes o similares que le impidan esa necesaria refrigeración.
Para nuestras pruebas con agentes recurrimos a un uso real de Hermes. Le pedimos que, usando el modelo local Qwen3.8-27B (importante, sin DFlash), realizara tres tareas sencillas: resumir un documento, buscar información en Internet y escribir algo de código con pruebas que debía también pasar.
La prueba la tenía que ejecutar 18 veces, 9 con la asignación de 64 GB de memoria para la GPU y otras 9 con 96 GB. Todas las tareas las completó con éxito y de media obtuvimos una velocidad de ejecución de 16 tok/s y un consumo de 57W. Importante hacer notar ya que el consumo medido se refiere exclusivamente al chip y no al equipo completo.
Como con los otros entornos de pruebas, además de nuestros test, pasamos un benchmark para tener cifras comparativas. En este caso, con MLPerf Client, la tarea de agente de programación (SWE Agent) tardó 44 segundos en completar el mismo con Llama 3.1 8B y Qwen3 8B.
Consumo, temperatura y throttling
Ya vas dándote cuenta de que este MSI EdgeMesa con NVIDIA Spark va a tener mucho sentido para trabajos donde se requiera un uso continuado de la IA local. Por eso queríamos valorar en esta review muy especialmente cómo era el consumo dependiendo de la tarea.
Cuando el Nvidia SPARK se encuentra trabajando es la escritura de tokens, el consumo del chip se mueve entre 27 y 55 W según nuestras pruebas y dependiendo del tipo de tarea y/o modelo. Cuando usamos modelos con contextos largos o que recurren a DFlash, el consumo se dispara hasta los 100W. También aumenta la temperatura que alcanza el chip, que pasa de los 67º de media con modelos “normales” a 87º.
También medimos qué ocurría con consumo y temperatura del equipo MSI con una prueba de lectura sostenida de 20 minutos y en ese caso, el consumo tuvo un pico de 113 W con una media de consumo de 107W y temperatura máxima de 88º. Lo mejor de esta prueba es que nos demostró que, incluso en la prueba más exigente en el uso de IA en local, la velocidad de generación de tokens no cae y no detectamos throttling en ningún momento.
Partiendo del hecho de que el coste de entrada de este equipo es muy alto, rozando los 5.000 euros, realizar cálculo del coste de tokens es un poco tramposo. Pero sí que nos sirve como referencia.
Si usamos una tarifa de referencia de 0,184 €/kWh podremos comparar coste con un equipo como el Mac Studio que analizamos recientemente también en el uso de IA local. Con este MSI, escribir un millón de tokens nos saldría a menos de 3 céntimos con Nemotron 30B o gpt-oss-120b, 16 céntimos con Qwen 3.8 27B en Q4 y 39 céntimos con el mismo modelo Qwen pero de 70B.
¿Y todo esto para qué? Qué modelo elegir según lo quieras hacer con el MSI
Tras toda esta retahíla de modelos, velocidad y datos de consumo que hemos volcado sobre el funcionamiento estas semanas del MSI EdgeMesa con NVIDA Spark, nos ha quedado claro que la IA local sí que empieza a tener sentido ... aunque todavía a un precio bastante alto. Pero todo se andará.
Una clave para sacar todo el partido a este miniPC con NVIDIA Spark está en la elección del modelo para la tarea o rol que queramos realizar. De ahí la ventaja de contar con un equipamiento que nos permite tener varios modelos, algunos enormes, listos para ponerse a trabajar para nosotros en cualquier momento. Y con total privacidad sobre el papel.
Según nuestras mediciones, una tabla de modelos para trabajar en el MSI EdgeMesa según la tarea sería la siguiente:
En cuanto a los perfiles candidatos para invertir en este equipo, hay un poco para todos.
Si tenemos rol principal de programador, este MSI es perfecto para tener un asistente de código y agentes que pueden estar trabajando en segundo plano realizando tareas de tests, migraciones, refactorizaciones ... todo ello sin pagar un solo euro por token más allá del que hemos visto por consumo y con la ventaja de que, como servidor compartido de IA local, podemos trabajar varios compañeros a la vez. Misma idea podemos coger para equipos de marketing.
La privacidad que nos otorga el uso de la IA en local es imprescindible para otros ámbitos donde la IA tiene sentido. Educación (mi campo), investigación o pequeñas empresas/autónomos asociadas a campos de la salud o lo legal que trabajen con datos confidenciales (contratos, informes médicos, procedimientos, presupuestos ...) tienen en NVIDIA Spark un aliado de precio inimaginable ahora mismo.
Un ámbito en el que le vemos ventajas a NVIDIA Spark pero no la solución completa es el del diseño y creatividad. Aquí tenemos buenas cifras de generación de imágenes y vídeo pero con más sentido para explorar ideas, probar cosas o realizar bocetos que para una producción seria.
En todos estos casos lógicamente hay que tener claro que estos modelos ejecutados en local no igualan en tareas largas o razonamiento a los modelos de frontera que día sí y día también nos hacen relamernos de sus posibilidades. Pero equipos con NVIDIA Spark nos dejan libre la vía híbrida para ejecutar en local lo que necesita privacidad, continuidad y trabajo masivo, y la nube para lo realmente difícil que requiere del último modelo de OpenAI, Google o Antrophic.
MSI EdgeMesa N1x N AI+, la opinión de Xataka
Que levante la mano quien, ya sea por trabajo o puro ocio, no se ha quedado compuesto y sin novio/a cuando el límite de cinco horas o semanal se le ha acabado usando modelos frontera de las grandes compañías. Y quizás solo estabamos creando un vídeo o imagen chorra o el enésimo proyecto personal “ahora que puedo o sé hacerlo”. Pues imagina esa sensación para profesionales que literalmente engullen tokens.
El mini PC MSI EdgeMesa con NVIDIA Spark llega para ofrecer una solución lista para usar y optimizada para muchos modelos gracias al músculo de un gigante. Al consumidor nos puede parecer que el precio de partida es alto pero para cierto perfil no creo que lo sea tanto.
NVIDIA Spark encaja perfectamente en este tipo de equipos que ya no deben ser enormes ni consumir recursos como loco ni tampoco consumir en exceso. Basta encender, poner a nuestro agente a configurar todo y descargar modelos y estaremos listos para, con modelos MoE de hasta 120.000 millones de parámetros, trabajar a un ritmo de 66 tokens por segundo. Sin apenas coste energético.
Tomar la decisión adecuada respecto a la cantidad de memoria unificada no lo es tanto para determinados modelos y tareas como lo puede ser el ancho de banda, único limitante de este equipo. Frente a equipos con gráficas dedicadas o los equipos más potentes de Apple, los 270 GB/s de quedan cortos si no priorizamos tareas de largo recorrido y continuas.

articles.title: Xbox Helix started as a PC in disguise, with free multiplayer and Steam, until plans changed
articles.text:
What we know so far: Microsoft has confirmed that the next Xbox, codenamed Helix, will support PC games, but the extent of that support remains unclear. Current messaging indicates a console-first experience, but rumors suggest the project initially leaned in a much more PC-centric direction. It remains uncertain how much Microsoft's current roadmap resembles that original plan.
Sources tell Windows Central that, before Asha Sharma became Xbox CEO earlier this year, Microsoft planned for its next console to essentially be a PC with an Xbox-style UI and support for Xbox console games. This would have required the company to drop its online multiplayer paywall.
As prior rumors suggested, the Asus ROG Xbox Ally was a rough draft of the experience the Xbox division intended for its next console while under Phil Spencer. The next Xbox would have run on Windows and booted into Microsoft's new Xbox Mode by default, but users could exit to the traditional desktop and install any Windows app, including Steam.
Microsoft's official messaging remains vague but implies the opposite approach while retaining some PC compatibility. The company recently described its next console, now codenamed Helix, as a console that plays PC games, not a PC that plays console games.
The device will feature a new interface that provides immediate access to games but also supports greater customization for advanced users and eliminates traditional barriers. However, it remains unclear what this means and how much Microsoft's plans have changed since Sharma replaced Spencer in February.
Xbox's new CEO aims to make the division more profitable, which could be difficult if Helix supports Steam and doesn't require an online multiplayer subscription. Steam's market share eclipses that of the Microsoft Store, and Valve's service is almost synonymous with PC gaming, so including access to it could mean forfeiting revenue from game sales. On the other hand, Microsoft's confirmation that Helix will play PC games means little in the practical terms without Steam.
The most concrete rumors regarding Helix concern its hardware. It reportedly includes a custom APU with 10 Zen 6 CPU cores, 20 threads, and a 40-TFLOP RDNA 5 GPU. It's far too early to predict pricing because storage and RAM costs have been chaotic for the past year, but an MSRP well over $1,000 is a real possibility.
Microsoft confirmed that developers will receive Helix alpha development kits next year, suggesting the console could hit store shelves in late 2027 or sometime in 2028.

articles.title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
articles.text:
This artist's illustration shows one take on what Homo erectus might have looked like in its rainforest home near Baxian Cave, Guangxi, China.
Credit:
Garciart/Joannes-Boyau
This artist's illustration shows one take on what Homo erectus might have looked like in its rainforest home near Baxian Cave, Guangxi, China.
Credit:
Garciart/Joannes-Boyau
Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China’s Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that’s vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.
The chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.
A handful of teeth with a lot to say
Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.
Proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA, so they’re more likely to survive a few hundred thousand years. But like DNA, proteins contain variations that can help identify the species they came from. Four of the five teeth in the study had distinctly Homo erectus proteins in their enamel; the fifth seems to be some other hominin species, most likely a Denisovan (more on that below).
The hominin teeth and the thousands of animal bone fragments had accumulated in a cement-like rock called breccia. Based on luminescence dating (a method that measures how long it’s been since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight) of the cave sediments, along with the ratios of uranium isotopes in the bones themselves, it looks like that breccia formed sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. That’s a wide range, but it’s enough to show that Homo erectus lived in what’s now southern China at least 60,000 years longer than we’ve previously realized.
Homo erectus emerged in Africa sometime before 2 million years ago, and they had reached East and Southeast Asia—including the islands of Indonesia—by around 1.7 million years ago. The most recent Homo erectus fossils anywhere else in mainland Asia date to somewhere between 420,000 and 400,000 years ago. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java, however, reveal that Homo erectus held on in the islands up until at least 177,000 to 108,000 years ago. That makes it a little surprising that nobody had found traces of Homo erectus on the mainland during that 200,000- to 300,000-year gap.
These nine teeth help fill in some of that gap, showing that Homo erectus was still around on the mainland all that time after all. On its own, that would be nontrivial, but the teeth also shed light on how these long-dead hominins lived, what the world around them looked like, and how this handful of hominins was related to the rest of their species. And it turns out we’ve been drastically underestimating Homo erectus.
Credit:
Kira Westaway, Macquarie University
Credit:
Kira Westaway, Macquarie University
Homo erectus and Denisovans were neighbors
Four of the five teeth that Welker and his colleagues sequenced proteins from clearly belonged to Homo erectus. Careful measurements of the other four—things like the shape and dimensions of the crown, the roots, and the place where the outer layer of enamel meets the inner layer of dentine—suggest these also belonged to Homo erectus.
But the ninth tooth, from Baxian, has proteins that don’t match any known Homo erectus variants, and the shape also looks decidedly un-Homo–erectus-like, “strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than Homo erectus in Baxian Cave,” wrote Welker and his colleagues in their recent paper in the journal Nature.
But who were those other hominins? The enigmatic ninth tooth looks like it belonged to a Denisovan (or Homo longi, if you prefer). But Welker and his colleagues can’t be absolutely sure, because its proteins don’t exactly match any known Denisovan sequence, either (and there’s no clearly identified Denisovan lower second molar enamel-dentine junction to compare it to). But we do know that Denisovans lived in the wider region of mainland Asia at the time, based on fossils from other sites, and there’s no evidence of any other species running around at the same time.
“It therefore seems plausible that the Homo erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian Cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins,” wrote Welker and his colleagues.
Now, to clarify, Naxian and Baxian Caves weren’t (as far as anyone knows) places where hominins actually lived. The bones and teeth there seem to have been carried in by porcupines, with the result that “why do porcupines collect bones?” is now part of your faithful correspondent’s search history [EDITOR’S NOTE: my search history now includes “there are porcupines in China?”]. So the presence of this tooth doesn’t mean that Homo erectus and Denisovans were roommates. But it does mean they were living in the same general area at around the same time; based on the territorial habits of modern porcupines, the teeth probably came from within an area of less than 100 square kilometers. So there’s a nonzero chance that Homo erectus and Denisovans might have interacted in some way, although we have no way to know what that interaction might have looked like.
Not long after this, our species showed up in the area, and we know for a fact that our species interacted, ahem, very closely with Denisovans in this part of the world. Exactly when Homo sapiens arrived is still a matter of some debate, but some fossils from southern China that may be Homo sapiens date as far back as 100,000 or 120,000 years ago, before the major out-of-Africa migration. So for a brief period of time, there may have been at least two and maybe three species of hominins living in the rainforests of what’s now southern China.
Professor Yingqi Zhang looks out the wide entrance of Baxian Cave toward the alluvial plain.
Credit:
Kira Westaway, Macquarie University
Professor Yingqi Zhang looks out the wide entrance of Baxian Cave toward the alluvial plain.
Credit:
Kira Westaway, Macquarie University
Tracing how Homo erectus populations moved around
While the enamel proteins from four of the Baxian and Naxian teeth are clearly Homo erectus, they have a slightly different version of one particular protein—one amino acid swapped for another in the sequence that makes up the protein ameloblastin. This variant is clearly different from every other Asian Homo erectus fossil with proteins that researchers have sequenced. That means they’re probably part of a different genetic population (a group of hominins that live in the same area and mostly interbred among themselves).
There are a handful of other Homo erectus fossils from elsewhere in Asia that share one amino acid substitution with these four, but the Baxian and Naxian ones have another substitution that the other four don’t have, which means that at some point, their population branched off from the others. By plotting that kind of information on what’s called a phylogenetic tree, anthropologists can begin to map out how different groups of Homo erectus are related and how they may have moved around in time and space. And what we’re learning is pretty cool.
“The phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population [at Baxian and Naxian Caves] might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans,” wrote Welker and his colleagues. That divergence happened more than 600,000 years ago. And half a millennium after that, it seems, one group of Homo erectus still living in southern Asia may have met some long-lost cousins.
This map shows the location of the study sites in China.
Credit:
Westaway et al. 2026
This map shows the location of the study sites in China.
Credit:
Westaway et al. 2026
Once again, Homo sapiens isn’t that special
Isotopes of the chemical elements carbon and oxygen in the enamel of not just the Homo erectus teeth, but teeth from several animal species like elephants (both the pygmy Stegodon and the full-size version), rhinos, apes, and relatives of modern cattle, strongly point to the area around Baxian and Naxian Caves having been a densely canopied tropical rainforest during the Middle Pleistocene.
Different types of plants use slightly different chemical processes to do photosynthesis, so they end up with different amounts of the isotopes carbon-12 and carbon-13; the ratios of those isotopes in the teeth of whatever ate the plants (in this case, pygmy elephants and Homo erectus, among others) can reveal the makeup of the local environment. At Baxian and Naxian Caves, those ratios point to a forest where the trees’ upper branches form a thick, closed canopy above the forest floor. Westaway and her colleagues say the signals look very similar to rainforests in the Amazon Basin today.
Meanwhile, the ratio of two oxygen isotopes, oxygen-18 and oxygen-16, can shed light on ancient climate conditions; higher amounts of oxygen-18, like the ones in all five teeth from Baxian and Naxian Caves, tend to signal warmer, wetter climates. All of those clues together point to tropical rainforest, a challenging environment that most anthropologists had previously assumed that only Homo sapiens were clever and adaptable enough to make a living in.
That idea, that we were the only hominins capable of making a go of it in tropical rainforests, was so entrenched that it has been considered a possible explanation for the lack of Homo erectus fossils in southern Asia after about 400,000 years ago. Around this time, the climate became warmer and wetter, allowing dense, closed-canopy tropical rainforests to spread.
“In southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of […] expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-Homo sapiens hominin taxa, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savanna-woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues.
Even on Java, where Homo erectus lasted until almost 100,000 years ago, those last groups seem to have lived in small patches of more open woodlands, while rainforests spread across the rest of the islands—another correlation that gives anthropologists reason to think the spread of rainforests may have had a hand in the extinction of Homo erectus.
However, the evidence from Baxian and Naxian Caves suggests Homo erectus could survive in the rainforest, “even if such habitats did not represent its primary ecological niche,” as Westaway and her colleagues put it. That doesn’t mean that every group of Homo erectus was as successful at adapting to spreading rainforests—it’s safe to assume there were cultural and social differences among the groups that might have made some more adaptable than others. But it does mean that we’ve been drastically underestimating our late cousins, and we may need to rethink what we’ve assumed were the limits of their world.
An image of the entrance to Naxian Cave revealing a small opening that stretches back ~50 m to a fossil chamber.
Credit:
Kira Westaway, Macquarie University
An image of the entrance to Naxian Cave revealing a small opening that stretches back ~50 m to a fossil chamber.
Credit:
Kira Westaway, Macquarie University
Well-traveled little hominins
Other evidence in the enamel of the Baxian and Naxian Caves teeth underscores that point, revealing that a few of these Homo erectus individuals spent their childhoods as much as 250 kilometers away from the cave where their teeth ended up. Bedrock in different places has different ratios of the isotopes strontium-87 and strontium-86; plants take up dissolved strontium through their roots, and eventually it replaces some of the calcium in the bones (or tooth enamel) of the animals that eat the plants. So the ratio of strontium isotopes in your bones can be traced to the area of bedrock where your food was grown during the final years of your life, while the ratio in your tooth enamel is a souvenir of the bedrock where your food was grown when you were around 2 to 6 years old and forming your adult teeth. (Modern food systems are going to be a massive headache for future archaeologists.)
All four Homo erectus teeth that Westaway and her colleagues studied suggested that their erstwhile owners had either moved around between different areas or ate food gathered from different areas when they were very young. Some of those strontium ratios match bedrock as far away as northern Vietnam, about 250 kilometers away from Baxian and Naxian Caves, mostly through closed-canopy rainforest.
In other words, a handful of teeth offer enough fragments of a story to show us “that Homo erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments and that long-distance mobility into those environments may have been a common behavioral pattern rather than exceptional behavior by isolated individuals,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues. “Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question.”

articles.title: Canada’s Scott Pilgrim is coming to Fortnite
articles.text:
Fortnite just got a little more Canadian.
Developer Epic Games has announced that skins based on Scott Pilgrim and Ramona Flowers are coming to its popular battle royale game sometime this week.
In a short trailer, we can see the Toronto couple in creator Bryan Lee O’Malley’s signature comic book style. Scott sports his jacket, star t-shirt, guitar and flaming sword, while Ramona has her punk outfit and hammer. Naturally, the trailer also riffs on Scott Pilgrim‘s fighting game-style battles with the evil exes and Envy Adams music.
Epic Games didn’t confirm the V-Bucks cost for Scott and Ramona or what else, if anything, this collab might include. In the meantime, though, O’Malley shared fun new artwork of the pair dropping from the Fortnite Battle Bus.
It’s been a good year for everyone’s favourite sword-wielding Torontonian. In March, Montreal-based Tribute Games released Scott Pilgrim EX, a brand-new beat ’em up featuring an original story by O’Malley.
Image credit: Epic Games

articles.title: Bcomp secures €20 million from EIB to scale flax fibre-based alternatives to carbon fibre, glass fibre and plastics
articles.text:
Bcomp, a Fribourg-based CleanTech startup specialising in high-performance bio-based materials, has secured €20 million from the European Investment Bank (EIB) to build a high-volume manufacturing plant in the Romanian city of Timișoara and continue research and development in Fribourg.
This EIB backing takes the form of €20 million in venture debt, supporting the company’s €47.6 million investment programme to expand manufacturing capacity in Romania and further develop its R&D activities in Switzerland. In April 2024, the company closed a €37.6 million Series C investment funding round led by EGS Beteiligungen AG (EGSB), and in April 2022, it closed its oversubscribed Series B financing round of €31.69 million (CHF 32.4 million/USD 35 million).
“Europe needs to turn technological innovation into industrial production if we are to strengthen our competitiveness and accelerate the green transition. By supporting Bcomp in Romania and Switzerland, we are helping European innovation reach industrial scale and unlock new opportunities for sustainable growth,” said EIB Vice-President Ioannis Tsakiris.
Founded in 2011 by Christian Fischer and Julien Rion, Bcomp develops composite materials based primarily on flax fibres instead of conventional carbon fibre, glass fibre and plastics. The company says its materials, which have a significantly lower environmental footprint, are designed for use in a range of industries, including automotive, motorsport, and recreational equipment.
Its proprietary natural fibre-based reinforcement materials — ampliTex and powerRibs — help decarbonise manufacturing and reduce environmental impacts while enabling lightweight performance, extensive design freedom and plug-and-play integration into existing processes in a wide range of high-performance applications.
“Scaling up our natural fibre composites production is an important step towards making these materials available to more manufacturers and applications, while supporting the EU’s transition towards a circular economy. The EIB’s support will allow us to expand production and continue investing in R&D, strengthening our ability to serve industrial customers and accelerating the adoption of our high-performance natural fibre materials,” said Christian Fischer, Bcomp’s Chief Executive Officer.
Its main manufacturing and development facilities are located in Fribourg, and it plans to carry out its investment project between 2027 and 2030. As a result, the company expects to significantly expand its workforce through 2030, with the Timișoara plant in Romania’s western region of Vest representing a key driver of future employment growth. Around 61% of Bcomp’s planned investment will take place in Vest, supporting regional development and economic cohesion in the European Union.
Bcomp says its production facility in Timișoara is on track to launch in 2027 and will meet growing global demand for its sustainable composite technologies.
The new production facility will significantly increase the company’s production of roving, the foundational yarn used to weave ampliTex. By increasing in-house roving supply, Bcomp highlights that it will have greater control over quality and a more resilient, near-shored supply chain. The production line itself will base production on its existing Fribourg site.
Sergiu Ureniuc, Plant Manager at Bcomp, concluded, “Preparations are already underway to have Timișoara operational by mid-2027 and we are working closely with the experts in Fribourg. Soon, we will be producing in Romania the ampliTex™ roving from European flax, building upon the innovations and lessons learned at Bcomp’s first production site, in Switzerland. There is growing momentum and energy within the local team as we prepare to commission equipment and hit the ground running.”

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
articles.text:
A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, including T-Mobile, Cisco, and Motorola.
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
The Chinese telecom giant was also found guilty of bank fraud.
The Department of Justice’s 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the arrest of the company’s CFO, Wanzhou Meng, whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the indictment against Meng was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei’s operations in Iran as part of a deferred prosecution agreement. The US government blacklisted Huawei in 2019 over national security concerns.
In total, the jury found Huawei guilty of 10 of 12 criminal counts, including money laundering, violating US sanctions, bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the US. The company was acquitted of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Huawei’s sentencing is set for September 14th, 2027, where it may face “financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution,” according to the DOJ.
“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” Tysen A. Duva, the assistant attorney general of the DOJ’s criminal division, says in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”
In a statement to NBC News, a Huawei spokesperson said the charges are “without legal or factual merit” and that it plans to appeal the decision. Huawei didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
Update, November 24th: Added information from the DOJ.

articles.title: Hope Is Not A Strategy: What First-Silicon Success Really Takes
articles.text:
Most re-spins are caused by logic and functional flaws, not hard-to-predict physical effects.
Only about one chip in twenty now works the first time it comes back from the fab. For an industry that invests years and millions in every tape-out, that is a disconcerting thought.
It was also the starting point for a recent episode of ‘Wearing Flip Flops’, where host Ronen sat down with Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari. The conversation traveled from AI silicon and power bugs to the place of formal engineers in a verification team. But one idea ran through all of it: Hope is not a strategy. Determinism is.
Here is what that idea means in practice and why we believe it matters more today than ever.
The latest Wilson Research Group functional verification study puts first-silicon success at around 5%, down from 14% in 2024. At Axiomise, that number doesn’t surprise us.
Look at who is building chips. Two years ago, the survey was shaped by a wave of new RISC-V teams, where design was moving faster than verification could follow. Today it is the turn of custom AI silicon, built not only for hyperscalers but for phones and cars too. For verification, this is an unknown territory.
Formal is in more projects than ever, perhaps 30 to 40% of them. But “using formal” can mean very different things. It might be a lint or connectivity app, assertions that only ever run in simulation, or formal trusted to sign off functional verification. Only the last really improves the chances of success at tape-out.
By our estimate, fewer than a dozen of the world’s 200-plus silicon houses use formal as a sign-off criterion today. The appetite is growing fast: at DVCon US this year, NVIDIA’s VP of graphics predicted that formal will eventually replace simulation. Yet the journey has barely begun.
That 5% is the latest point in a long slide. For years, roughly three projects in ten got silicon right first time. The figure fell to 24% in 2022 and to 14% in 2024, which Harry Foster of Siemens EDA called the lowest point in more than twenty years of tracking. In 2026 it reached 5%, while around three in four projects are still missing their original schedules.
Every one of those failures means a re-spin: fixing the design and manufacturing the chip again. At 3nm, a mask set alone costs tens of millions of dollars, and a single re-spin at an advanced node can wipe out an entire product cycle. Half of all projects need more than one re-spin, and some large chipmakers now plan for as many as four.
The data also shows where the trouble starts. Logic and functional flaws remain the most common reason chips fail and around 70% of re-spins trace back to design errors caused by changing specifications. In other words, most re-spins are not caused by hard-to-predict physical effects. They are functional bugs that verification should have caught and that exhaustive methods such as formal are designed to find.
Back in the days of the 386 and the Pentium, life was simpler. A processor was built to run a known version of Windows, and everyone understood the scope of the job. Today, an AI chip must run models from OpenAI, Anthropic and many others, and those models change far faster than any hardware schedule.
The hardware has changed too. Many AI chips grew out of GPUs, which were originally designed for graphics, so older graphics hardware now sits alongside new AI-specific units. To squeeze out more speed, designers add layer upon layer of coherency, the mechanisms that keep every part of the chip working with the same up-to-date data: one coherent NoC, then another, then coherency across whole clusters. Every layer creates interactions that never existed before, and many are never reached in simulation.
Power adds its own surprises. One story from the episode stays with us: a GPU on a test chip that refused to start. The failure showed up at system, FPGA and OS level, but the root cause was an X value read from an uninitialized FIFO, left behind by a low-power optimization. A tiny functional bug had brought down the whole chip.
Clock gating tells a similar tale. On paper, proving that a gated design behaves exactly like its ungated twin is a well-defined problem, and one that formal sequential equivalence checking is built to solve. In practice, the constraints come from firmware and software, and on large designs they are hard to capture. So, clock-gating checks tend to land at the very end of sign-off, just when there is least time to deal with what they find. The answer is not a different tool, but bringing formal in earlier, with the firmware and software teams at the table.
The people behind the study are reaching a similar conclusion. Harry Foster argues that verification has succeeded for decades by splitting the problem into specialist domains and that the next challenge is interaction complexity: parts that work perfectly alone but fail together across hardware, firmware, power, safety and security.
At Axiomise, this is the problem we work on every day. Simulation samples behavior: it checks the scenarios someone thought to write. Interaction bugs live in the scenarios nobody thought of, such as an interrupt, a power transition and a coherency request arriving in just the wrong order. Formal starts from every possible input sequence and asks whether any of them can break the design. That is why we built our apps around the places where interactions hide: nocProve for networks-on-chip, formalISA for processors, floatrix for floating-point units and footprint for redundant logic.
None of this replaces simulation. It means using each method where it is strongest. Formal excels at concurrent, control-heavy logic such as NoCs, coherency, arbiters and FIFOs. Simulation and emulation remain essential for software, performance and end-to-end system behavior. Our role is to help teams combine them in the right measures, at the right time, for the right reason and to prove, with mutation and scenario coverage, that the formal part has truly done its job.
Formal has a measurement problem. With equivalence checking, the answer is clear: the proof converged, synthesis broke nothing, job done. Functional formal is less tidy. Some proofs are bounded rather than exhaustive, and any VP of silicon will reasonably ask: “If you haven’t got the proofs, what have you got?”
At Axiomise, we answer that question by measuring formal in six dimensions. Alongside the familiar counts of assertions written, passed and failed, and the coverage figures EDA tools already provide, two measures do the heavy lifting.
Mutation means planting bugs on purpose and showing that the checkers and constraints catch each one. If they don’t, you have found a gap before the silicon does.
Scenario coverage means proving that each scenario in the verification plan can happen and always happens. Instead of claiming “every RISC-V instruction works”, a team can show that debug was checked against interrupts, that loads and stores complete under every dependency, and that each result traces back to a requirement. We built this approach into formalISA, our RISC-V app, and it gives designers, verification engineers and managers something rare: a shared language.
Tying results to requirements matters more than ever. If around 70% of re-spins begin with a changing specification, verification that isn’t linked to requirements can quietly end up checking the wrong thing. With scenario coverage, a changed requirement points straight to the scenarios and proofs that need revisiting.
That matters, because today’s leaders receive formal numbers and simulation numbers that cannot easily be compared. Without a way to bring them together, the tape-out decision becomes “let’s try it and see.” And that is how you arrive at a 5% success rate.
The big three EDA vendors build excellent tools for linting, X-propagation, CDC and connectivity checking. These apps tend to sit at either end of a project. Axiomise works in the space between, using formal for full functional verification, safety and security.
Our apps run on the axiomiser platform and work together: nocProve for complete NoC grids, floatrix for floating-point units, formalISA for RISC-V processors and footprint for redundancy and power. Their strongest results come from designs that were already considered verified, where they still find bugs others missed.
A security core, and a fix that broke something else. cheriot-ibex, Microsoft’s CHERI-extended RISC-V core, had already been verified with both simulation and formal. Within days of integrating it with formalISA in 2024, a standard RTYPE check failed in JasperGold in 20 seconds. An illegal CHERI load was never squashed: it went out to memory and the data it brought back corrupted the AND instruction behind it, putting stores, and therefore memory, at risk too. The designers pointed us to a fix. On re-running, the load bug was gone, but bit-manipulation proofs that had previously passed now failed. A fix in one corner had opened a hole in another, exactly the kind of interaction that formal is built to catch.
A vector FPU in ninety minutes. On the Tenstorrent Ocelot core, floatrix was surfacing bugs within an hour and a half of cloning the repository, on a design that had already been extensively tested.
Late, but not too late. For Akeana, our team ran footprint before tape-out, covering unexpected scenarios. Redundancy is the bug nobody looks for. In one AI design, a control bug meant that each 512-deep FIFO in a chain only ever used a single location. Reachability analysis reported 99.998%, every flop toggled, and standard coverage saw nothing wrong. Yet the chip was burning area and power on storage it never touched. It is like renting an entire hotel for a single guest.
LLMs can now produce SystemVerilog assertions, constraints and even whole testbenches. That is a genuine productivity boost, and we use AI agents in-house at Axiomise. But walk the floor at DAC this year and one question came up again and again among experienced designers: how do we know we can trust it?
AI-generated checks still need auditing. Even when they produce proofs, someone has to confirm that every corner case was actually expressed. In inexperienced hands, AI can even slow a team down, because every line needs a human review.
This is where determinism earns its place. On every engagement, we build a full mutation coverage plan. Customers can plant bugs themselves without telling us, or hand us a plan to script into the environment, while we inject our own mutations independently to avoid shared blind spots. When every planted bug is caught, you have evidence rather than hope. Our rule is simple: if we can’t show that every bug that could be planted is caught, we won’t put our name to the result.
In many companies, “DV” still quietly means simulation, and formal engineers are called in late, as rescuers rather than partners. We would like to see a different picture: formal and simulation engineers sitting at the same table as architects, designers, and firmware and software teams, from the moment the specification is written.
For teams planning their next tape-out, that starts with a few practical shifts:
- Bring formal in at the planning stage, not only at the end.
- Agree what “formal” means on your project, from apps to full functional sign-off.
- Measure the quality of formal with mutation and scenario coverage, not proofs alone.
- Tie every result back to requirements, so formal and simulation can live in one plan.
- Treat AI-generated verification as a first draft and prove that it really catches bugs.
One chip in twenty is not a law of nature. It is the result of choices, and better ones are available. Hope is not a strategy. Determinism is.
Listen to the full conversation between Ashish and Ronen on ‘Wearing Flip Flops’.
Curious what formal could find in your design? Get in touch with the Axiomise team.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Meta brings its Muse AI assistant directly into Instagram DMs
articles.text:
Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday. The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.
The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.
Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.
Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.
Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.
Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.
Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.
Meta says that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram. Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

articles.title: De los juegos a la TV: Deborah Ann Woll repetirá como Faye en la serie de ‘God of War’
articles.text:
La serie de God of War ha confirmado a un nuevo fichaje de primer nivel. Se trata de Deborah Ann Woll, quien interpretará a Faye en la adaptación que Amazon MGM Studios prepara para la plataforma Prime Video. De esta manera, la actriz regresará al papel que ya interpretó en los videojuegos.
Deborah Ann Woll dio vida a Faye por primera vez en God of War Ragnarok (2022), prestando su voz como guía de Kratos y Atreus en su aventura. Muy pronto, tendrá la oportunidad de liderar su primera aventura en solitario de la mano de God of War Laufey, que llegará en 2027. Dicho juego no solo utilizará la voz de la intérprete, sino también su apariencia.
Todavía no se sabe cuánto peso en pantalla tendrá Deborah Ann Woll en la adaptación televisiva de God of War, pero Faye es un personaje crucial en la historia. Tengamos en cuenta que la serie se basa en el juego de 2018, que se inicia con el fallecimiento de la esposa de Kratos y madre de Atreus. Esto llevará a que los protagonistas pongan en marcha un largo peregrinar para arrojar sus cenizas en el pico más alto de los nueve reinos.
"God of War sigue a Kratos y a su hijo Atreus mientras emprenden un viaje para esparcir las cenizas de Faye, esposa de uno y madre del otro. A lo largo de sus aventuras, Kratos intenta enseñar a su hijo a ser un mejor dios, mientras que Atreus trata de enseñarle a su padre cómo ser un mejor ser humano", indica la sinopsis oficial de la serie de Prime Video.
Deborah Ann Woll será Faye en la serie de God of War
Respecto del personaje de Faye en la serie, Amazon indica lo siguiente: "El repentino fallecimiento de Faye, la misteriosa difunta esposa de Kratos y madre de Atreus, pone en marcha los acontecimientos de God of War. A lo largo de su viaje, Kratos y Atreus descubren secretos sobre Faye que les llevan a preguntarse hasta qué punto la conocían realmente".
El personaje de Faye aparecerá por primera vez en un rol protagónico en God of War Laufey, que se lanzará en PS5 el 20 de mayo del próximo año. Según se pudo ver en el primer gameplay del juego, la esposa de Kratos y madre de Atreus despierta en el Everywhen, la otra vida de los dioses, tras su fallecimiento. A partir de allí, debe combatir contra dioses y otras criaturas mitológicas en un escenario con peligros permanentes.
Deborah Ann Woll se suma a un elenco de God of War con varios nombres importantes. Recordemos que el rol de Kratos ha quedado en manos de Dave Bautista, quien reemplazó a Ryan Hurst tras una grave lesión. El papel de Atreus está en manos de Callum Vinson, mientras que otros nombres confirmados son Mandy Patinkin (Odín), Ed Skrein (Baldur), Max Parker (Heimdall), Ólafur Darri Ólafsson (Thor) y Teresa Palmer (Sif), por citar solo algunos.
La serie live-action de God of War todavía no tiene fecha de estreno en Prime Video. No obstante, su showrunner ha confirmado que tendrá al menos dos temporadas en la plataforma de streaming.

articles.title: GTA 6 ha sido el mayor lanzamiento en la historia de PlayStation: tuvo más de 39 millones de jugadores
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) alcanzó más de 39 millones de jugadores únicos en PlayStation 5 durante sus primeros días y se convirtió en el mayor lanzamiento en la historia de la marca, según informó Sony. La cifra corresponde a personas que jugaron el título en la consola, no a unidades vendidas, y forma parte de los datos internos recopilados entre el 19 y el 22 de noviembre de 2026.
La compañía también confirmó que GTA 6 estableció un nuevo récord de jugadores simultáneos para un videojuego en PlayStation. El registro superó las marcas previas de títulos multijugador, gratuitos y para un solo jugador. Sony no precisó cuántos usuarios estuvieron conectados al mismo tiempo.
GTA 6 acumuló 683 millones de horas de juego
En el mismo periodo, los jugadores de PS5 sumaron 683 millones de horas dentro del juego. De acuerdo con Sony, cada usuario dedicó un promedio de 17,4 horas a explorar Leónida durante los primeros días. La cifra da cuenta del tiempo total de juego registrado en la consola y no incluye una medición publicada para Xbox Series X|S.
El dato de los 39 millones también se refiere exclusivamente a jugadores únicos en PS5. Por eso, no debe interpretarse como el total de personas que jugaron en todas las plataformas ni como una cifra de ventas. PlayStation presentó el resultado como un récord para la historia de sus consolas, que abarca cinco generaciones y tres décadas.
La compañía atribuyó el logro a la comunidad que se sumó al lanzamiento, tanto a quienes siguen la saga desde hace años como a quienes probaron por primera vez un título de Grand Theft Auto. En su mensaje de agradecimiento, Sony destacó la recepción del juego y el trabajo de Rockstar Games.
El lanzamiento impulsó nuevas conexiones de PS5
El estreno también coincidió con otro hito para la consola. PlayStation registró el mayor número de PS5 conectadas por primera vez en un solo día desde el lanzamiento del sistema, fuera del periodo de las fiestas de fin de año. La marca no divulgó cuántas consolas se activaron.
Además, Sony indicó que GTA 6 fue el primer juego utilizado en el 70 % de las nuevas PS5 conectadas durante ese periodo. El dato sugiere que el título tuvo un papel importante en la actividad de las consolas recién estrenadas, aunque el comunicado no especifica cuántas de ellas fueron compradas expresamente para jugarlo.
El resultado llega tras una larga espera por la nueva entrega de la franquicia, que conduce a los jugadores por el estado ficticio de Leónida y por Vice City. La historia sigue a Jason y Lucía, protagonistas de una trama criminal ambientada en un mundo abierto. Su lanzamiento en PlayStation 5 y Xbox Series X|S movilizó a jugadores de distintas generaciones.
Qué significan las cifras de PlayStation
Las estadísticas divulgadas por Sony describen la actividad dentro de su ecosistema durante la ventana inicial del lanzamiento. No permiten calcular las ventas totales de GTA 6 ni comparar el número de jugadores entre PlayStation y Xbox, pues la empresa no compartió datos equivalentes para la consola de Microsoft.
También conviene distinguir entre jugadores únicos y usuarios simultáneos. Los primeros son las cuentas o personas que accedieron al juego en el periodo informado; los segundos corresponden a quienes estuvieron jugando al mismo tiempo. Sony afirmó que el título rompió el récord de concurrencia en PlayStation, pero no reveló el máximo alcanzado.
Con estas cifras, GTA 6 ya dejó una marca inédita para PlayStation en sus primeros días. La compañía señaló que los datos se basan en registros internos recopilados del 19 al 22 de noviembre de 2026, por lo que el balance cubre el lanzamiento y su fin de semana inicial, no el desempeño posterior del juego.

articles.title: 'Save manually all the time if you don't want this to happen to you': gamers have been frustrated by GTA 6's buggy autosaves — but the first update just arrived with a fix
articles.text:
GTA 6's first update delivers 3 key fixes for PS5 and Xbox gamers — cures autosave and mission-failing woes, and makes dynamic weather actually work
Don't trust the game's autosave? These issues should hopefully be a thing of the past
- Rockstar has released the first update for GTA 6
- It fixes a nasty bug whereby autosaves have been failing or vanishing, leaving players with many lost hours of gameplay
- There's also a remedy for mission-blocking bugs where phone calls fail to trigger, and dynamic weather is fixed
GTA 6 hasn't been out for long, but the first update for the game is now here for PS5 and Xbox gamers.
It's a relatively small patch from Rockstar, but within the release notes there are some critical fixes that a lot of gamers will be pleased to see. Something that's badly needed is a remedy for autosaves going awry, and Rockstar has implemented that — as well as fixes for bugs that derail missions, alongside a cure for the dynamic weather failing to be, well, dynamic.
I'll go over these three key fixes first, then round up what else has been applied by Rockstar to make GTA 6 a more enjoyable experience.
1. Fixed autosaves failing or disappearing
There has been quite a lot of vocal complaining about autosaves failing to work with GTA 6. This generally involves gamers playing for a few hours — or a lot of hours in some cases — and quitting, or having their PS5 shut off (maybe due to a power cut), then getting back into the game to find that an autosave has vanished.
Here's a typical post from Reddit: "Had a power outage, but before the outage I recently checked the autosave and it saved my game. When I booted up the PS5 after the outage, the autosaved file is gone, whole day worth of progress lost."
There are lots of similar stories, and in a post entitled 'Autosave didn't work and I've lost 5 hours of progress', another Redditor explains: "I thought autosave was working after completing missions and stuff. Nope. Save manually all the time if you don't want this to happen to you."
In this new update, Rockstar assures us: "Fixed an issue that resulted in the game not autosaving correctly."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Hopefully that has rectified the situation with autosaves either not working at all, or appearing to work, and then the save file seemingly vanishing the next time you boot up GTA 6. Unless there are multiple issues at play here — let's hope not, because saves are not an area of a game that you want to be particularly buggy.
Regardless, I'd be wary of relying on autosave too much anyway. I'm playing GTA 6 myself, and I'd always advise manually saving fairly often — and rotate those save spots, too (meaning don't just save in one slot, just in case a manual save ends up corrupted somehow).
2. Fixed mission-blocking bugs
There are some bugs that mean that during a mission, you fail to receive a necessary phone call that you need to progress the plot.
These are pretty aggravating glitches in general, especially in the case where you don't realize that a call is supposed to have come through, and you end up wondering what to do, searching online to find out where you went wrong, only to discover it wasn't your fault and the mission has just fallen over due to a bug.
Rockstar tells us: "Fixed several issues that resulted in phone calls not triggering correctly, including those that progressed the story or unlocked mission content."
Obviously, missing incidental phone calls scripted for color and background isn't really a big deal, but a story- or mission-blocking bug is very bad news — and hopefully these worst offenders have now been stamped out.
3. Fixed dynamic weather
While the above two problems represent bugs that may prove irritating or even infuriating, the lack of dynamic weather isn't quite such an issue — indeed, you may not even think about it or notice that the sun has remained shining for quite some time.
Nevertheless, it's a known bug in GTA 6 that the changing weather Vice City is supposed to experience isn't switching up dynamically as it should.
In the patch notes, Rockstar says: "Fixed an issue that resulted in the weather not changing for extended periods."
So, if you've lacked a little rain in your GTA 6 adventures, that should no longer be the case. That said, based on early reports from Reddit, some folks are getting more varied weather, but others are still saying it's mostly sunny all the time. Some of that may depend on how far you are through GTA 6, but some gamers are claiming that this fix doesn't work — or at least that it isn't fully implemented, and the weather changes feel too sudden when they happen.
The jury is still out on this one, then, but it does appear that it's somewhat rainier in Vice City after this first patch — but the weather patterns may yet need some further tuning.
Other fixes
Here's a list of the other fixes applied by Rockstar in this initial update for GTA 6:
- Fixed several issues that caused the game to crash
- Fixed an issue that resulted in the player being unable to lose their Wanted Level
- Fixed an issue that resulted in the player being unable to use the deadlift bar in the Gym
- Fixed an issue that resulted in partners not handing over bags so that players could sell them to fences
I must admit that I've not played a huge amount of GTA 6 (about 12 hours thus far; it would have been more, except real life got in the way) — but I haven't encountered any bugs except for some minor issues. I've experienced gym equipment failing to work, and a similar issue with one of the early house repair tasks, as well as the odd traffic light staying on red for an overly long period of time.
As noted, though, my playtime has been fairly limited, but I'm certainly glad to see some of these fixes come through before I've got too far in the game — especially when it comes to the mission-blocking glitches.
