articles.title: The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
articles.text:
Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politicothat Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) could be attached to the National Defense Authorization Act. It’s the latest in a grueling fight over a major spying rule that hasn’t technically lapsed.
The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
Warrantless wiretapping proponents are rushing to beat the looming blue wave.
“We don’t have two weeks to work just on FISA,” said Rounds, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “But if it’s amended onto the NDAA then you can move it forward and get that done in time.”
FISA allows for the warrantless surveillance of certain foreigners’ communications, ostensibly on national security grounds. In part because of FISA’s broad scope, Congress revisits it every few years, both to reauthorize the authority and to reform it. The last effort to do both failed. Despite pressure from President Donald Trump, Congress failed to reauthorize FISA over the summer, in part because leadership wouldn’t allow any amendments — particularly attempts to limit its sweeping scope — to be debated or introduced. (Trump didn’t help matters when he made Bill Pulte the acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, who reportedly bragged about purging one-third of the DNI staff, is now the director of federal housing.) But the surveillance authority didn’t actually lapse because the FISA court rectified surveillance under Section 702 back in March, meaning the surveillance state can keep chugging along as is for another four months.
So why the urgency? If you haven’t heard, there’s about to be a new Congress in town — one that is even less likely to give Trump seemingly unlimited spying powers without some semblance of reform.
Support for — and opposition to — FISA isn’t a clear-cut partisan issue. Last time around, a bipartisan coalition led by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), the ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, led the campaign for a “clean” reauthorization of FISA. Their efforts were defeated largely because of holdouts from the Freedom Caucus, whose privacy concerns echoed those of liberal lawmakers. FISA’s critics wanted reform, not abolition. Their goal was to make it harder for intelligence agencies to use the statute, which is intended for foreign targets, to access Americans’ communications.
“It was remarkable watching two dozen House Republicans stand up to the establishment, stand up to Mike Johnson, and fight to reform FISA,” said Michael Baick, an organizer with the OpenAI boycott campaign QuitGPT, which has been advocating for FISA reform to stop AI surveillance. “This has always been a bipartisan issue where Americans of all stripes can agree, and trying to make deals with the establishment to maintain the status quo, while the ground is shifting, is just short-sighted and missing what this moment really is.”
I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time.
Johnson and Himes were adamantly opposed to any reining in of Section 702, stressing the need for a so-called “clean reauthorization.” Both claimed there had already been reforms. “It ain’t the same FISA,” Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) declared in April.
But the changes reformers most wanted were missing. Among them were a warrant requirement and an end to what critics say are major loopholes. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can pull the communications of non-US persons not in the United States — that is, foreign nationals outside the country. But federal agencies like the FBI and NSA can buy Americans’ data from private brokers, a practice FBI director Kash Patel admits is ongoing. And intelligence agencies can use Section 702 to obtain the communications of non-US persons who are communicating with Americans — a workaround known as the “backdoor search loophole.”
“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Constitution Project of the Project on Government Oversight, told The Verge. “This is something everyone knew was coming down the pike. There have been months to do this, and I don’t think anyone is saying don’t reauthorize at all. The argument is this is an incredibly powerful surveillance tool, and there needs to be guardrails in place to protect people’s constitutional rights.”
Himes, arguably the Democratic Party’s biggest champion of FISA, seems willing to give Trump one more win before the blue wave crashes down in Washington. “I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck,” he told The Hill, “because it’s, you know, going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”
But Himes didn’t have the votes this summer, and it’s even less likely that he’ll have the votes for a clean reauthorization now.

articles.title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic
articles.text:
Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland.
The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press. Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara.
Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli.
Casualties from the strikes included at least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, Libyan National Army officials told The Associated Press. They also mentioned some wounded crew members of the Russian warship being transferred to local hospitals.
Merkury was a Steregushchiy-class missile corvette, designated by Russia as Project 20380, that can carry both anti-ship and air-defense missiles. They are also armed with torpedoes to counter submarines and have a naval cannon mounted on the deck.
Corvette-class warships are typically smaller than the destroyers or frigates that often act as workhorses of modern navies, although NATO has designated Russian missile corvettes such as the Merkury as being equivalent to frigates.
Merkury was originally meant to join Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. But after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Russian warship was unable to enter the Black Sea because Turkey invoked the 1936 Montreux Convention to restrict warships from entering or leaving the Black Sea. Instead, the Merkury mainly operated from Russia’s Northern Fleet bases in Arctic waters, according to naval analyst HI Sutton.

articles.title: De volta à Nvidia, Jensen Huang fala de terapia, nega influência de Trump e descarta plano de sucessão
articles.text:
O CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, pediu desculpas aos funcionários da empresa nesta terça-feira (24), durante sua primeira reunião geral desde que foi reconduzido ao cargo. O executivo reconheceu que violou o código de conduta da companhia, admitiu ter cometido erros pessoais e afirmou que está fazendo terapia. A reunião também foi marcada por declarações sobre seu retorno à liderança, a influência do governo de Donald Trump e a estrutura de comando da fabricante de chips.
“Cometi alguns erros terríveis”, afirmou Huang, segundo relatos publicados pelo The New York Times. O executivo também reconheceu que foi infiel à esposa, Lori, e que suas atitudes prejudicaram os filhos e os funcionários da Nvidia. “Eu decepcionei todos vocês”, disse, de acordo com fontes ouvidas pela CNBC.
Jensen Huang reconhece violações ao código de conduta
Durante a reunião, Huang afirmou que não era aceitável ter violado o código de conduta da Nvidia. Ele também lembrou que participou da elaboração de parte das regras internas da companhia e reconheceu que seu comportamento levou o conselho de administração a avaliar seu futuro na empresa.
O executivo deixou o cargo em novembro, após a divulgação de relatos sobre relacionamentos extraconjugais, incluindo um caso com uma empresária chinesa apontada como possível espiã de Pequim. Também foram divulgadas informações sobre supostos relacionamentos com funcionárias da Nvidia, entre elas Kimberly Powell, vice-presidente da divisão de saúde da companhia.
A saída foi anunciada em meio a questionamentos sobre a conduta pessoal de Huang e possíveis implicações para a segurança nacional dos Estados Unidos. O presidente do conselho da Nvidia, Harvey Jones, afirmou anteriormente que a decisão havia sido motivada pela divulgação de comportamentos pessoais incompatíveis com o código de conduta, os padrões e a cultura da empresa.
Huang também afirmou que está fazendo terapia. Segundo a Bloomberg, o executivo frequenta sessões diariamente.
CEO nega influência de Donald Trump em seu retorno
Outro assunto abordado por Huang foi a participação do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, em seu retorno à liderança da Nvidia. O executivo classificou como “completamente falsa” a interpretação de que a decisão teria sido resultado de pressão política.
Trump havia afirmado publicamente que participou das articulações para trazer Huang de volta, inclusive com a colaboração do vice-presidente JD Vance e de outros integrantes do governo. O presidente também disse à CNBC que ajudou a viabilizar o acordo que permitiu a recondução do executivo.
Na reunião com os funcionários, Huang afirmou que o conselho de administração avaliou a situação, reuniu informações e tomou a decisão de restabelecê-lo no cargo. Segundo o executivo, o governo norte-americano também forneceu garantias de que ele não representava uma ameaça à segurança nacional e deveria receber uma segunda oportunidade.
Huang ainda rejeitou a ideia de que seu retorno tenha ocorrido por uma suposta cultura de impunidade entre executivos de tecnologia. Ele afirmou que não estava de volta por ser um “tech bro” que estaria acima da lei ou das regras internas da companhia. Também descreveu a Nvidia como uma empresa apolítica.
Nvidia não precisa de plano de sucessão, diz Huang
A estrutura de liderança da Nvidia também foi discutida durante a reunião. Huang afirmou que não acredita na necessidade de um plano de sucessão tradicional para a empresa, mesmo diante das dúvidas sobre o futuro de sua liderança após a renúncia.
Segundo relatos publicados pela CNBC, o CEO argumentou que a Nvidia possui um modelo de negócios particular e vários executivos capazes de liderar diferentes áreas da companhia. Na avaliação dele, um plano formal de sucessão poderia criar uma hierarquia desnecessária entre esses profissionais.
Huang também contestou críticas à estrutura organizacional da fabricante de chips. O executivo tem cerca de 60 subordinados diretos e afirmou que não pretende mudar esse modelo. Ele argumentou que a quantidade de pessoas que se reportam diretamente a ele faz parte da maneira como a Nvidia opera.
A declaração ocorre depois de investidores e analistas questionarem o futuro da companhia durante o período em que Huang esteve fora do cargo. O executivo foi reconduzido à posição de CEO, presidente e integrante do conselho de administração na segunda-feira (23).
Apesar do retorno, os questionamentos sobre a Nvidia ainda não terminaram. A empresa conduz uma investigação interna sobre os relatos envolvendo uma possível tentativa de espionagem chinesa relacionada a Huang. O executivo também deverá prestar depoimento ao Congresso dos Estados Unidos em 1º de dezembro, quando deve responder a perguntas sobre questões de segurança nacional e as circunstâncias de sua volta à liderança.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
articles.text:
Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

articles.title: La película live-action de ‘Naruto’ ficha a Hiroyuki Sanada para un papel clave
articles.text:
La película live-action de Naruto acaba de cerrar uno de sus primeros fichajes. Y se trata de un nombre de muchísimo nivel. Hiroyuki Sanada, legendario actor de series como Shogun o películas como El Último Samurai, John Wick 4 o Mortal Kombat, se une a las filas de este esperado remake en imagen real. Además, ya se ha revelado el papel que interpretará y, desde luego, no podían haber elegido a nadie mejor.
Tal y como ha informado Deadline, Hiroyuki Sanada será Hiruzen Sarutobi en la película live-action de Naruto. Sarutobi era el Tercer Hokage de la Aldea Oculta de la Hoja. Es decir, el líder ninja del pueblo natal del joven protagonista. Conocedor de las cinco naturalezas del chakra, se trata de uno de los personajes más poderosos e importantes de todo el manga y el anime.
Por el momento, Hiroyuki Sanada se ha convertido en el primer actor confirmado para el reparto de la película live-action de Naruto. Con su fichaje, el proyecto gana no solo a uno de los mejores y más queridos actores japoneses del mundo, sino a un auténtico experto en el cine de artes marciales.
Se sabe también que el director de la película live-action de Naruto será Destin Daniel Cretton. El cineasta es conocido por el gran público gracias a su trabajo en Marvel. En dicha saga ha dirigido Shang-Chi y la Leyenda de los Diez Anillos, la serie de Wonder Man y, sobre todo, la reciente Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Y, además, el joven actor Charles Melton (Riverdale) está en negociaciones para unirse al filme, aunque todavía no hay nada cerrado.
De qué va Naruto
Naruto fue publicada entre 1999 y 2014 en la popular revista Shonen Jump y ha vendido más de 250 millones de copias en todo el mundo. Su trama sigue la historia de un muchacho huérfano que vive en la Aldea Oculta de la Hoja. En su interior vive encerrado el espíritu de un temible demonio, el Zorro de las Nueve Colas. Un monstruo que años atrás atacó y arrasó la aldea. Por eso mismo, Naruto Uzumakivive marginado y aislado.
Ante esta situación, el protagonista se lanza a cumplir su sueño. Para ganarse el respeto y la admiración de todos, deberá convertirse en Hokage, el líder ninja de la aldea. Pero si quiere conseguirlo, deberá entrenar muy duro y sortear todo tipo de aventuras. Entre sus aliados encontrará a Sasuke y Sakura, que le ayudarán a hacer frente a las misiones y amenazas que se crucen en su camino.

articles.title: Ariane 6 retente sa chance ce mardi avec 36 satellites Amazon Leo, suivez le décollage en direct
articles.text:
Après le report de la veille, Ariane 6 a rendez-vous ce mardi pour son dixième vol. Le décollage avec 36 satellites Amazon Leo est prévu entre 11h45 et 12h14 depuis Kourou, à suivre en direct et en vidéo.
Le lancement d'Ariane 6 et de ses 36 satellites Amazon Leo est programmé ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, entre 11h45 et 12h14 heure de Paris, depuis Kourou. Arianespace le retransmet en direct et en vidéo sur sa chaîne YouTube, et vous pouvez suivre l'événement à nos côtés ici même, au lendemain d'un report dû à un problème technique sur les installations au sol. Ce dixième vol d'Ariane 6 doit placer les satellites en orbite basse en un peu plus de deux heures.
Ariane 6 en direct, rendez-vous à 11h45
Le compte à rebours a repris ses droits pour Ariane 6. La fenêtre de tir s'ouvre à 11h45, heure de Paris, et se referme à 12h14, pour s'élancer depuis le Centre spatial guyanais, sur son pas de tir habituel, où il sera alors 7h45. Arianespace diffuse ça en direct et propose son émission Road to Space, que vous pouvez également suivre ci-dessus. Mieux vaut se connecter un peu en avance pour ne rien manquer des dernières secondes.
Ce nouveau créneau, ouvert 24 minutes plus tôt que celui de lundi, faite suite au contretemps de la veille. La chronologie avait alors été interrompue avant même le retrait de la tour mobile, à cause d'un souci technique sur les systèmes au sol, qui servent à préparer et à lancer la fusée. Selon Arianespace, les équipes ont depuis mené les analyses et vérifications nécessaires, et l'élégante fusée comme ses satellites demeurent bien « dans des conditions stables et sécurisées », comme l'expliquait la compagnie franco-européenne il y a quelques heures. La nature exacte de ce coup d'arrêt temporaire n'a pas été précisée.
Si tout se passe bien, le spectacle commencera sept secondes avant le décollage, avec l'allumage du moteur principe Vulcain 2.1, et non Vulcan, qui pourrait rappeler de mauvais souvenirs à Amazon Leo. Les quatre boosters se détacheront au bout de 2 minutes 23, puis la coiffe sera larguée à 3 minutes 12. Moins de huit minutes après le départ, l'étage supérieur et son moteur Vinci prendront le relais, avant de libérer les 36 satellites entre 1h39 et 2h04 de vol, vers 460 km d'altitude. Un dernier allumage le fera ensuite retomber vers la Terre.
Un dixième vol aux airs de revanche pour Amazon Leo
Ce lancement est tout à fait symbolique pour Arianespace, qui lui a consacré un dossier de vol en édition spéciale. Depuis son vol inaugural qui nous ramène en juillet 2024, Ariane 6 a multiplié les profils de mission, avec le satellite militaire CSO-3, la météo avec Metop-SGA1 et MTG-I2, l'observation de la Terre avec Sentinel-1D, la navigation avec Galileo, et trois vols pour Amazon Leo. VA271 doit être son dixième décollage, et le cinquième d'Arianespace en 2026.
Et pour ce rendez-vous très attendu, Ariane 6 volera en version Ariane 64, avec quatre boosters P160C. Sans changer de taille extérieure par rapport à la génération qui avait propulsé sous nos yeux les premiers satellites Amazon Leo, ils importent chacun 156 tonnes de propergol, contre 142 contre leurs prédécesseurs. Ils font ici leur deuxième sortie. Au décollage, l'ensemble pèse 900 tonnes et développe pas moins de 16 600 kN de poussée, l'équivalent d'environ 1 700 tonnes, de quoi emporter autour de 22 tonnes en orbite basse.
Du côté d'Amazon, l'attente est d'autant plus forte que la fusée américaine Vulcan a échoué le 15 novembre, emportant 40 satellites Leo avec elle. Ariane 6, elle, a déjà placé 100 satellites de la constellation en orbite sans le moindre accroc. En cas de succès, le compteur passera à 136, dans le cadre d'un contrat qui prévoit, après sa prolongation récente, désormais 24 lancements. Amazon fera ensuite grimper les nouveaux venus entre 590 et 630 km d'altitude.

articles.title: Why an international advocacy group is bringing its fight for safer social media to Canada
articles.text:
A UK-based digital advocacy group that has had high-profile spats with the likes of X and the US government is taking on Canada’s proposed Safe Social Media Act—arguing it doesn’t go far enough.
The news: The Center for Countering Digital Harm (CCDH), which recently rebranded from the Center for Countering Digital Hate, opened an Ottawa office in September. The organization currently has one Ottawa staffer working remotely, supported by research, comms, and advocacy teams in the US, EU, and UK.
CCDH is currently focused on Bill C-34, which the organization views as an opportunity to strengthen platform accountability and improve protections. It also plans to monitor policies and legislation that touch on issues like deepfakes, tech-facilitated gender-based violence, online fraud, election integrity, and consumer protection.
From the source: “Canada has an opportunity to lead the world in building a safer, more accountable digital ecosystem,” Nicole Fournier-Sylvester, Canada senior manager at CCDH, told BetaKit in an emailed statement. “As concerns about online harms, AI, and platform accountability grow, Canadians are looking for practical, evidence-based solutions.” She added that CCDH wants to bring “independent research and real-world evidence” to that conversation.
The context: CCDH’s Canadian expansion was first reported by the Globe and Mail. It’s being funded by the Ronald S. Roadburg Foundation, a private foundation established through the estate of the late Vancouver philanthropist and real estate mogul. The organization’s latest report found that safeguards in ChatGPT for teens are easily bypassed, giving users harmful responses about eating disorders, suicide, and substance abuse.
Final thought: CCDH was sued by X and accused of running a scare campaign in 2023 after CCDH used data scraping to report on disinformation spreading on the platform; the suit was dismissed. CCDH’s CEO was also denied a US visa last year, as US officials called the organization “radical” activists who aimed to censor US big tech companies.
Its focus in Canada, Bill C-34, is currently under review by a House committee. The bill aims to create a new digital super regulator and restrict social media accounts for youth under age 16 unless platforms establish safeguards. Open Media, a Canadian non-profit digital advocacy org, said on Tuesday in a post to its website that if done right, the bill “can be a win for both fundamental freedoms and common-sense regulation,” but “done wrong, it could become a blueprint for censorship and privacy violations dressed up as safety.”

articles.title: Check Point Security Management Servers Hacked in AI-Assisted Campaign
articles.text:
A threat actor has been using AI-enabled offensive tools in a broad campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, threat intelligence firm GreyNoise reports.
As part of the campaign, which the security firm started tracking in early October and is likely still ongoing, a threat actor tracked as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) has been conducting scanning, exploitation, and control activities from 99 IP addresses, many associated with disposable network infrastructure.
According to GreyNoise, GT13 targeted at least 22 organizations from the energy, engineering, financial services, government, manufacturing, mining, and transportation sectors across the US, the UK, Australia, Austria, China, France, Germany, Hong Kong, the Netherlands, South Korea, and other geographies.
GreyNoise believes the threat actor has been using agentic harnesses and systems to weaponize vulnerabilities, find vulnerable assets, and automatically exploit them. The automated operations were complemented by hands-on-keyboard activity.
“We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created,” GreyNoise says.
In one instance, GreyNoise tracked the activity to October 2, when the threat actor forged a signed admin session cookie to gain administrative access to an HFS server. The attacker obtained SSH access to the server, which was used to scan the environment and exfiltrate data.
“The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets,” the company notes.
The attacker deployed tools such as Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and other Python utilities and scripts, performed reconnaissance, lateral movement, and privilege escalation. They used one victim’s server as a hop to save command results and data exfiltrated from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers.
Between October 20 and 26, in addition to gaining deeper access to the victim’s environment, the threat actor conducted bulk actions against 21 other victim Check Point devices. GT13 issued a bulk certificate-management task to 24 servers across the 22 organizations. The task failed, but the threat actor collected the responses on the relay server in text files.
“These files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices holds the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop,” GreyNoise says.
The activity within the first victim’s environment also involved the use or attempted exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2023-4966 and CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF), CVE-2020-1472 and CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473 (Microsoft Exchange), and CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter).
GreyNoise says it confirmed threat actor activity against Check Point Security Management servers between October 17 and November 2, when it stopped observing it. However, the company believes the campaign is still ongoing as GT13 had persistent access to the compromised servers.
“We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations,” GreyNoise notes.

articles.title: Black Friday: Diese Samsung-Angebote lohnen sich
articles.text:
Black Friday: Diese Samsung-Angebote bei Amazon und Mediamarkt lohnen sich
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Offiziell findet der Black Friday zwar erst am 27. November statt, die Preisschlacht hat aber schon jetzt begonnen. Besonders viel sparen können Schnäppchenjäger:innen dann, wenn mehrere Shops versuchen, sich mit ihren Rabattaktionen gegenseitig zu unterbieten. Aktuell ist das bei den Konkurrenten Amazon und Media Markt der Fall, die beide Samsung-Smartphones deutlich reduziert anbieten. Wir haben die Black-Friday-Deals geprüft und zeigen dir, wo du derzeit am meisten sparst.
Samsung Galaxy A18 jetzt noch günstiger
Samsung bietet mehrere Smartphone-Serien an, die sich in Ausstattung und Preis teils deutlich voneinander unterscheiden. Die A-Reihe umfasst günstigere und mittelpreisige Modelle. Sie richtet sich an Nutzer:innen, die ein solides Gerät für den Alltag suchen, aber auf teure Spitzenfunktionen verzichten können. Zu den günstigsten Einstiegsmodellen der Reihe zählt das Samsung Galaxy A18.
Es hat ein 6,7-Zoll-Display und 128 Gigabyte internen Speicher. Mithilfe des „RAM Plus“-Features soll das Smartphone auf bis zu vier Gigabyte virtuellen Arbeitsspeicher zusätzlich zu den festen vier Gigabyte RAM zugreifen können. Dabei greift das Gerät dann auf den Datenspeicher zu. Einen sehr großen Leistungsschub sollte man sich davon nicht erwarten.
Die unverbindliche Preisempfehlung liegt bei 279 Euro. Bei Amazon ist das Modell aktuell für 209 Euro erhältlich. Im Onlineshop von Mediamarkt ist das Galaxy A18 allerdings noch günstiger zu haben. Hier liegt der Preis bei 179 Euro. Wer jetzt zuschlägt, spart rund 36 Prozent gegenüber der Preisempfehlung. Laut etablierten Preisvergleichsportalen war das Smartphone bislang kaum irgendwo günstiger zu haben.
So viel kannst du jetzt bei Foldables sparen
Auch die Foldables von Samsung sind aktuell reduziert. Das Galaxy Z Flip 8 misst aufgeklappt 6,9 Zoll, das Frontdisplay 4,1 Zoll. Die Dualkamera kombiniert ein 50-Megapixel-Weitwinkel- mit einem 12-Megapixel-Ultraweitwinkel-Objektiv. Bei Amazon ist das Modell derzeit ausverkauft. Im Samsung-Shop kostet es mit 256 Gigabyte internem Speicher 1.069 Euro, bei Media Markt 749 Euro. Hier sparst du also 320 Euro beziehungsweise knapp 30 Prozent.
Auch das Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 ist jetzt günstiger. Es eignet sich für alle, die sich ein möglichst großes Display für Videos oder E-Mails wünschen. Das Frontdisplay misst 5,5 Zoll, aufgeklappt sind es 7,6 Zoll. Die Hauptkamera auf der Rückseite löst mit 50 Megapixeln aus. Laut Herstellerangaben ermöglicht der große Akku bis zu 26 Stunden Videowiedergabe. Bei Samsung kostet das Foldable mit 256 Gigabyte ab 1.799 Euro, bei Mediamarkt 1.649 Euro und damit 150 Euro weniger. Bei Amazon ist es ausverkauft.
Der Preisvergleich zeigt: Bei beiden Modellen fällt die Ersparnis geringer aus als von Mediamarkt angegeben. Der Händler legt eine höhere unverbindliche Preisempfehlung zugrunde, obwohl die Geräte beim Hersteller selbst günstiger sind. Auch ein Blick in etablierte Preisvergleichsportale lohnt sich: Laut Analyse sind beide Foldables in kleineren Onlineshops aktuell noch günstiger.
Galaxy A57: Warum sich der Vergleich lohnt
Auch das Samsung Galaxy A57 ist Teil der Black-Friday-Aktion. Das höherwertige Mittelklassemodell bietet mehr Leistung und eine bessere Kameraausstattung als das A18. Es unterstützt 5G und hat 256 Gigabyte Speicher. Das Display misst ebenfalls 6,7 Zoll, bietet aber eine Bildrate von 120 Hertz. Die 50-Megapixel-Hauptkamera verfügt über eine optische Bildstabilisierung. Dazu kommen eine 12-Megapixel-Weitwinkelkamera und eine 5-Megapixel-Makrokamera. Mit KI‑Funktionen wie dem Objektradierer, der störende Elemente aus dem Hintergrund entfernt, lassen sich die Bilder bearbeiten.
Bei Amazon zählte das Galaxy A57 über Wochen zu den meistverkauften Smartphones, inzwischen ist es dort vergriffen. Mediamarkt bietet es aktuell noch zum reduzierten Black-Friday-Preis von 379 Euro an. Das Angebot ist allerdings weniger gut, als der Händler suggeriert. Er nennt eine unverbindliche Preisempfehlung von 659 Euro, was eine Ersparnis von 42 Prozent bedeuten würde. Beim Hersteller selbst kostet das Modell aber nur noch 459 Euro.
Dass es sich nicht um ein einmaliges Schnäppchen handelt, zeigen auch Vergleichsportale: Laut ihrer Analyse ist das Modell in anderen Shops noch günstiger. Zudem lag der Preis vor einigen Monaten regelmäßig bei etwa 300 Euro. Zwar sparen Käufer:innen bei Media Markt jetzt 80 Euro gegenüber dem Herstellerpreis. Ein Preisvergleich zeigt aber, dass sich der Kauf im Rahmen der Black-Friday-Aktion nur bedingt lohnt.
Ist das Samsung Galaxy S26 wirklich günstiger?
Ähnliches gilt für das Galaxy S26. Bei diesem Smartphone handelt es sich um das aktuelle Premium-Modell von Samsung. Dessen Prozessor, der Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, ist speziell auf KI-Anwendungen ausgelegt und geht darüber hinaus zu den leistungsstärksten Chips in der Android-Welt. Das Smartphone ist in verschiedenen Ausführungen erhältlich. Das Standardmodell verfügt über ein 6,3-Zoll-Display und 256 Gigabyte integrierten Speicher. Die Dreifachkamera besteht aus einem 50-Megapixel-Weitwinkel-, einem 12-Megapixel-Ultraweitwinkel- und einem 10-Megapixel-Teleobjektiv.
Mediamarkt nennt für das Galaxy S26 eine unverbindliche Preisempfehlung von 1.099 Euro, der Hersteller verlangt inzwischen aber nur noch 699 Euro. Der Black-Friday-Nachlass fällt daher geringer aus als im Onlineshop angegeben. Statt der versprochenen 42 Prozent sparen Käufer:innen beim Angebot von 679 Euro nur 20 Euro, also weniger als drei Prozent. Laut Vergleichsportalen schwankte der Preis zuletzt stark und lag in anderen Shops oft bei 650 Euro oder weniger.
Black Friday: Lass dich nicht täuschen
Anlässlich der Black Week locken viele Onlineshops mit hohen Rabatten. Ein Preisvergleich zeigt allerdings, dass diese nicht immer so hoch ausfallen wie angegeben. Oft sind aktuelle Smartphones beim Hersteller günstiger, als die unverbindlichen Preisempfehlung suggeriert. Kaufinteressierte sollten sich daher nicht von vermeintlichen Schnäppchen blenden lassen. Ob ein Angebot wirklich gut ist, zeigt nur der direkte Preisvergleich.

articles.title: Vehicle-to-Grid: Great Idea or Unrealistic Dream?
articles.text:
You’re undoubtedly familiar with the idea of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) automobile energy transfer. It’s been a “hot” topic for the last few years, largely due to the number of pure electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid vehicles on the road. In the U.S., these EVs/HEVs account for roughly 8% to 10% of all new cars sold (but they are a much lower fraction of cars on the road, of course); the worldwide numbers are higher depending on the region.
What is V2G? In short, V2G enables the energy stored in car battery packs to become a part of the grid, using some percent of each battery’s energy storage capacity to meet grid-level peak demand (Figure 1).
V2G appears poised for increased adoption by automakers due to the release of a new certification program for V2G technologies based on the recently issued UL 1741 Supplement SC standard. (Note that one variation of V2G is V2H, or vehicle-to-home, but we’re focusing just on V2G here.)
This adjunct standard creates a formal testing and certification pathway for bidirectional electric vehicle supply equipment (BEVSE) under UL 1741, the primary North American safety and performance standard for inverters, converters, charge controllers, and interconnection system equipment (ISE) used in distributed energy resources (DERs), such as solar panels, wind turbines, and home battery-storage systems (Figure 2).
The certification program covers AC-based V2G connections, known as V2G-AC. Under this approach, EVs equipped with certified bidirectional onboard inverters can connect to the electric grid through AC wallboxes. The wallbox oversees the connection between the vehicle, home wiring, and grid rather than relying on an external inverter.
What’s the plan?
Since energy storage is one of the bigger challenges facing efficient and environmentally friendly energy generation and distribution, using cars for transitional storage of any excess energy can minimize the need to build new generating capacity. It can also help create a more resilient grid, in principle.
The premise of V2G is that many car owners usually use only a fraction of their battery capacity, so V2G lets them offer more “use” of their cars as battery energy storage systems (BESS). Vehicle owners who send their unneeded energy back to the grid get some payment.
I’m not going to delve into the operational details of the proposed V2G operation, as that information is widely available. The idea is simple in concept: A car that is connected to a home charger when not in use can either recharge or allow its “excess” stored energy (which is temporarily unneeded) to be transferred back to the grid.
This capability would be especially useful to bolster the grid when its capacity is low compared to demand. In operation, power would flow from the grid to the car or vice versa, depending on the supply/demand balance and energy pricing at that moment.
In engineering and economic terms, everything will be optimized: supply, demand, pricing, costs—you name it. On top of that, it comes with a host of “green” virtues. So, what’s not to like?
The second part explores some issues and concerns associated with V2G.

articles.title: From Vulnerability Noise to Resilience: Rethinking Security in the AI Era
articles.text:
Written by: George Manuelian, Chief Strategy Officer, RapidFort
The modern software stack has become an iceberg. The application code customers and security teams see at the surface is only a small portion of what is being shipped. Beneath it sit operating systems, frameworks, libraries, packages, and transitive dependencies, with much of it drawn from open source or third parties.
As AI accelerates software development, that hidden complexity has become an even more critical security challenge.
For business and technology leaders, the question is no longer simply how many vulnerabilities exist. It is where does meaningful risk live, which vulnerabilities can be exploited in our environment, and how we can reduce that risk without turning developers into full-time vulnerability managers.
The answer requires a fundamental shift from vulnerability accumulation to continuous software resilience.
First step: Recognizing composition of modern software
The typical containerized stack is layers of base operating system software, packages, libraries, language frameworks and dependencies, and the application itself. The application a company writes may represent only a small portion of what it ultimately ships.
That is important because vulnerabilities multiply. A vulnerable package in a base image is not necessarily one vulnerability in practice; it can be replicated across every application and container that uses that image.
In light of this, executives should ask a different question of their security programs: How much of the reported risk is relevant to the way our software operates? Traditional scanning frequently identifies the presence of a vulnerable component without establishing whether that component is loaded, executing, reachable or exposed.
A software bill of materials (SBOM) identifies what exists; a runtime bill of materials (RBOM) can pinpoint what is actually being used. That distinction can dramatically reduce noise.
For example, in the real world from a customer, an NGINX image containing 152 packages and 48 CVEs had only 47 packages actually running in the application. More than 80% of the software was not being exercised. The lesson is not that every unused package is harmless, but that security teams need operational context before assigning remediation urgency.
This is also why severity alone has become an inadequate basis for prioritization. A high or critical Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score can command attention, but the business question is whether the vulnerable code is relevant and exploitable in the environment.
There are four contextual factors increasingly shaping remediation decisions: Whether a vulnerability is exposed, whether it is a known exploited vulnerability, whether exploitation is automatable, and whether exploitation would have meaningful technical impact.
The shift from severity to exploitability and reachability is important because it changes the operating model. Instead of asking engineering teams to chase the largest number on a scanner dashboard, leaders should ask whether the organization has enough visibility to determine what is running, what is reachable, and what is exposed.
As a result, security becomes a business-risk exercise rather than a race to close tickets.
Eliminate Up to 99.9% of Container CVEs Without Code Changes
RapidFort Curated Images give your team 35,000+ near-zero CVE container images, rebuilt and hardened every 24 hours.
Swap in a hardened base image and remove exploitable vulnerabilities at the source, with no code, OS or pipeline changes.
Learn More
Hardening is the important next step
Hardening should not mean merely passing a configuration benchmark. It should also mean removing software and functionality that the application does not need
. Every unnecessary library, shell, package manager, build utility, or default component increases the amount of software that must be maintained and potentially gives an attacker additional tools if a container is compromised.
Runtime profiling is a proven approach for identifying these unused components and removing them systematically.
AI makes this discipline more important
AI-assisted development can rapidly generate code and pull in packages, but developers may not always know which dependencies were introduced or whether they remain necessary as the application evolves.
For example, a development environment in which developers may have to ask the AI system which Python version or packages were used because the model generated much of the implementation is a warning sign for governance.
Speed of development cannot come at the expense of knowing what is being shipped.
No one is going to slow AI development. The answer is to put security controls into the pipeline so developers do not have to perform every security task manually. Clean, curated base images; runtime profiling; removal of unused components; vulnerability context; and automated rebuilding can become repeatable parts of CI/CD.
The objective is to make the secure path the default path.
Introducing Zero Trust software architecture
Zero Trust has traditionally been associated with network access and identity. But when organizations continuously ingest open source and third-party software, they also need to question the software entering their environments.
Software should be verified, trusted components should be maintained in controlled registries, and the software should be continuously evaluated as it moves through development, testing and production – following the common principles of Zero Trust.
This represents a meaningful change in how software supply chain security should be managed. The goal should not be a perfect vulnerability dashboard.
The goal should be a development system that continuously produces software with less unnecessary code, fewer meaningful vulnerabilities, and a smaller attack surface.
For example, one customer reduced an initial 5,286 findings to three unresolved vulnerabilities within 48 hours by combining profiling, curated images, and removal of unused components.
The strategic lesson learned
Vulnerability remediation should become a manufacturing process, not a recurring emergency. If organizations wait until a scanner produces a massive backlog, they have already allowed complexity to become technical debt.
If instead they control what enters the software supply chain, understand what actually runs, prioritize based on reachability and impact, remove what is unnecessary, and continuously rebuild from cleaner components, security becomes part of software production itself.
This approach also changes the conversation between security and engineering. Developers should not be expected to fix every finding simply because a scanner found it. They need context, automation and a clear understanding of which risks require action.
Security leaders need visibility into runtime behavior and the ability to distinguish a theoretical exposure from a vulnerability that can actually affect the business.
The future of software security in the AI era
The future of software security belongs to organizations that manage complexity continuously. AI will accelerate development, it’s a given. Open source will remain foundational, that’s understood. Neither trend is going away, nor should it of course.
But both make it more important to establish disciplined software intake, strong supply-chain controls, runtime visibility, effective hardening, and automated remediation.
Ultimately, the objective is not simply to reduce the number of CVEs on a report. It is to build software that contains less unnecessary functionality, relies on cleaner components, exposes fewer opportunities to attackers, and can be continuously refreshed without overwhelming those responsible for delivering it
. Software supply chain security works best when profiling, verification, clean images, and removal of unused components are built directly into the pipeline.
The executive mandate for the AI era must stop treating vulnerability management as a downstream cleanup exercise. Build security into the way software is assembled, tested and deployed.
When continuous remediation becomes part of the normal development life cycle, organizations can move faster without accepting vulnerability volume as an unavoidable cost of innovation.

articles.title: Ecologistas quieren soltar en el Pirineo catalán un felino superdepredador extinto desde 1930
articles.text:
En 1930 se cazó el último lince boreal en libertad del que hay constancia en Cataluña, y su piel acabó expuesta en la comarca del Ripollès, tal y como recoge la Fundación para la Conservación del Quebrantahuesos. Casi un siglo después, dos asociaciones ecologistas plantearon en octubre de 2025 devolver este felino al Pirineo catalán con una prueba piloto que todavía está lejos de convertirse en realidad.
Quién lo propone y cómo. La idea parte de Amics del Parc Natural de l’Alt Pirineu y de ADLO Pirineo, que quieren soltar varios machos castrados en el Parque Natural del Alt Pirineu, el espacio protegido más grande de Cataluña. Los animales podrían llegar de Rumanía, cuya población de los Cárpatos se mantiene sin grandes cambios o crece poco a poco, según el balance de la Comisión Europea para 2017-2023. ¿Y por qué castrados? Pues porque, según sus impulsores, así no podrían reproducirse, y el experimento se quedaría en un ensayo controlado para ver qué efecto tiene su presencia en el ecosistema.
Un felino mucho mayor que el ibérico. El lince boreal (Lynx lynx), también llamado euroasiático, es el mayor felino de Europa. También es bastante más corpulento que el lince ibérico, al que WWF presenta como su pariente más pequeño. Puede medir entre 60 y 75 centímetros de altura y pesar hasta 30 kilos, según la ficha de la especie del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica, y entre sus presas están los corzos y los rebecos y, en ocasiones, los ciervos.
La propuesta ha despertado inquietud en algunos sectores ligados al medio rural y a la gestión de la fauna, que temen que su llegada afecte a las poblaciones de ciertas especies silvestres y altere el equilibrio actual del territorio. Los promotores defienden lo contrario, que su presencia ayudaría a recuperar procesos ecológicos perdidos hace décadas y que, al ser ejemplares estériles, el riesgo sería menor. Vamos, que no podrían crear por su cuenta una población estable. Eso sí, el debate ya va más allá del ensayo, porque la gran pregunta es qué pasaría si algún día se planteara soltar linces fértiles.
La sombra del lince ibérico. Otro de los puntos que generan dudas es la posible relación con el lince ibérico (Lynx pardinus), cuya recuperación ha costado lustros de trabajo y más de 100 millones de euros, según la estrategia de conservación de España y Portugal. De hecho, un estudio liderado por la Estación Biológica de Doñana, del Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas (CSIC), concluyó en enero de 2024 que ambas especies llegaron a cruzarse en el pasado.
Los investigadores analizaron el ADN de linces prehistóricos hallados en Andújar, Alcanar y el Algarve, y vieron que “los linces modernos compartían más material genético con su especie hermana, el lince euroasiático, que los linces más antiguos”, según explicaba María Lucena, primera autora del trabajo, en la nota de prensa de la Estación Biológica. Aquella hibridación pudo ayudar a aumentar la diversidad genética del lince ibérico, pero José Antonio Godoy, coautor del trabajo, advierte en la misma nota de que no se pueden predecir las consecuencias de una futura hibridación, natural o intencionada, en una especie cuya viabilidad genética todavía no está garantizada.
Un camino administrativo largo. En octubre de 2025 la propuesta estaba en una fase muy inicial. Según la misma fundación, el borrador del plan tiene que pasar primero por el parque natural, que lo elevaría a la Generalitat de Cataluña, y el Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico únicamente lo estudiaría si la Generalitat diera su visto bueno. Las asociaciones, por su parte, insistían en que se trataría de una experiencia limitada y sin posibilidad de reproducción.
Pero un año después el planteamiento ha cambiado. El 13 de octubre de 2026, las dos asociaciones y otras cuatro entidades ecologistas pidieron a la Dirección General de Políticas Ambientales y Medio Natural de la Generalitat que recuperara y actualizara el plan de viabilidad para reintroducir el lince boreal anunciado en 2016, que nunca llegó a ejecutarse. En ese comunicado ya no hablan de machos castrados, sino de traer ejemplares no esterilizados de otras regiones europeas si los estudios lo avalan.

articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
  November 13, 2026
- Source:
  Princeton University
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Princeton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- John Mark P. Martirez. A Chemist’sGuide to Solid-State Qubits: DiamondColor Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules. ACS Central Science, 2026; 12 (10): 1578 DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548

articles.title: The Best CPUs - Late 2026 Update
articles.text:
If you're building a new PC or considering a platform upgrade, choosing the right CPU in late 2026 presents an unusual dilemma. There are plenty of good processors covering a wide range of prices, and some holiday deals, particularly on Intel CPUs, are outstanding. But with DDR5 memory prices through the roof and new processors from both Intel and AMD on the horizon, this might not be the best time to invest in an entirely new platform.
In fact, if you can afford to wait, that's exactly what we'd recommend. Intel's next-generation Nova Lake processors are expected in early 2027, potentially within the first quarter, with AMD's Zen 6 series likely following a little later. Faster CPUs are just around the corner, and their arrival should put downward pressure on pricing for existing hardware.
Of course, not everyone can wait. If you need a new PC today, there are some excellent deals worth considering, including a few that challenge our usual advice about avoiding dead-end platforms.
Intel's Core Ultra 5 250K Plus and Core Ultra 7 270K Plus are particularly attractive right now, with some frankly insane discounts. Amazon has been among those offering the most aggressive deals, though it's hard to say how long those will last. Availability and pricing vary considerably by region, however. In Australia, for example, the 250K Plus is still around $300 AUD, though that's considerably less than the Ryzen 7 9700X, which costs $385 AUD even after Amazon's discount.
As we've noted repeatedly, we normally wouldn't recommend investing in Intel's LGA1851 platform, given its limited upgrade path. But at current prices, you're effectively getting the motherboard for free compared to competing AMD configurations. The other major consideration is memory pricing. DDR5 has become painfully expensive, making older DDR4 platforms attractive again, especially for anyone who already owns a decent memory kit.
The AI bubble also looks like it might be losing some air, it's impossible to predict what will happen, but NAND flash prices have been dropping lately, falling by around 20% in recent weeks.
With all that in mind, we've updated our CPU recommendations to reflect current pricing and the unusual state of the market. We'll start with the best affordable DDR4 options, move on to DDR5, and then look at the processors offering the most performance for your money.
Best Entry-Level Platform Upgrade (DDR4)
Ryzen 7 5700X or Core i5-14400F
Let's start with the cheapest worthwhile hardware options available right now. The premise for this category is simple: you need a new PC or a complete platform upgrade, but don't want to pay current DDR5 prices, perhaps because you already own a decent DDR4 kit.
As it stands, a basic 16GB DDR5 memory kit costs roughly twice as much as DDR4, at around $260 versus $130. For budget builders who can get away with 16GB of memory, DDR4 is considerably more attractive, even if it means investing in older platforms such as AM4 or LGA1700.
So what are the options? As usual, availability and pricing will depend on your region, especially since many of these processors are quite old now.
Starting with AMD, the cheapest AM4 processor worth considering is the Ryzen 5 5600 or 5600X, whichever is cheaper or more readily available. The Ryzen 5 5500 has been a popular choice at $90. While its name suggests it's simply a slightly downclocked 5600, it's actually a much worse processor, featuring an entirely different design with just half the L3 cache. As a result, it performs more like a Ryzen 5 3600 than a 5600, making it difficult to justify the $45 saving over the 5600X.
Beyond the 5600 models, there's the Ryzen 7 5700X, currently on sale for $160, just $25 more than the 5600. Frankly, it's well worth coughing up the extra cash if you can. The 5700X packs two additional cores and is generally a little faster for gaming, while offering a much more substantial improvement in productivity performance. We should also point out that there's a Ryzen 7 5700 (non-X), which you should avoid like the plague. Essentially, it's an 8-core version of the Ryzen 5 5500, meaning it features a cut-down 16MB L3 cache rather than the 32MB found in the 5700X and 5800X.
Turning to Intel, your DDR4 options are limited to the LGA1700 platform, which supports 12th-, 13th-, and 14th-generation Core processors. Again, availability and pricing will vary considerably.
In the US, the Core i3-14100F costs around $105, but it's only a quad-core processor, so we'd avoid it. That leaves the Core i5-14400F at $155 as Intel's best budget DDR4 option. It packs six P-cores, four E-cores, and 20MB of L3 cache. The 14400F is slightly faster than the Ryzen 5 5600 for gaming while offering superior productivity performance, largely thanks to those additional E-cores. It currently costs about 15% more, but the extra performance helps offset the price increase.
Beyond that, you're looking at spending over $200 on something like the Core i5-14600KF at $230 or the Core i7-12700KF at $285, which is well beyond entry-level territory.
So which DDR4-compatible CPU should you buy for under $200? Your main options are the Ryzen 5 5600 at $135, the Core i5-14400F at $155, and the Ryzen 7 5700X at $160.
We think the 5700X is a better buy than the 5600 at those prices, so it really comes down to the 5700X versus the 14400F. There's no wrong choice here. They're quite similar in performance, especially for gaming, so the decision will largely depend on pricing and availability in your region.
Best Gaming Platform Upgrade (DDR4)
Intel Core i5-14600KF
What if you want to build the fastest gaming PC you can while still using DDR4 memory, either because you don't want to pay today's DDR5 prices or because you already own a good DDR4 kit?
Right now, the most viable options include the Intel Core i5-14600KF at $230, the Core i7-12700KF at $285, and the Ryzen 7 5800X3D at $320. In a normal market, the 14600KF at $230 wouldn't be particularly appealing. You'd be better off investing in AMD's AM5 platform or buying something even cheaper and slightly faster, such as the Core Ultra 5 250K Plus.
Sadly, we're not in a normal market, and those alternatives all require DDR5 memory. For anyone specifically looking for a DDR4 solution, the 14600KF is therefore extremely attractive and easily our top recommendation.
Overall gaming performance is very similar to the 5800X3D, but at almost a 30% discount, the Core i5 represents considerably better value. The 14600KF also outperforms the 12700KF, offering better single-core and multi-core performance, so there's little reason to spend another $55 on the older Core i7.
If you're after the best-performing processor that still supports DDR4 memory without breaking the bank, the 14600KF is the one to get. Obviously, the fastest LGA1700 processor is the Core i9-14900K, but even the KF variant starts at $430, and it's absolutely not worth paying almost twice as much as the Core i5-14600KF.
The 13th- and 14th-generation Core i7 and Core i9 processors have also been plagued by stability issues. While Intel has introduced fixes intended to address those problems, we can't say for certain that every affected processor is in the clear.
On that note, we strongly recommend avoiding second-hand 13th- or 14th-gen Core i7 and i9 processors. Many have suffered degradation that can lead to stability problems or poor performance, and there's no reliable way to know what you're getting.
Best Entry-Level Platform Upgrade (DDR5)
AMD Ryzen 5 7500F
Sadly, budget CPU options remain pretty miserable, especially if you want to move to AMD's or Intel's latest platform. On Intel's side, the Core Ultra 5 225F is its cheapest current-generation offering, and at $160, it's pretty horrible. Despite packing six P-cores and four E-cores, it only delivers multi-core performance comparable to the Ryzen 5 7500F while being considerably slower for gaming.
Several factors hurt the 225F's performance. One is its 4.9GHz boost clock, but the bigger issue is the measly 20MB L3 cache, the smallest cache capacity of any Core Ultra 200 series processor. That's a significant problem given that these CPUs aren't particularly impressive for gaming to begin with. Even if the 225F were considerably more competitive, you'd still have the problem of buying into a dead platform.
The LGA1851 socket won't support any future CPU architectures, making it effectively a dead end. Intel's upcoming Nova Lake-S desktop processors will use the new LGA1954 socket, which is incompatible with LGA1851.
So if you're building a new PC or performing a complete platform upgrade with DDR5 memory, it's difficult to justify investing in a platform with no future CPU upgrade path. That really leaves AMD's AM5 platform as the only viable option for budget builders right now.
This is why we continue to recommend the Ryzen 5 7500F for budget gamers, though the older Core i5 processors are potentially better investments for productivity workloads. For gaming, however, the 7500F is only slightly slower than those older Core i5 models, making it an excellent value choice, particularly given AM5's much stronger upgrade path.
The main downside is availability, as the 7500F isn't officially sold in every region. In the US, it's not generally available through local retailers, but you can order it from AliExpress for around $120. Alternatively, the Ryzen 5 7600X costs $185 at most retailers, although AMD's store on Amazon currently has it for just $165, making it a reasonable alternative to the imported 7500F.
Best CPU for ~$200
Intel Core Ultra 5 250K Plus
If we ignore future platform upgrades and simply focus on getting the most CPU performance for your money, there's one standout option that's become irresistibly cheap. Whether you're gaming, working, or doing just about anything else, the Core Ultra 5 250K Plus is the CPU to get right now.
Retailers such as Newegg have the 250K Plus for around $170, but Amazon is currently offering it for just $140 to eligible Amazon Visa cardholders, thanks to a $60 discount on its $200 list price. At that price, it's an absolute steal.
The 250K Plus packs six P-cores clocked up to 5.3GHz with a shared 30MB L3 cache, along with 12 E-cores. It also features a 43% increase in die-to-die frequency, jumping from 2.1GHz to 3GHz. This improvement addresses many of the latency issues found in the original Arrow Lake processors, leading to substantially better gaming performance.
AMD is currently floundering at this price point. While the Ryzen 7 9700X might deliver similar gaming performance, the 250K Plus is up to 50% faster in core-heavy productivity workloads.
To get comparable gaming and productivity performance from AMD, you'd need to spend at least $300 on the Ryzen 9 7900X, though that processor can be a bit sketchy for gaming at times. Ideally, you'd want the Ryzen 9 9900X, but that processor costs around $330, making it more than twice as expensive as the 250K Plus at Amazon's promotional price.
That means you can currently buy the 250K Plus along with a quality Z890 motherboard for roughly the same price as the Ryzen 9 9900X alone, making Intel's dead-platform issue a complete non-issue from a financial perspective. So while we normally wouldn't recommend investing in Intel's dead-end LGA1851 socket, especially with Nova Lake and its new socket expected in early 2027, the 250K Plus is cheap enough that the deal makes sense.
Frankly, at these prices, it's much better value than anything AMD has on offer right now.
Best Value Productivity CPU
Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus
If you have more than $200 to spend, the good news is that you don't actually need to spend much more than that on a CPU right now. In fact, Amazon is currently selling Intel's Core Ultra 7 270K Plus for just $221, which is complete madness.
The 270K Plus is a one-stop shop for just about any workload. Whether you're gaming or tackling demanding productivity tasks, if you want a CPU that handles everything with a high degree of efficiency, this is the one to get.
This model packs eight P-cores clocked at up to 5.5GHz, along with 16 E-cores that can reach 4.7GHz. There's also 36MB of L3 cache, and Intel has specified a maximum turbo power rating of 250 watts.
In multi-threaded, core-heavy productivity workloads, it performs within 2 – 5% of the AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, a processor that often retails for twice the price. That makes the 270K Plus, by far, one of the most cost-effective ways to get high-end workstation-class performance on a mainstream desktop.
Not only that, but unlike the original Core Ultra 7 265K, the Plus version addresses internal latency issues, greatly improving gaming performance to the point where it's no longer embarrassing.
Of course, AMD's X3D processors still hold the crown for pure gaming performance, but we think the 270K Plus is now close enough that the price savings make it more attractive for most people, especially if you're looking for strong performance across a variety of workloads.
The fact that you're getting productivity performance approaching that of the 9950X, along with very capable gaming performance, at a fraction of the price makes concerns about future platform support largely irrelevant. As with the 250K Plus, you're effectively getting the motherboard for free.
The cheapest Ryzen 9 9950X we could find at the time of writing was $490. Meanwhile, shoppers can get the 270K Plus at Amazon for just $221, along with a really nice $200 Z890 motherboard, for less than the price of the Ryzen 9 alone.
Once again, the motherboard is effectively free, and at that point, the lack of a future upgrade path becomes much less of a concern. For anyone who needs serious productivity performance without spending a fortune, it's an incredibly compelling deal.
Best Gaming CPU
AMD Ryzen 7 9850X3D or Ryzen 7 7700X3D
There's no debating which company makes the fastest gaming CPUs. AMD continues to dominate with its X3D processors, and the Ryzen 7 9850X3D remains the fastest gaming CPU money can buy.
What's changed in the last few months is pricing, and right now the 9850X3D is a much more attractive option. Amazon has discounted the 9850X3D to just $399, matching the price of the 9800X3D. Given that the 9850X3D is ~5% faster on average, there's really no reason to buy the 9800X3D at the same price.
Of course, that 4-5% improvement isn't exactly exciting, and as we found in our original review, the additional performance comes at the cost of substantially higher power consumption. Still, both processors are relatively efficient compared to Intel's previous flagships, and at identical prices, we'd take the extra performance.
The 9850X3D is also around 15% faster than the Ryzen 7 7800X3D in our CPU-limited gaming benchmarks, and a massive 40% faster than Intel's Core Ultra 9 285K. AMD's lead is particularly impressive in titles such as Baldur's Gate 3, Cyberpunk 2077, and Assetto Corsa Competizione, where the additional L3 cache makes a significant difference.
But do you really need to spend $400 on a gaming CPU? Absolutely not.
The older Ryzen 7 7800X3D remains an option at around $339. It's roughly 15% slower than the 9850X3D, but costs 15% less, making it a reasonable alternative. There's also the newer Ryzen 7 7700X3D, which launched in July at $329 and is currently available for $299. This is essentially a slightly downclocked 7800X3D, and in our 13-game benchmark we found it was just 7% slower on average, while trailing the 9800X3D by 15%.
At these prices, the 7700X3D is arguably the best-value X3D processor for gamers. It delivers excellent gaming performance, and you're saving $100 compared to the 9850X3D. All of these processors use AMD's AM5 platform, so you're also getting a much better upgrade path than Intel's current LGA1851 offerings.
One important consideration is that all these CPUs require DDR5 memory, which has become painfully expensive. The good news is that AMD's X3D processors aren't particularly sensitive to memory speed. In our testing, the 9850X3D lost very little performance when switching from DDR5-6000 CL30 to slower DDR5-4800 CL40 memory, making cheaper DDR5 kits a viable option.
For most gamers, our Core Ultra 7 270K Plus recommendation will be more than sufficient, especially considering its outstanding productivity performance and current pricing. But if gaming is your priority, AMD's X3D processors remain the top choice.

articles.title: Tesla FSD v15 : cette mise à jour évite les nids-de-poule, freine devant les radars et ajoute la réalité augmentée
articles.text:
À défaut de sortir de nouveaux modèles, Tesla continue d’affiner son FSD. La dernière mise à jour en date promet en ce sens de corriger les faiblesses structurelles de la version actuelle. Le FSD v15 lit ainsi mieux les panneaux, évite plus habilement les nids de poule et réagit plus rapidement aux zones scolaires. Au bout du compte, la marque assure une gestion « 25 fois plus performante des situations critiques ».
Cerise sur le gâteau, une représentation ultra-réaliste en réalité augmentée de l’environnement s’invite sur l’écran central. Mais qu’apporte concrètement cette nouvelle mise à jour ? Dans le détail, la navigation est améliorée grâce à l’utilisation d’un modèle d’apprentissage de bout en bout basé sur les données d’autres véhicules ayant déjà emprunté un itinéraire similaire.
Stationnement personnalisé et détection des radars au programme
Ensuite, une fois arrivé à destination, le stationnement pourra se faire de plusieurs manières via l’historique de stationnement personnalisé. Le véhicule offrira de fait une poignée d’options pour se garer en fonction du lieu sur lequel il se trouve. D’autre part, le dispositif de surveillance de l’attention du conducteur gagne en efficacité lorsque la personne porte un chapeau ou des lunettes de soleil.
La caméra placée au-dessus du rétroviseur demeure en revanche la même. Les petits animaux et les débris sur la chaussée sont d’autre part mieux détectés pour éviter une collision. Les zones inondées seront aussi contournées si la profondeur d’eau est trop importante pour envisager un passage. Enfin, le FSD pourra ralentir à l’approche d’un radar et deviendra compatible avec l’usage d’un porte-vélos.
 FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network
Safety
25x better handling of safety critical cases
Tesla Reality View 
Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to do
Navigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW
— Tesla (@Tesla) November 21, 2026
Tesla Reality View : une nouvelle interface en réalité augmentée
Mais le plus impressionnant demeure la fonction Tesla Reality View permettant de visualiser tout ce qui se passe autour du véhicule. La représentation actuelle modélisant l’environnement de manière simpliste devient ainsi complètement obsolète. Qu’en est-il alors de la promesse d’une efficacité 25 fois supérieure formulée initialement ? Tesla ne fournit aucun chiffre précis. Le magazine Electrek a mené sa petite enquête.
Puisque le FSD v14 pouvait parcourir quelques milliers de kilomètres sans intervention critique du conducteur, il serait raisonnable de penser que le FSD v15 soit capable de rouler environ 80 000 km sans aucune manipulation d’urgence. La promesse est grande, mais possible à tenir vu les derniers ajustements du FSD. Rappelons en effet que le système ne peut plus faire de gros excès de vitesse en dépassant seulement la limite de 10 % au maximum.
Une allure plus faible permettra à l’ensemble de mieux gérer les situations critiques comme décrit. De quoi permettre à Tesla de creuser à nouveau l’écart avec ses concurrents chinois, qui investissent aussi massivement dans la conduite entièrement autonome.
