articles.title: How to Run NVIDIA Cosmos 3 on Local AI Devices Using Hugging Face Diffusers
articles.text:
Running video generation models locally can be challenging when model weights and intermediate data exceed available GPU memory. NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano is a world foundation model that generates videos from text, images, and other inputs to support physical AI development. Learn more about NVIDIA Cosmos for physical AI.
This tutorial walks you through how to run Cosmos 3 Nano on a GPU with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by storing most model weights in system RAM and transferring them to the GPU as needed. Using Hugging Face Diffusers, you’ll generate your first video, explore sound and additional input types, and use an FP8 checkpoint to further reduce memory requirements.
This streaming adapter builds on top of the native group offloading approach from the Hugging Face library to enable generation on a smaller GPU. The tradeoff is that this requires increased system RAM use and PCIe transfers for a smaller GPU-memory requirement. Note that this approach does not provide interactive latency or stream weights directly from disk during inference.
Step 1: Generate your first video
Use an existing Linux environment with Python 3.12 and a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build compatible with your GPU. The tested consumer-GPU hosts had approximately 128 GB of system RAM; this is not a measured minimum.
Clone Cosmos-Framework and install its standalone offloading package in your active environment. Run all examples and benchmark commands below from the package directory:
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/cosmos-framework.git
cd cosmos-framework/packages/diffusers-cpu-offloading
uv pip install '.[benchmarks]'
Pass the Hugging Face repository ID directly to build_pipeline. The first load downloads the checkpoint. Subsequent loads reuse cached files. Safety checking is enabled by default.
import torch
from cosmos3_streaming import StreamingConfig, build_pipeline
device = "cuda:0"
config = StreamingConfig(device=device)
pipe = build_pipeline(
    "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano",
    config=config,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
With no revision argument, the BF16 load uses the repository’s default branch. The default configuration chooses appropriate memory-saving behavior automatically.
Start with BF16 and PyTorch scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), the baseline used on all four tested GPUs.
Set the video options
This example generates 189 frames at 720p. For faster iteration on a 12 GB GPU, change height and width to 480 and 848, or 240 and 432.
common_video_args = {
    "negative_prompt": "",
    "num_frames": 189,
    "height": 720,
    "width": 1280,
    "fps": 24.0,
    "num_inference_steps": 35,
    "guidance_scale": 6.0,
    "add_resolution_template": False,
    "add_duration_template": False,
}
Generate and save the video
Next, generate and save the video using the following script:
t2v = pipe(
    prompt='{"scene":"A robot arm working in a kitchen"}',
    generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(123),
    output="videos",
    **common_video_args,
)
# Save the returned video frames as an MP4 file:
from diffusers.utils import export_to_video
export_to_video(t2v, "cosmos3_t2v.mp4", fps=common_video_args["fps"])
Step 2: Offload weights storage
The central idea is to store model weights in system RAM and use the GPU for computation.
To run large models within tight VRAM limits, this execution model manages memory and compute across the CPU and GPU in four ways:
- Checkpoint weights that are not currently needed remain in system RAM, in BF16 or the checkpoint’s FP8 representation.
- The next transformer block is transferred to the GPU when required.
- Every matrix multiplication and attention operation runs on CUDA.
- The adapter manages memory for denoising, the variational autoencoder (VAE) that encodes and decodes video, and safety checking.
With this approach, system RAM acts as the backing store for model weights. More demanding requests, including 720p Transfer on a 12 GB GPU, use an automatic lower-memory execution mode while keeping model computation on CUDA.
Move weights from system RAM to the GPU
Next, move weights from system RAM to the GPU. Figure 1 shows the path from checkpoint storage to GPU computation. Checkpoint files remain on disk between runs. During generation, system RAM is the backing store for weights that are not currently on the GPU. This is why a fast SSD helps with model loading, while sufficient system RAM and PCIe bandwidth matter during generation.
Reuse understanding context during generation
Diffusers provides sequential, model-level, and group-level CPU offloading to move model components between CPU and GPU memory. The Cosmos adapter builds on those mechanisms and coordinates when the model’s understanding and generation pathways run.
NVIDIA Cosmos 3, an open omnimodal world foundation model for physical AI, has two complementary pathways inside its transformer:
- The understanding pathway interprets the prompt and other conditioning inputs. These inputs remain fixed during generation.
- The generation pathway processes the evolving video, sound, or action representation at every denoising step while using the understanding result as context.
The transformer contains both understanding and generation computation. With fixed conditioning and precision, the adapter prepares the understanding context once and reuses it during generation. If native FP8 precision changes during denoising, that context is refreshed to match.
Video 1 shows how generation traverses the transformer blocks at each denoising step. A 35-step request runs denoising steps 1 through 35. Each step traverses 36 transformer blocks, indexed 0 through 35. After block 35, the scheduler updates the generation state and the next step starts at block 0. After the final denoising step, the pipeline decodes the output.
Classifier-free guidance (CFG) in Hugging Face combines predictions with and without prompt conditioning at each denoising step. The adapter reuses each streamed block across these predictions instead of transferring its weights for each branch. Transfer can add a control branch, which the automatic low-memory mode handles through the same API.
Keep the official Diffusers pipeline
The adapter uses the official Diffusers modular pipeline for:
- Prompt processing
- Conditioning and latent preparation
- Sequence preparation
- The denoising loop and UniPC scheduler
- Masking and classifier-free guidance output handling
- VAE decode
- Safety checking
- Output conversion
Manage memory across the complete request
Block offloading alone is not enough for the complete Cosmos pipeline. The adapter applies the following behavior automatically.
Reuse fixed understanding work
With fixed precision, the understanding pathway runs once for fixed conditioning inputs and its context is reused during denoising.
Stream generation blocks
Transformer weights remain in system RAM until their block is needed. The active block moves to the GPU, performs its CUDA work for the current denoising step, and makes room for the next block. Guidance predictions share the same block placement whenever possible.
Overlap transfers with computation
When the GPU has enough headroom, the next block can begin moving while the current block computes. Larger workloads automatically use the safer lower-memory schedule. There is no user-facing transfer schedule to configure.
Manage decoding and safety checks
VAE processing and safety checking have different memory requirements from denoising. The adapter manages those phases separately and automatically uses memory-efficient VAE execution on constrained cards. Users do not choose device-specific tuning values.
Handle larger Transfer requests
Transfer Modality performs more guidance work than text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V). At 720p on a 12 GB GPU, the adapter automatically selects a lower-memory execution mode. The full GeForce RTX 5070 modality results include its generation time and guardrail settings.
Step 3: Generate other modalities ( sound, action, etc )
Reuse pipe, device, and common_video_args from Step 1 for the examples in this section. Replace the input image and video paths with your own files. The prompts are illustrative; use the benchmark scripts for the exact measured inputs. Video-only calls return a list of frames. Calls requesting sound or action return a mapping of the requested outputs.
Image-to-video
Condition generation on an image with image=.
from diffusers.utils import load_image
image = load_image("/path/to/conditioning_image.jpg")
i2v = pipe(
    prompt='{"scene":"A vehicle approaches a rockfall on a coastal road"}',
    image=image,
    generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(1111),
    output="videos",
    **common_video_args,
)
Video-to-video
Pass a source video and choose the conditioning frames for video-to-video (V2V) generation.
from diffusers.utils import load_video
source_video = load_video("/path/to/source_video.mp4")
v2v = pipe(
    prompt='{"scene":"A robot pours liquid into a cup"}',
    video=source_video,
    condition_frame_indexes_vision=[0, 1],
    condition_video_keep="first",
    generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0),
    output="videos",
    **common_video_args,
)
Text-to-video with sound
Set enable_sound=True and include an audio description to generate video and sound together.
t2v_sound = pipe(
    prompt=(
        '{"scene":"A robot arm working in a kitchen",'
        '"audio_description":"Soft servo whirring and a ceramic clink."}'
    ),
    enable_sound=True,
    generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0),
    output=["videos", "sound", "sampling_rate"],
    **common_video_args,
)
Image-to-video with sound
Combine the image input with enable_sound=True to generate both outputs.
i2v_sound = pipe(
    prompt=(
        '{"scene":"A vehicle travels along a coastal road",'
        '"audio_description":"Road noise, wind, and distant waves."}'
    ),
    image=image,
    enable_sound=True,
    generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0),
    output=["videos", "sound", "sampling_rate"],
    **common_video_args,
)
Action generation
Use CosmosActionCondition to select the action domain and provide the conditioning video.
from diffusers import CosmosActionCondition
action_result = pipe(
    prompt="Put the pot to the left of the purple item.",
    action=CosmosActionCondition(
        mode="policy",
        chunk_size=16,
        domain_name="bridge_orig_lerobot",
        resolution_tier=480,
        video=load_video("/path/to/bridge_input.mp4"),
        view_point="ego_view",
    ),
    fps=5,
    num_inference_steps=30,
    guidance_scale=1.0,
    use_system_prompt=False,
    generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0),
    output=["videos", "action"],
)
Control-guided generation
Pass a control video with the control_videos argument. Safety checking remains enabled in this example; the benchmark’s guardrails-off exception is documented with the results.
transfer = pipe(
    prompt='{"scene":"Transform the input using edge guidance"}',
    negative_prompt="",
    control_videos={
        "edge": load_video("/path/to/control_edge.mp4"),
    },
    num_frames=121,
    height=720,
    width=1280,
    fps=30.0,
    num_inference_steps=35,
    guidance_scale=3.0,
    control_guidance=1.5,
    generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0),
    output="videos",
)
Diffusers routes each call to the appropriate workflow and loads the required components through the same pipeline.
Step 4: Use the FP8 checkpoint
Use nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano with the FP8 branch for the dedicated FP8 checkpoint. From the same package directory, install the FP8 extra, which includes NVIDIA Model Optimizer, before loading the checkpoint:
uv pip install '.[benchmarks,fp8]'
Select the FP8 branch through the same Hub API by passing revision="fp8":
pipe = build_pipeline(
    "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano",
    revision="fp8",
    config=StreamingConfig(device="cuda:0"),
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    checkpoint_precision="fp8",
)
The adapter uses the checkpoint’s native Diffusers precision policy. W8A8 uses 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations. W8A16 reuses the stored 8-bit weights, dequantizes them for a linear operation, and uses 16-bit activations. The tested Nano video checkpoint selects W8A16 for the first three and last three denoising steps and W8A8 for the middle steps. Note that attention remains BF16 SDPA; the entire pipeline does not run in FP8.
Step 5: Choose a GPU and resolution
Use Table 1 to choose a starting resolution. The default configuration adapts automatically to the requested resolution, modality, and available GPU memory.
| GPU class | Recommended use | 
|---|---|
| 12 GB | Start at 240p or 480p for iteration. Full 720p is supported, including Transfer, but can be substantially slower. | 
| 16 GB | 480p is a practical iteration mode; 720p is supported with automatic memory management. | 
| 24 GB | Full-resolution generation has more working room and is materially faster in the tested configuration. | 
| 32 GB | Best measured consumer-GPU latency for the 720p BF16 workload. | 
These are guidance ranges rather than fixed limits. Resolution, frame count, modality, checkpoint precision, available system RAM, and PCIe bandwidth all affect fit and runtime.
Step 6: Benchmark setup and results
The presented results cover text-to-video across four GeForce RTX cards and all seven generation modalities on the GeForce RTX 5070. Use Table 4 to estimate memory requirements and wait times. Hosts, software revisions, and safety settings can affect latency, so these single-run measurements are not a controlled GPU ranking or a multiseed BF16-versus-FP8 comparison.
Reproduce the benchmarks
From the package directory used in Step 1, run the BF16 and FP8 benchmarks separately to measure your system. These commands cover all seven modalities and three resolution tiers. Install the FP8 dependency from Step 4 before running the FP8 command.
python benchmarks/benchmark_bf16.py --output-dir artifacts/benchmark-bf16
python benchmarks/benchmark_fp8.py --output-dir artifacts/benchmark-fp8
The benchmark guide in benchmarks/README.md explains the pinned inputs, per-case logs, summary tables, --resume, and --preflight-only. Safety checks are enabled by default. Reproducing the labeled Transfer timings requires an explicit Transfer-only run with --transfer-without-guardrails. The FP8 runner records the exact checkpoint revision and uses the native Diffusers policy.
Test settings
The benchmark workloads use the bundled model-card inputs. Each saved video was checked for its output dimensions, frame count, and frame rate. Sound cases also produced WAV files, and Action cases produced action JSON. Table 2 lists the generation and timing settings.
| Control | BF16 T2V | RTX 5070 modalities | 
|---|---|---|
| Output | 189 frames, 24 fps | 189 frames for video/sound; 17 for Action; 121 at 30 fps for Transfer | 
| Resolution tiers | 432×240, 848×480, 1280×720 | 432×240, 848×480, 1280×720; action uses corresponding tiers | 
| Denoising | 35 UniPC steps, CFG 6, seed 123 | 35 steps for video/sound/Transfer; 30 for Action; fixed per-modality inputs and seeds | 
| Safety | Enabled | Enabled except the explicitly labeled guardrails-off Transfer rows | 
| Timing | Pipeline call through returned frames | Pipeline call through returned modality tensors | 
| Excluded | Construction, checkpoint loading, MP4 encoding | Construction, checkpoint loading, file encoding | 
Tested hardware
Table 3 lists the tested GPUs. Each host had approximately 128 GB of system RAM. CPU offloading exchanges GPU memory pressure for system RAM use. The measured consumer-GPU hosts had approximately 128 GB of system RAM.
| GPU | Architecture | Compute capability | VRAM | System RAM | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GeForce RTX 5070 | Blackwell GB205 | SM120 | 12 GB | 128 GB class | 
| GeForce RTX 5080 | Blackwell GB203 | SM120 | 16 GB | 128 GB class | 
| GeForce RTX 4090 | Ada AD102 | SM89 | 24 GB | 128 GB class | 
| GeForce RTX 5090 | Blackwell GB202 | SM120 | 32 GB | 128 GB class |

Get started with Cosmos 3 Nano on GeForce RTX GPUs
Weight streaming enables you to experiment with NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano on RTX GPUs with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by storing model weights in system RAM while keeping computation on the GPU.
To get started, install the Cosmos-Framework offloading package and run the BF16 text-to-video example at 240p or 480p. Then explore image- and video-conditioned generation, sound, actions, and control inputs through the same Diffusers API. Try the FP8 checkpoint and use the included benchmarks to compare generation time and memory use on your hardware.
- Download the Cosmos 3 Nano checkpoint and its FP8 branch on Hugging Face.
- Find examples and code in the Cosmos-Framework offloading package.
- Review the Diffusers memory optimization guide for CPU offloading and the Cosmos 3 pipeline documentation for supported generation workflows.
- Join the community, open issues, and contribute to the Cosmos ecosystem on GitHub and Discord.

articles.title: Logitech G lança teclado G316 X 75 no Brasil com 8 kHz, switches hot-swappable e display LED por R$ 584,90
articles.text:
Com taxa de resposta de até 8 kHz, formato de 75% e preço sugerido de R$ 584,90, a Logitech G anunciou a chegada do teclado Logitech G316 X 75 ao Brasil. O novo modelo gamer com fio está disponível nas cores preto e branco e aposta em desempenho, personalização e melhor aproveitamento do espaço no setup.
A proposta é oferecer uma experiência completa de jogo sem ocupar muito espaço na mesa. Segundo a empresa, o teclado amplia o acesso a recursos de personalização e a tecnologias que fazem diferença para os jogadores.
Desempenho e personalização do G316 X 75
O principal diferencial é a taxa de resposta de até 8 kHz, que garante uma comunicação rápida entre o teclado e o computador. Os switches são hot-swappable, ou seja, podem ser trocados com facilidade, o que permite ajustar a experiência de digitação e de jogo.
No visual, as keycaps são de PBT e têm hastes cross hatch, o que abre mais possibilidades de personalização.
Construção e display LED
O G316 X 75 usa o sistema gasket mount, com estrutura de silicone e camadas de amortecimento acústico. Segundo a Logitech G, o resultado é uma digitação mais suave e responsiva, com sonoridade diferenciada. A ideia é oferecer conforto e uma experiência tátil aprimorada durante o uso.
Outro destaque é o display LED de matriz de pontos integrado, que exibe animações e permite controlar configurações direto pelo seletor. Entre as funções disponíveis estão ajustes de volume, reprodução de mídia, brilho e taxa de resposta, sem interromper o jogo.
Iluminação RGB LIGHTSYNC e software G HUB
A iluminação usa a tecnologia RGB LIGHTSYNC e permite configurar cada tecla individualmente, além de até 30 zonas diferentes na barra de luz. Pelo software G HUB, o jogador cria macros, personaliza atribuições de teclas, configura o modo de jogo e ajusta outras funcionalidades do equipamento.
Preço e onde comprar o Logitech G316 X 75
O G316 X 75 chega à Logitech Store com preço sugerido de R$ 584,90, ou R$ 497,17 para quem optar pelo PIX.
“O G316 X 75 chega para ampliar o acesso a recursos de personalização e tecnologias que fazem diferença na experiência dos jogadores. Sabemos que cada gamer tem seu próprio estilo e suas preferências na hora de montar um setup”, afirma Leandro Rocha, gerente de produtos da Logitech G no Brasil.
Com o G316 X 75, a Logitech G amplia seu portfólio de teclados gamers no Brasil, reunindo recursos de personalização, desempenho e design compacto em uma opção voltada a diferentes perfis de jogadores.
É técnica em audiovisual e community manager com 7 anos de experiência no universo gamer.
Amazon Prime também é feito para jogadores!
Todo mês, obtenha itens exclusivos, jogos grátis, uma assinatura gratuita na Twitch.tv e muito mais com sua assinatura Prime. Clique aqui para um teste gratuito de 30 dias.

articles.title: Das Ramageddon ist real: So sehr sind Preise für PCs, Konsolen und Speicher gestiegen
articles.text:
Chipkrise: So stark sind Preise für PCs, Konsolen und Speicher gestiegen
Laptops, Spielekonsolen und andere Elektronikartikel haben sich mit dem Boom um Künstliche Intelligenz deutlich verteuert. Wie das Statistische Bundesamt mitteilte, waren Laptops im Oktober fast 15 Prozent teurer als ein Jahr zuvor und Desktop-PCs gut 13 Prozent. „Ein Grund dafür ist der gestiegene Bedarf an Speicherkapazität für KI-Rechenzentren, der sich auch in der Entwicklung der Verbraucherpreise für Speichermedien widerspiegelt“, heißt es in der Mitteilung.
So verteuerten sich Festplatten im Oktober zum Vorjahresmonat um 40,8 Prozent, Speicherkarten, USB-Sticks und Ähnliches waren gut ein Fünftel (22,1 Prozent) teurer. Auch bei anderen digitalen Geräten gebe es Preiserhöhungen: Spielekonsolen verteuerten sich um 13 Prozent, Mobiltelefone ohne Vertrag um gut zwölf Prozent, Smartwatches, Fitnesstracker oder Ähnliches um rund sechs Prozent. Die Preise für E-Book-Reader blieben dagegen fast unverändert. Zum Vergleich: Die Verbraucherpreise insgesamt stiegen im Oktober zum Vorjahresmonat um 2,8 Prozent.
Preise für Computer mittelfristig gefallen
Den jüngsten Preisanstiegen für Laptops und Co gingen allerdings teils deutliche Preisnachlässe in den Vorjahren voraus. 2025 waren Desktop-PCs gut 16 Prozent und Laptops rund 9 Prozent günstiger als 2020, so die Statistiker. Mobiltelefone ohne Vertrag wurden in dem Zeitraum 11,7 Prozent günstiger, Spielekonsolen 4,2 Prozent und Smartwatches, Fitnesstracker und Co 3,3 Prozent. „Diese Preissenkungen resultierten vor allem aus dem Abbau von Überproduktionen, die während der Covid-19-Pandemie entstanden waren“, hieß es.
Unterhaltselektronik und Haushaltsgeräte billiger
Während Computer zuletzt deutlich teurer waren als vor einem Jahr, verbilligte sich Unterhaltungselektronik. So mussten Verbraucher für Fernsehgeräte im Oktober 9,2 Prozent weniger zahlen und für Kameras 2,5 Prozent weniger.
Auch Haushaltselektrogeräte verbilligten sich: Die Preise für Geschirrspülmaschinen lagen im Oktober sieben Prozent niedriger als ein Jahr zuvor. Kaffeevollautomaten oder Espressomaschinen verbilligten sich um 5,4 Prozent, Waschmaschinen um gut vier Prozent, Toaster oder Grillgeräte um 1,5 Prozent.

articles.title: How Canada’s Pharmacy Shift Prepared MedMe for the US Market
articles.text:
When Canadians talk about healthcare access, the conversation often centres on finding a family doctor. But for many of us, a pharmacy is closer to home, making it one of the most convenient places to get expert advice and treatment.
According to Purya Sarmadi, CEO and co-founder of MedMe Health, 90 percent of North Americans live within about five miles (eight kilometres) of a neighbourhood drugstore. He sees an opportunity to use that access better as provinces expand pharmacists’ responsibilities, from treating common infections to helping patients manage chronic conditions like diabetes and asthma.
“We invest in this because the distance between installing software and delivering care is where most clinical programs stall.”
Purya Sarmadi, MedMe
His company provides an AI-enabled platform for connecting the whole patient journey, from booking and intake to clinical documentation and billing. Since 2019, the Toronto-based digital health startup has grown to serve over 40 percent of the Canadian pharmacy market, supporting more than 30 million patient interactions, according to the company.
MedMe is now bringing that experience to the US, where pharmacies are beginning to take on the clinical role that their Canadian counterparts have been developing, albeit with the added challenge of navigating a more complicated payment system.
“We have shown in Canada what pharmacists can do once they are authorized, paid, and equipped to practice to their full scope, and we intend to make that the standard for pharmacy practice everywhere,” Sarmadi told BetaKit.
Canada’s head start
MedMe deliberately chose Canada as a place to develop its platform alongside pharmacies already putting new models of care into practice.
“Canadian provinces expanded pharmacists’ scope of practice and began paying pharmacies for clinical services years before most US states,” said Sarmadi.
By 2020, the pandemic was bringing more patients into pharmacies for vaccinations and testing, broadening their view of what pharmacists could offer, he added. As demand grew, the number of locations using MedMe rose from about 100 to nearly 1,200 in ten weeks, according to the company.
Working with those businesses revealed two recurring problems, said Sarmadi. Patients didn’t always know what was available at their local pharmacy, leaving appointment slots unfilled, while manual intake systems, phone scheduling, and documentation completed after hours made consultations time-consuming and costly to deliver.
Among its solutions, MedMe introduced Patient Concierge, an AI agent that answers the phone and contacts patients to coordinate refills or schedule deliveries. Its Clinical Assistant drafts consultation notes for pharmacists to review and sign. One Calgary pharmacist puts the cost at about 18 cents a consult, the company says.
But introducing clinical programs also changed how the whole store operated, from staffing and training to measuring returns, Sarmadi said. It meant MedMe’s approach had to go beyond technology. The company built READY, an implementation framework that involves pharmacists and managers in designing routines that fit appointments around dispensing, trains staff one-on-one during launch, and monitors adoption. Locations go live only when their teams are prepared.
“We invest in this because the distance between installing software and delivering care is where most clinical programs stall,” said Sarmadi.
He points to Nova Scotia as an example of how technology can support a larger clinical role for pharmacies. Since 2023, the province has funded a network of Community Pharmacy Primary Care Clinics, which is credited with a decline of close to 10 percent in emergency room visits for non-urgent and less urgent cases.
The Pharmacy Association of Nova Scotia selected MedMe to build and run the booking platform for all 44 clinics, giving patients a direct way to arrange a visit as pharmacies become an established part of the province’s primary care network. The province’s 811 health advice line also directs callers there when it’s the right setting for their care.
That experience gives MedMe a model to draw on as US states invest in community pharmacies to improve access to care in rural areas.
Taking the experience south
MedMe is drawing on its Canadian experience to support its US rollout; it’s now live in more than 350 US pharmacies, with further launches planned through 2027. Critically, they bring an understanding of the correct sequence of steps needed to make clinical care viable.
“Scope expands first, billing pathways follow, and then comes the operational work of building patient demand, delivering care efficiently, changing how the pharmacy runs and, fundamentally, what it is for,” explained Sarmadi. “We entered the US having already built for each of those stages.”
The company also brought its Canadian-built online booking and patient outreach tools, along with experience helping teams adapt to new ways of working. Sarmadi likens that shift to a large company adopting a new customer relationship management system, which requires rethinking roles, processes, and reporting, rather than simply installing software.
“The point is to get the pharmacist in front of the patient at exactly the right moment, and far more often than happens today.”
Purya Sarmadi, MedMe
“Every rollout we run in the US therefore covers the whole operation,” he said.
Unlike Canada’s provincially funded programs with set fees, however, American pharmacies face multiple payers with different coverage and billing requirements. Rejected or denied claims can leave staff chasing payments, making expanding clinical roles more challenging. MedMe’s platform is designed to handle rejection and denial management on its customers’ behalf.
At Pucci’s Pharmacy in Sacramento, Calif., for instance, the owner previously relied on four separate systems for scheduling and intake, documentation, dispensing, and outside billing. He and his clinical pharmacist spent days calling health plans, while some denied claims went unpursued, according to Sarmadi.
Since moving onto MedMe in September 2025, the store has logged about 2,700 clinical appointments. It now handles around 300 a month, up from 140 last winter, and 41 percent of patients book online themselves.
Processing claims across multiple businesses also gives MedMe insight into which payers deny particular treatments, and why. The company incorporates those findings into billing rules and automation used across its platform, reducing the need for each customer to learn through its own trial and error.
Future of pharmacy care
Sarmadi sees a future where pharmacy care continues between appointments. Pharmacists would have access to patients’ medication histories and readings from home monitors, while AI would help coordinate follow-up and routine outreach. If blood pressure readings change or a refill goes uncollected, for example, the team could reach out rather than wait for the patient’s next visit.
“What AI shouldn’t do is make the clinical call,” he said. “The point is to get the pharmacist in front of the patient at exactly the right moment, and far more often than happens today.”
Aaron Bast, managing director at Graphite Ventures, which has invested in MedMe, sees the company’s Canadian roots as a key strength as it pursues its global ambitions.
“MedMe is exactly what we mean by Scale Canadian,” he said. “Purya and the team built where pharmacy care was changing first, earned the trust of Canada’s pharmacies, and are now bringing a proven playbook to a much larger market. Canadian companies don’t have to leave to win globally. They can take what they’ve built in Canada as a model for international success.”
PRESENTED BY
Check out Scale Canadian for more stories of those building in Canada and scaling globally.
Feature image courtesy MedMe.

articles.title: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
articles.text:
Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.
David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.
Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”
Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.
It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.
Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.
At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.
Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.
Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

articles.title: Prepare Market Data for Forecasting with NVIDIA Megatron Core
articles.text:
Market data arrives as a stream of trades and quotes: every execution, bid, and ask, timestamped to the microsecond. Preparing this data for AI-based market forecasting requires turning price and volume histories into consistent inputs for model training and inference. A common first step is aggregating the data into bars—one row per instrument per time unit—with price, volume, and other statistics. Neural networks can learn patterns from these histories across instruments and forecast horizons.
NVIDIA Megatron Core is an open-source library of GPU-optimized components for training transformer models at scale. Megatron-LM is a GitHub repository that combines that library with preconfigured training scripts. A preprocessing script turns intraday market bars into model-ready tensors, and a dataset provider feeds them into Megatron’s distributed training loop.
This post shows how to preprocess market-bar data and train a model with Megatron-LM to forecast returns and trading volume across multiple horizons.
Forecast returns and trading volume
Price and volume remain continuous features. A learned patch embedding turns each group of observations into a model input without converting market values into text.
A common data interface supports training a shared forecasting model on histories from many instruments. Each training window belongs to one instrument and includes its identifier, so the model can learn instrument-specific behavior within shared parameters. You can also explore longer contexts, different sampling frequencies, and additional features through the same interface.
The example forecasts returns and trading volume at several horizons from the same context. Quantitative researchers can use these outputs to study short-term market behavior, trading activity, or execution timing. Point and interval forecasts address different research questions while using the same input representation.
You can change the model architecture, optimizer, or training duration while reusing a prepared dataset. Preprocessing records the patch size, context length, and forecast horizons in the saved metadata, making the data configuration an explicit part of each experiment.
A consistent representation also separates the source feed from the model. Data from a new vendor or sampling scheme can follow the same row schema, while the dataset provider supplies the same batch fields. Figure 1 shows the pipeline from market bars to training.
From price and volume to model-ready sequences
The input is a directory of Parquet files with one row per bar and Symbol, Date, Timestamp, Close, and Volume columns, plus optional numeric feature columns. Bars can come from different vendors and sampling schemes, such as one-minute or sub-minute aggregates of tick data. Keep each instrument’s trading day in one file and the files in chronological order. The script sorts each instrument’s daily observations by timestamp. The script derives within-day log returns and log volumes itself, so the overnight gap never enters the inputs. The preprocessor treats rows as observation steps and leaves gaps unchanged. Align the data upstream if you need a regular time grid.
preprocessing.py groups consecutive bars for one instrument on one trading day into patches—the model’s tokens—and slides fixed-length context windows over them.
Each patch retains the features of its constituent rows. For example, eight bars per patch and 32 patches per window provide 256 observations in a sequence of 32 model positions. An instrument ID identifies the series, and each patch carries its position within the trading day (Figure 2).
Run preprocessing and training
Before running the example, see the preprocessing README for environment setup, input-file requirements, configuration options, and output tensor formats.
First, preprocess the market bars into training-ready tensors:
python examples/financial_timeseries/preprocessing.py \
    --data-dir /data/bars --out-dir /data/tensors \
    --patch-len 8 --context-len 32 --window-stride 16 \
    --time-units-per-day 390 --horizons 1,2,5,15 \
    --target-mode cumulative --no-allow-overnight-targets
Then, run the Megatron training example with the saved tensors:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 -m examples.financial_timeseries.pretrain_ts \
    --ts-data-path /data/tensors --dataloader-type cyclic \
    --num-layers 4 --hidden-size 256 --num-attention-heads 4 \
    --seq-length 32 --max-position-embeddings 32 \
    --micro-batch-size 64 --global-batch-size 256 --train-iters 2000 \
    --lr 3e-4 --min-lr 3e-5 --lr-decay-style cosine --lr-warmup-iters 100 \
    --tokenizer-type NullTokenizer --bf16 \
    --log-interval 50 --eval-interval 500 --eval-iters 20 \
    --save /data/ckpt --save-interval 2000
This small model shows the expected input and output formats. Use it to check that preprocessing, the data loader, target masking, and loss computation work together before substituting your forecasting architecture.
You can replace this model while keeping the data layer unchanged. forward_step calls the model with patches (B, L, P, F), inst_id (B,), and patch_tod (B, L). loss_func expects a dictionary with return and volshare tensors of shape (B, L, H), with one forecast per context position and horizon. Any MegatronModule that takes those three inputs and returns that dictionary can replace it.
Defining forecast targets
Each window includes future targets for every context position, so one forward pass produces forecasts throughout the context rather than only at the end. A causal forecasting model uses only the history available at each position.
Forecast horizons can be defined in observation steps or patches. A point target uses the return and volume at a future step; a cumulative target uses the summed log return and total volume over the interval. Volume targets are represented on a log scale. Figure 3 shows both target definitions for the same context.
For regular one-minute bars, a horizon of five observation steps corresponds to five minutes. For event-based data, it counts events.
Efficient data loading for distributed training
The data pipeline consists of two stages: preprocessing and data loading. Preprocessing builds the features, patches, windows, and targets offline, then writes them as PyTorch tensor files: train.pt, val.pt, test.pt, and meta.pt. Training reads these saved tensors, keeping Parquet parsing and target construction outside the training loop.
Prepare once, reuse across runs
During preprocessing, the script handles files in order and uses array operations for regular bar layouts, with a per-instrument path for irregular observations. It computes each instrument’s target sequence once and reuses it across overlapping windows. Temporary memory-mapped arrays hold the completed split tensors before they are saved to disk.
The saved metadata records instrument mappings, feature names, patch and context lengths, forecast horizons, and normalization statistics. Model and dataset settings can be checked against the same description before training.
Map tensors and share batches
The data loader reads the saved splits and supplies batches for training or inference. Validation checks that required keys are present, sample counts align, and the stored context length matches the model. Each worker opens the saved file lazily through memory mapping; fetching a sample copies only its selected rows into private memory.
Within each tensor-parallel group, rank zero reads the microbatch and broadcasts it to the other ranks. Megatron’s sampler handles data-parallel sampling and can reshuffle and cycle through the saved windows for the requested number of training iterations. This connects the market-data interface to the training loop, parallelism, and checkpointing used by the forecasting model.
Preserving time in financial modeling
The outputs are split by date into training, validation, and test sets. A window is retained only when its entire context and future observations needed for the longest forecast horizon fall within the same split. This keeps validation or test observations from entering training windows or training targets.
An embargo removes trading days from the end of the training period before validation begins; validation and test are adjacent. The script also checks that the context patches used by different splits do not overlap. These safeguards address cross-split leakage that could introduce forward-looking bias.
Per-horizon target statistics are computed from the training split only. If you standardize targets, use these statistics during training, validation, and testing. Future evaluation data therefore does not determine the target scaling applied in training. The example trainer leaves targets unscaled.
Session boundaries are configurable. Input log returns reset at the start of each day. For cumulative forecasts, targets can include the overnight move; intraday-only targets instead mask horizons that cross the close. A separate setting keeps the input context within one trading day when that matches the task. The loader reconstructs valid-target masks from the saved values, so the loss can exclude unavailable targets.
These settings make the forecasting question explicit: which history is visible, how far ahead the target reaches, and whether the model is predicting within a session or across sessions.
Getting started
Use the preprocessing script and Megatron dataset provider with your own market-bar Parquet files. The input schema, tensor formats, and configuration options are documented in the preprocessing README, alongside a training example that connects the data interface to a forecasting model.
Choose the sampling frequency, context length, and forecast horizons that match your research question. Prepare the dataset, check its metadata and split counts, and use the saved tensors in a Megatron training run. Then experiment with other instruments, feature sets, and model configurations.

articles.title: What’s New for Game Developers: AI Animation and RTX Tools
articles.text:
This month’s NVIDIA game development updates help teams bring new graphics, animation, and local AI capabilities into their engines while balancing image quality, performance, and creative intent.
This post covers:
- Developer lessons from the War Thunder NVIDIA DLSS 5 integration
- NVIDIA Kimodo animation generation in Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview
- NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 updates for RTX Spark, speech recognition, and Vulkan
- NVIDIA RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 and RTX Path Tracing 1.9 improvements for lighting, integration, and debugging
- Nsight developer tools updates for Fall of 2026
How Gaijin raised War Thunder’s realism using NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering
In an interview, Gaijin Entertainment shares how it integrated DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering into War Thunder’s Dagor Engine while preserving the game’s established visual identity. The team explains how it adapted its color management pipeline to evaluate DLSS 5 in sRGB before post-processing and UI, then map the results back to linear HDR, saying “DLSS 5 delivers improved highlights and shadows while introducing a new level of microcontrast that we simply haven’t been able to achieve before. The result is a more natural, lifelike image, with finer detail and a stronger sense of realism.”
The team also discusses tuning DLSS 5 against its reference look to preserve vehicle markings, surface wear, and material properties, as well as evaluating image quality and performance separately across air, ground, and naval combat. The interview offers developers practical lessons on balancing lighting and material enhancements with their game’s art direction, with ON/OFF comparisons highlighting rainy, overcast scenes.
Read the full War Thunder interview.
NVIDIA Kimodo is the first model in Unreal Engine 5.9’s guided animation framework
Kimodo brings its animation research into Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview, which introduces a guided animation framework and a set of Sequencer tools that help animators work directly with AI motion-generation models. Kimodo is the first model integrated with it, enabling animators to generate character motion right inside Sequencer. The integration pairs GPU-accelerated motion generation with the familiar timeline editor workflow.
Animators can describe a motion with a text prompt, draw a spline path for the character to follow, and set target poses at specific frames. The model generates motion that follows these constraints, so teams decide where characters move and how they pose at key moments, bringing creative control into the animation.
Explore the Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview release notes and the Kimodo research project.
NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 expands platform and model support
The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK helps developers integrate NVIDIA ACE on-device. ACE is a suite of AI technologies designed to help middleware and game developers build knowledgeable, actionable, and conversational in-game characters. The SDK supports multiple inference backends across GPU and CPU hardware, giving teams a common interface for running AI alongside game graphics.
Version 1.8 focuses on platform support and the inference components used in language and speech workflows. Key updates include:
- RTX Spark: Hardened platform support for developers building applications
- Updated inference backends: Newer llama.cpp and whisper.cpp versions
- Expanded speech recognition: Support for the Parakeet automatic speech recognition (ASR) model through whisper.cpp
- Vulkan integration: Added support for the Vulkan priority API
- Additional bug fixes across the SDK.
Explore the NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK.
NVIDIA RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 adds sampling improvements and reservoir debugging tools
RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 is available on GitHub with updates for developers integrating ReSTIR lighting into their renderers. The release adds new sampling options for ReSTIR DI, adds RTX Spark support, and expands the tools used to inspect lighting reservoirs.
Release highlights include:
- Stratified low-discrepancy sampling for ReSTIR DI spatial resampling
- A fallback sample feature for ReSTIR DI
- Enhanced reservoir visualization for direct illumination, global illumination, and path tracing, giving developers more ways to inspect the samples used by each technique
- RTX Spark support
- Updated Donut and NVRHI components, along with bug fixes
Explore the RTXDI SDK and samples on GitHub.
NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 brings live acceleration structure inspection to D3D12 and Vulkan
NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 is now available on GitHub. The utility shows ray tracing acceleration structures while a game or renderer is running. It helps developers understand TLAS and BLAS contents, validate acceleration structure updates, and debug geometry-related ray tracing issues.
The viewer integrates at the graphics API level through Direct3D 12 and Vulkan libraries. Developers send acceleration structure builds, copies, queue submissions, and frame boundaries to the viewer, which displays the results in a separate window. Separate windows with its own camera allows it to inspect TLAS independently from the in-game camera.
To inspect an existing title without changing its code, developers can use the included sampler. It attaches the viewer to a running D3D12 or Vulkan process and serves as an integration sample.
Release highlights include:
- Visualization modes for primitive, geometry, instance, and cluster IDs, BLAS addresses, instance masks and flags, and acceleration structure update state
- Per-pixel trace time heatmaps that show which parts of a scene cost the most to trace
- Support for various geometry filters: flags, types and ray culling
- Support for Clustered geometry in D3D12
- Vendor-agnostic integration with optional vendor-specific paths, plus builds for Windows x64 and RTX Spark
Access the BVH Viewer on github and download the v1.0.0 release.
RTX Path Tracing 1.9 adds an introductory sample and SHaRC integration
NVIDIA RTX Path Tracing 1.9 gives developers a more accessible starting point for adding ray-traced lighting and studying a real-time path tracing pipeline.
The intro sample uses a hybrid deferred renderer to introduce lighting features one at a time across nine selectable steps. Developers can progress from image-based lighting and screen-space effects to ReSTIR DI, path-traced indirect lighting, and SHaRC radiance caching.
SHaRC is also integrated into the main real-time path tracer and enabled by default, providing additional indirect-lighting information to DLSS Ray Reconstruction. Other updates include:
- RTX Spark support
- Performance optimizations including real-time subsampling, overlapping DLSS Ray Reconstruction with the next frame’s path tracing, and GPU-side acceleration-structure instance generation
- Expanded NEE-AT light sampling support for up to two million lights and clustering of emissive triangles into light levels of detail
- A new design document describing the real-time path tracing pipeline, plus updated dependencies, fixes, and rendering improvements
Read the RTX Path Tracing 1.9 release notes and explore the Intro Sample.
RTX Global Illumination 2.9 adds improved diffuse GI sample and SER support
Release highlights for NVIDIA RTX Global Illumination 2.9 include:
- A new IndirectDiffuse sample introducing a deferred renderer that uses NRC or SHaRC for indirect diffuse illumination, complete with shadow mapping, sky lighting, and visualization modes
- Shader Execution Reordering (SER) support for Direct3D 12 (Shader Model 6.9) and Vulkan, toggleable directly from the UI
- Additional bug fixes and performance enhancements
NVIDIA Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems Introduce DLSS-FG Support, Agentic AI Tooling
Video 1. NVIDIA Nsight Graphics 2026.4 release spotlight, highlighting DLSS Frame Generation analysis and agentic AI tooling
NVIDIA Nsight Graphics 2026.4 and Nsight Systems 2026.6 introduce support for analyzing applications using DLSS Frame Generation (DLSS-FG). When integrating DLSS Frame Generation and Multi-Frame Generation into a title, it is important to understand both the work submitted by the application and the pacing of the frames presented to players.
In Nsight Graphics, GPU Trace now displays application and presented frames on separate timeline rows, while Graphics Capture preserves the DLSS-FG workload for inspection during capture and replay. Nsight Systems distinguishes generated frames from application frames and correlates them with CPU frame ranges. DLSS-FG support in both tools requires Streamline SDK 2.12 or newer.
The new releases also introduce agentic AI tooling for graphics development. A new Nsight Graphics MCP server enables compatible AI agents to capture applications, inspect and debug captures, and analyze GPU traces. Nsight Systems includes skill files that guide AI agents in diagnosing CPU bottlenecks, frame stutter, and CPU-GPU synchronization overhead.
Download Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems.
Resources for game developers
Check out the full list of game developer resources and stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news:
- Subscribe to our newsletter (select gaming as your industry)
- Follow us on social: X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube
- Join our Discord community

articles.title: Databricks has “very strong growth plans” for Canada
articles.text:
San Francisco-based data and AI platform Databricks, which already employs more than 500 people across Canada, intends to expand its presence in the country over the coming years.
The privately held software giant first began building a presence in Canada about seven years ago. Today, Databricks has around 300 employees at its Vancouver research and development hub, and “well over” 200 in Toronto, predominantly in go-to-market (GTM) positions.
Canada is a “tier-one” market
Since 2024, Databricks has grown its Canadian business by over 125 percent. In an interview with BetaKit, Databricks vice-president and general manager of Canada, Jim Lambe, said the firm sees a lot more room to expand with Canadian companies operating in energy, financial services, retail, technology, and telecommunications, as well as public sector organizations.
Lambe said Databricks considers Canada a “tier-one” market, revealing that the business has some “very strong growth plans for the country over the next 12 to 24 months,” as it builds out its local GTM, solution engineering, and forward-deployed engineering (FDE) teams.
Since 2024, Databricks has grown its Canadian business by over 125 percent.
“We’re building out all of those teams here in Canada,” Lambe added.
Databricks sells software designed to help other businesses and organizations store, manage, and analyze data, and build AI products. The company’s Canadian clients include Hydro-Québec, Rogers Communications, and TD Bank.
Two of Databricks’ co-founders, CTO Matei Zaharia and chief architect Reynold Xin, also have ties to Canada: Zaharia grew up in Toronto and attended the University of Waterloo, while Xin studied at the University of Toronto.
Lambe, who joined Databricks in June 2025 to help expand the company’s presence in Canada, did not disclose any specific hiring targets.
At the moment, Databricks’ current job postings list 27 open roles in Canada across both technical and sales-oriented functions.
RELATED: Databricks and Ada execs on what’s fuelling the Gen Z AI backlash
Lambe said FDEs in particular will be “a huge focus” as prospective customers seek “a more guided journey” to adopting AI.
On the back of strong investor demand for companies supporting the AI boom, The Wall Street Journal recently reported that Databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars in a new funding round that would value the company at about $225 billion USD ($323 billion CAD).
Lambe said Databricks’ Canadian customers are leveraging AI for everything from real-time financial fraud detection to analyzing investor calls and regulating how oil and gas flow.
“What’s really interesting about what we’re starting to see in Canada is each one of the industries that we talked about … are going deeper and deeper and deeper into their use and adoption of AI,” Lambe added.
Feature image courtesy Databricks.

articles.title: Verifying UCIe.mem: Flexible Verification For Compute And Memory Chiplets
articles.text:
Validate UCIe.mem implementations across development stages while reusing a common verification environment.
By Ujjwal Negi and Prashant Dixit
As chiplet-based designs become increasingly common, connecting compute and memory dies efficiently is an important part of building scalable systems. The Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) standard provides a common die-to-die interconnect, while UCIe.mem defines a standardized protocol for memory transactions between compute and memory chiplets.
Modern systems can combine compute chiplets with different memory technologies, including HBM, DDR, and LPDDR. Traditionally, integrating these components can involve technology-specific interfaces and custom mechanisms. UCIe.mem addresses the growing need for scalable and flexible memory architectures in modern computing systems by providing a common, memory-technology-agnostic way to communicate memory requests and responses across chiplets.
This standardization provides a foundation for more modular and scalable chiplet-based architectures. It allows compute and memory chiplets to be developed independently and integrated across implementations from different vendors, reducing reliance on custom, technology-specific interfaces. By decoupling memory communication from the underlying memory technology, UCIe.mem gives system designers greater flexibility to combine, reuse, and scale compute and memory resources to meet different application requirements.
Fig. 1: Memory and compute chiplet over UCIe.
While a common protocol helps streamline integration, verifying UCIe.mem introduces challenges at multiple levels. The protocol must be validated across initialization, credit management, transaction handling, packing, and data integrity. Verification must also account for concurrent requests, different channel configurations, and the correct association of responses with their originating requests.
A further challenge is accommodating different DUT interfaces and levels of integration. Early-stage designs may not yet implement UCIe.mem and may expose only a conventional memory interface, such as AXI. Other designs may implement UCIe.mem and expose FDI, allowing the DUT to generate and receive control and memory payload flits directly. At the system level, verification must extend beyond protocol compliance to include realistic interactions with the memory subsystem.
A flexible verification environment must support these different scenarios while maintaining consistent protocol validation and end-to-end checking.
Questa One Avery UCIe VIP provides a versatile verification platform that adapts to different DUT interfaces and system configurations. Rather than limiting verification to a single integration model, it enables teams to validate UCIe.mem implementations across development stages while reusing a common verification environment.
For early-stage DUTs that do not implement UCIe.mem, the VIP can bridge conventional memory interfaces (such as AXI to UCIe.mem transactions) enabling memory-access functionality to be verified before the DUT incorporates the protocol. For UCIe.mem-compatible DUTs that expose FDI, the VIP acts as the link partner, allowing the DUT’s own protocol implementation and generated traffic to be directly validated.
Beyond protocol-level testing, the solution enables realistic system-level verification by modeling the compute and memory sides of a chiplet-based system. A CXL.mem root host VIP can model the compute-side host while the DUT acts as the memory chiplet. Alternatively, a memory subsystem VIP, comprising a memory controller and memory model, can represent the memory side while the DUT acts as the compute chiplet. These configurations allow verification to go beyond basic request-response exchanges, exercising the DUT under realistic system conditions. Configurable latency, timing, and memory operating parameters help model different system behaviors and evaluate how the DUT handles them.
Complementing this integration flexibility, the VIP offers an exhaustive UCIe.mem compliance test suite, comprehensive protocol checking, and end-to-end data and transaction score-boarding. Together with transaction tracking for easier debug, these capabilities help ensure protocol compliance and identify design issues.
Teams can begin with early-stage memory-access validation, progress to direct UCIe.mem protocol testing, and extend verification to realistic system-level scenarios—all within a flexible verification environment.
Fig. 2: Questa One Avery UCIe.mem solution.
As chiplet architectures continue to develop, verification environments need to accommodate different implementation choices and levels of design maturity. With support for varied DUT interfaces and memory subsystem integration, Questa One Avery UCIe VIP makes UCIe.mem verification more adaptable across development stages and system configurations.
The result is a flexible approach to validating memory communication between chiplets, helping design teams begin verification early and extend it as their implementations mature.
For a detailed look at the UCIe.mem verification architecture, capabilities, and supported integration topologies, refer to the whitepaper, Verifying UCIe.mem: A Scalable Framework for Chiplet-Based Compute and Memory Systems.
Prashant Dixit develops verification solutions for UCIe-based designs and manages the Storage Verification IP team at Siemens EDA. Prior work included the design and verification of IP and SoCs in the networking and storage domains at Samsung. Dixit earned a Bachelor of Technology in Electronics and Communication from Uttar Pradesh Technical University in 2004 and a Master of Engineering degree in Microelectronics from BITS Pilani in 2006.

articles.title: Why Canada invested in Cohere
articles.text:
Today we have another edition of what is becoming a quarterly accountability check-in with Canada’s AI Minister, Evan Solomon.
“Simply put, Canada is not gonna wait for others to build the AI—maybe people we don’t know or don’t trust. We’re gonna build it now.”
The last time the minister was on the podcast, it was shortly following the release of Canada’s AI strategy. This time, we’re checking in right after Budget 2026, and we talk through some of the budget components the minister is most passionate about in their support of entrepreneurs. We also cover how some of those steps are designed to help prevent more AI companies like Taalas and Tenstorrent from being acquired or fleeing south—for his part, Minister Solomon said it’s his job to give those companies reasons not to leave.
But we also talk about the big news that dropped right before the budget: the federal government’s investment in AI champion Cohere. If you’ve seen the minister on The BetaKit Podcast before, or are familiar with BetaKit’s coverage generally, this news should not surprise you.
But public investments in private companies are relatively novel in Canada, and now that every Canadian has skin in the game, they’re coming armed with a lot of questions. As Build Canada’s Lucy Hargreaves put it, “Ottawa is becoming the owner, the funder, the customer and the regulator of the same companies.” How is that going to work?

I put the question to the minister directly alongside these two: why did the feds choose this approach, and how much can Canadians expect to know about their growing tech portfolio?
Do you want to know the answers? Let’s dig in.

articles.title: Vale, Chris Dickman: Australian science grieves the loss of a giant of ecology and conservation
articles.text:
Australia has lost one of its most distinguished ecologists and conservation champions, Emeritus Professor Chris Dickman.
Chris’s achievements and legacy are vast, much like his beloved Simpson Desert that he and his research team – known as “the ratcatchers” – have studied for well over 30 years. He and his team would camp out under the stars, carefully trapping and monitoring the desert’s animals and plants.
Without Chris, we wouldn’t know just how important even small but ferocious predators are in structuring ecological communities. One example is the brush-tailed mulgara, which preys on and regulates numbers of other predators, including the lesser hairy-footed dunnart.
Chris touched many in both his personal and professional roles. The authors of this article each knew Chris for many years.
Chris was honoured in a celebratory forum and festschrift, a collection of written tributes, in June that was attended by about 200 people and another 140 online. He died on November 17, 2026.
Science and service
Chris’s impressive career was marked by a dedication to the scientific field and service to the wider community.
He was an internationally renowned leader in wildlife conservation who studied everything from the small marsupial Antechinus to dunnarts, long-haired rats, mulgaras, quolls, sandy inland and spinifex hopping mice and the Tasmanian devil, to name but a few species.
His work shed light on the remarkable lives these animals lead as well as the challenges they face, including feral cats and foxes. Chris was among the first to draw attention to the contentious issue of dingo management by bringing experts together for a scientific forum.
With Lily van Eeden, Chris also led a team of researchers who first estimated three billion animals had been affected by Australia’s 2019-20 bushfire crisis, garnering global attention.
A living legacy
What follows are our personal reflections about Chris. We hope they help convey who he was, both as a person and a professional.
Glenda Wardle
Professor of Ecology and Evolution, University of Sydney
Chris was a true intellect, polymath and gentleman of science. He welcomed me to the University of Sydney in 1995 and led by example in all aspects of academic life. It would be hard to find a better role model.
Over several decades we shared a commitment to discovering the ecological secrets of the red sand country of the Simpson Desert. We faced adversity in the field through floods, fires and flies, but would always smile and keep working.
I will miss the hilarious stories we shared around campfires with the many wonderful students and volunteers that joined our research efforts. Together, we would dig and delight in the way the desert came to life, particularly after big flooding rains. I will miss Chris’s writing, which was both edifying and entertaining. I will remember him when listening to the Simon and Garfunkel song, The Sounds of Silence.
Aaron Greenville
Senior Lecturer of Spatial Agricultural and Environmental Sciences, University of Sydney
It was 1998 and I was a young second-year zoology student. We had just finished a lecture that sounded like an in-person BBC wildlife documentary. The lecturer was Chris Dickman.
Soon after, Chris encouraged us students to join the Royal Zoological Society of New South Wales and I promptly signed up. Little did I know that moment would change my life.
His enthusiastic, kind and generous nature has supported many a student, colleague and friend. His door was always open, regardless of how busy he was. Chris’ passion for the Simpson Desert was contagious and persuaded many people, including myself, to make a trip to the desert year after year. Chris led by example, creating a supportive and caring environment that has ultimately shaped how I lead my own research and teaching programs.
Chris was a true gentleman scientist, mentor and friend. I will miss him greatly.
Euan Ritchie
Professor of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, Deakin University
As a young PhD student, I attended the 2003 annual scientific meeting of the Australian Mammal Society in Sydney. At the time, Chris Dickman was president of the society. I was instantly struck by a few of his qualities, which in the years since have greatly shaped my own career.
Chris and his team were diligently uncovering the dynamics of the mighty Simpson Desert. Their work underscored the importance of long-term, systematic monitoring of wildlife to documenting the complex lives of mulgaras, dunnarts, native rodents and other sand-dwelling denizens. This is no mean feat, especially in an environment as unpredictable and ever-changing as the Simpson.
Chris was also a master communicator. He spoke with such clarity and with his distinctly dulcet tone, both qualities that gave his science such impact.
Most notably, Chris was incredibly generous with his time. He would ask me about my research and was always genuinely interested in what I had to say. He made young scientists like myself feel like we belonged, particularly in academia where imposter syndrome is rife. His mentorship and kind, thoughtful and supportive nature has helped me and many others pursue careers in ecology and conservation. For this, we are all forever grateful.
Thomas Newsome
Associate Professor of Global Ecology, University of Sydney
I was so lucky to have Chris as a lecturer during my undergraduate studies at The University of Sydney.
I fondly remember my first field trip with Chris, which involved sampling small mammals in the ancient forests of Barrington Tops in New South Wales, also known as Dungog. My peers and I slid around in the mud, attempting to reach the sampling sites, and learnt about the history of the area and its inhabitants. These early experiences shaped me as an ecologist.
I also had the privilege of working with Chris as a masters and then PhD student. I would approach him with so many ideas, some better than others. Chris always listened but, in his own style, would gently guide me in the right direction and towards fascinating topics. In our time together, we asked and answered questions about dingoes in the Tanami, foxes and cats in the Simpson, wolves in the United States and scavengers in Australia.
I owe Chris so much for his time and support. And I will forever treasure the memories of our adventures, alongside an appreciation for his knowledge and kindness.
Vale, Chris, our dear friend, mentor and colleague.
We farewell Chris here with an excerpt from his forthcoming festschrift, a collection of reflections written in his honour:
For science at its very best is not a solitary quest — It helps us see, to care and to learn what we all share
Know that in the shimmering moonlight on a distant dune crest or beside a dry creek’s trace,
The scientist with the stellar moustache was listening, and learning, with patience, skill and grace.

articles.title: Q&A: How Everstone Brings Where Winds Meet to Life with NVIDIA DLSS 5
articles.text:
Where Winds Meet moves between distant mountain landscapes, bustling streets, and quiet moments with its characters. For Everstone Studio, bringing more realistic lighting and materials to this wuxia world means keeping its aesthetics, recognizable characters, and carefully composed atmosphere intact.
The team’s ongoing work with NVIDIA DLSS and Streamline provided a foundation for integrating DLSS 5. Artists and engineers evaluated its lighting and material enhancements against the game’s art direction, balancing visual gains with additional performance overhead.
We sat down with art director Muzi Li and engine tech lead Cory Zhou to discuss the studio’s integration approach, preserving character identity, the changes that stood out in Jiangnan, and why developers should account for DLSS 5 early in their rendering budgets.
What made DLSS 5 a fit for Where Winds Meet?
The world of Where Winds Meet encompasses landscapes and towns, as well as countless details in how people interact with their surroundings. Players might be gazing into the distance from a mountain one moment, then walking down a bustling street the next. We want these scenes to be more than beautiful; we want players to feel their different weather conditions, times of day, and moods.
What attracts us to DLSS 5 is the room it gives us to explore lighting and materials further. It builds on the image already produced by the game engine, using neural rendering to enhance lighting and material details.
Our goal isn’t to pursue greater visual impact for its own sake. It’s to make these details work in harmony with the original art direction: distant landscapes should retain their poetic atmosphere, while nearby buildings and characters should have a believable sense of texture.
What were your art team’s first thoughts of DLSS 5?
Our first impression was that the interplay of light and shadow had gained greater depth. When sunlight falls on buildings, fabrics, and characters, the result feels more than just a sharper image. DLSS 5 identifies and tones down overly bright highlights while bringing out more detail in those areas. It also fills in ambient-light details and subtle highlights in the shadows, and recognizes the properties of materials.
How did you integrate DLSS 5 into your pipeline?
We have consistently integrated the latest DLSS technologies and kept our NVIDIA Streamline integration up to date. As a result, our rendering pipeline already had strong support for DLSS, providing a solid foundation for adopting DLSS 5. This ongoing investment made the upgrade a natural extension of our existing technology roadmap and helped ensure a smooth integration process.
How did artists and engineers use DLSS 5 controls to preserve art direction across characters, materials, and lighting?
In any given scene, we look at whether characters remain recognizable, whether materials such as fabric, leather, and metal are still visually distinct, and whether changes in lighting and shadow disrupt the scene’s original mood.
NVIDIA provides developers with options for model selection and controls over aspects such as structural and tonal strength. For us, artists and engineers need to communicate and iterate based on what we see on screen. One setting might make the environment more striking, but if faces or the overall color palette drift away from the intended look, we need to find a different balance.
We want to strike the right balance between visual gains, performance cost, and player preferences, while giving players choices wherever possible.
How did you evaluate DLSS 5 image quality and performance?
Our evaluation focuses on three key areas: visual quality, performance overhead, and alignment with the game’s artistic direction. Our testing to date indicates that enabling DLSS 5 introduces additional performance overhead, so we assess that cost alongside the visual improvements it delivers.
In developing Where Winds Meet, we have consistently explored different graphics technologies to support a wide range of player preferences. In our internal playtesting, DLSS 5 delivered a distinct visual experience, enhancing the overall presentation of our environments and their sense of immersion.
Based on these findings, we plan to give players the option to enable or disable DLSS 5. Our approach to visual tuning will be guided by the art team’s creative vision, including selecting the DLSS 5 model that best matches the intended aesthetic. We also aim to make relevant visual controls available to players wherever possible, allowing them to tailor the image to their preferences.
On balance, our evaluation has been positive, taking into account the visual improvements, performance overhead, and flexibility offered to players.
How does DLSS 5 affect characters?
What matters is whether characters feel more naturally part of the world while retaining their own distinctive presence.
For example, when a character walks from sunlight into the shade beneath an eave, changes in lighting and materials can help them feel more naturally grounded in the environment. The way different clothing materials respond to light can also give them a stronger presence. At the same time, we pay close attention to whether faces and costumes remain recognizable.
Which scene best demonstrates the improvements?
We find that Jiangnan is where DLSS 5 makes the biggest visual improvement. \When adjusting the settings, we use DLSS 5 to soften highlights in the original scene lighting that can appear too harsh, while adding a greater sense of depth between buildings. DLSS 5 can recognize ambient color from the sun and fill in details in darker areas, giving shadows more depth and material detail. Many buildings in Jiangnan feature wood and tiled roofs; DLSS 5 can fill in lifelike wood and roof-tile details.
As for the image that best showcases the effect, it will reveal itself during each player’s own journey: perhaps at a street corner just after the rain has cleared, or at an old ferry crossing bathed in the setting sun—a quiet moment that makes you stop and linger.
What advice would you give other developers adopting DLSS 5?
First, account for DLSS 5 performance requirements early in your rendering budget. For projects targeting high frame rates, reserve sufficient performance headroom and evaluate the balance between visual benefits and performance cost in representative gameplay scenarios.
Second, work closely with the NVIDIA team throughout integration and tuning to understand the technology’s capabilities and available controls. Align that work with your project’s artistic direction and performance targets.
